title: Too Short to Be Noticed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I want you to attend the Technology Steering Committee for me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they are all tall members of senior management. They won't even acknowledge my existence.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Phfft.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Hey, Andy, this seat is free. I'll just move my coffee.

situation: The Boss sends Asok to represent him at the Technology Steering Committee, explaining that the senior managers there are all tall and ignore him. At the meeting, an executive places his coffee cup on the seat where the short Asok is sitting, not noticing him, and offers the 'free' seat to another executive.
punchline: Asok is so short and so low in status that the executives literally overlook him and treat his chair as empty, just as the Boss said would happen to himself.
summary: A boss dodges a meeting of tall executives by sending his underling, who is promptly ignored and mistaken for an empty seat.

title: Wizard of Landfill Grants Wishes

transcript.speaker: Man in purple shirt
transcript.text: Oh great Wizard of Landfill, can you show me how to go home?... Also, my pals need experience and ambition.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: You're here because you ran out of good ideas... Here are a few gems about the idiots who manage my company.

transcript.speaker: Man in purple shirt
transcript.text: There's no place like my home office... There's no place like my home office...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He was creepy.

setting: Beside a dumpster at a landfill
situation: A coworker approaches a garbage man as though he were a mystical Wizard of Landfill, asking to be shown how to go home and for his friends to gain experience and ambition. The garbage man instead picks him up, apparently as payment for the ideas he handed over, and dangles him in the air while he chants a Wizard of Oz line. The coworkers who came along watch, and Wally calls him creepy.
punchline: The man's desperate wish-making at a dumpster turns into a Wizard of Oz parody, with him being carried off chanting 'no place like my home office' while his friends shrug that he was creepy.
summary: A worker treats a trash collector like a magical wizard to wish his way home and ends up lifted off the ground in a parody of a famous movie.

title: Meetings Until Difference Disappears

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I had a choice of doing something important that no one would ever realize...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...or doing something useless that would look like an accomplishment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I attended meetings until I could no longer appreciate the difference.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Keep up the good work.

setting: Outdoor walk and fence beside a grassy field
situation: Dilbert strolls outside with Dogbert and explains his dilemma: do important work that nobody would notice, or do useless work that looks like an accomplishment. He says he chose to attend meetings until he could no longer tell the two options apart. Dogbert encourages him to keep it up.
punchline: Attending endless meetings has so dulled Dilbert's judgment that he can no longer distinguish meaningful work from looking busy, and Dogbert approves.
summary: After pondering whether to do invisible important work or visible pointless work, Dilbert sits through so many meetings that the distinction blurs, earning Dogbert's praise.

title: Literal Carrot Dangled Over Contractor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll bring you on as a contract employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll keep you motivated by dangling the carrot of becoming a regular employee.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your first mistake was assuming that he understands metaphors.

setting: Boss's office, then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: The Boss sits at a desk offering a job candidate a contract position, explaining he will motivate him by dangling the carrot of permanent employment. In the last panel, the new hire stands with an actual carrot dangling from a stick attached to his head while Alice, holding a coffee mug, comments on it.
punchline: The Boss's carrot-and-stick metaphor gets taken literally because he assumed the new hire understands figurative language, so a real carrot ends up dangling in front of him.
summary: A manager's figure of speech about a motivational carrot gets implemented as an actual vegetable on a stick, to a coworker's dry commentary.

title: Congratulations on Your Worthless Acquisition

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO visits

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: We bought our competitor and we plan to integrate their product line into ours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did anyone tell you that their products are worthless pieces of garbage? Maybe that's why they sold the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean congratulations.

setting: Conference room during a CEO visit
situation: The CEO visits a meeting and announces that the company has bought its competitor and will merge their product line into its own. Dilbert bluntly points out that the acquired products are garbage and that this is probably why the competitor sold. Seeing the boss's angry glare, he awkwardly tacks on a belated congratulations.
punchline: Dilbert's honest warning about the acquisition's flaws gets clumsily patched with a fake 'congratulations' once he realizes he has angered the executives.
summary: An engineer undermines a CEO's acquisition announcement by suggesting the rival only sold because its products were junk, then half-heartedly retracts it.

title: Dilbert Ignores Colleague's Possible Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey Mort, are you coming to the... Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you dead? Hello! Hello!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to let that problem work itself out.

situation: Dilbert stops by coworker Mort's cubicle to invite him somewhere and finds him slumped motionless in his chair. He pokes Mort and calls out to see if he is dead, gets no response, and simply walks away, deciding to let the problem resolve itself.
punchline: Dilbert responds to a possibly dead coworker with the lazy workplace strategy of ignoring a problem and hoping it goes away, which is absurdly inappropriate for a medical emergency.
summary: Finding a coworker apparently lifeless at his desk, Dilbert shrugs and leaves, treating the situation like any other problem best left alone.

title: Never Tell The Boss Anything

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's one thing you should know. . .

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Whoa, whoa, Asok!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Never tell him anything when he's distracted.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: He won't remember what you say. Later he'll blame you for not telling him.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Also avoid telling him anything when he's angry, late, or busy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And don't tell him anything when he's tense or hungry.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That doesn't leave much.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I usually wait for a yawn.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yawn!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My project is behind schedule because the vendor lied!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The next one is all yours.

situation: Alice coaches new employee Asok on the many moments when it is unsafe to tell the Boss anything, since he forgets and later blames the messenger. When Asok points out that leaves almost no opportunity, she says she waits for the Boss to yawn. She then dives in and blurts out her bad news the instant he yawns, and hands the next one to Asok.
punchline: Alice's trick for delivering bad news is to ambush the Boss mid-yawn, when his mouth is busy and he can't react, and she cheerfully passes the dirty job to Asok.
summary: A veteran coworker teaches a newcomer the narrow window for giving the boss bad news and demonstrates by pouncing on him mid-yawn.

title: Cost-Benefit Study Proves Itself Stupid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to add a $3 component to our product to comply with federal law.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The product review committee will need a cost-benefit study before we decide.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: And you know it's accurate because I used math!

setting: Boss's office, then a meeting room with a projected slide
situation: The Boss announces that a $3 component must be added to the product to comply with federal law. His assistant Carol insists the product review committee needs a cost-benefit study first. She then presents the study to the committee, with a slide reading 'DUH' to the power of 100, and boasts that it's accurate because she used math.
punchline: Complying with a legal requirement leaves no real choice, so the cost-benefit study is a pointless exercise, and Carol's 'math' is just 'duh' raised to the 100th power.
summary: A routine legal requirement gets run through a committee study whose only conclusion is the obvious, dressed up with a joke equation.

title: Job Hopper Has Unrealistic Expectations

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear you're a job hopper.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in bunny ears
transcript.text: I like to think I have high standards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that all jobs require you to do things you'd rather not do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's why they have to pay you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perhaps your expectations are unrealistic.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in bunny ears
transcript.text: I quit! I'm going someplace where my coworkers will never waste my time!!!

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, talks to a coworker wearing bunny ears who has a reputation for changing jobs frequently. The coworker claims to have high standards, but Dilbert points out that every job involves unpleasant tasks, which is why employees get paid. The coworker is so offended that he quits on the spot to find a workplace with perfectly respectful coworkers.
punchline: Dilbert's gentle advice that the coworker is wasting his time drives him to quit, ironically proving he's a job hopper with unrealistic expectations while Dilbert is the one who wasted his time.
summary: A chronic job-switcher is told that disliking some tasks is normal and storms off to hunt for a utopian workplace.

title: Worthless Product, Worthless Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, the marketing department requested your help.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new product is worthless, much like yourself. They figured you'd have some insight.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: All it does is occupy space and smell bad.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, it's definitely a gift item.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that marketing wants his help with a new product, insulting him by calling the product worthless like Wally. In a meeting, a coworker describes the product as doing nothing but taking up space and smelling bad. Wally, unfazed, suggests it would make a perfect gift item.
punchline: A product that is useless and smelly is sarcastically declared ideal as a gift, implying people give each other junk they don't want.
summary: Marketing asks the office slacker to weigh in on a useless, smelly gadget, and he pegs it as the ideal present to give someone.

title: Arbitrary Deadline Versus Arbitrary Process

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it more important to follow our documented process or to meet the deadline?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only ask because our deadline is arbitrary and our documented process was pulled out of someone's lower torso.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's your artificial sense of urgency?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Teamwork killed it.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he should prioritize following the documented process or meeting the deadline. He points out that both the deadline and the process are essentially made up. The boss responds by asking where Dilbert's artificial sense of urgency has gone.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically blames 'teamwork' for killing his urgency, implying that collaborative effort drains the motivation that manufactured deadlines depend on.
summary: An employee questions whether to obey a made-up process or a made-up deadline, and his manager complains that his sense of urgency has vanished.

title: Unluckiest Insurance Agent Loses Customer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob, the unluckiest insurance agent.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: You're making a good decision.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Gaaak!

situation: Bob, an insurance agent, sits across the desk from a customer who is signing paperwork. Bob assures him he's making a good decision, and the customer suddenly cries out and keels over. In the last panel Bob stands holding his tie while the customer is slumped back, apparently dead.
punchline: Bob's bad luck is so extreme that his customer drops dead right as he is about to sign the insurance policy, costing Bob the sale.
summary: A salesman's run of terrible fortune continues when his client collapses mid-signing.

title: Dead Guy Dragged to Marketing

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We've got a dead guy in cubicle D-32.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any idea how much paperwork it causes when someone dies in one of my cubicles?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Ten more feet to the Marketing Department.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's desk
situation: An employee reports a dead body in cubicle D-32. The Boss is concerned only about the paperwork a death in his cubicles creates. In the last panel the employee is shown dragging the body and thinking that the Marketing Department is just ten more feet away.
punchline: To dodge the paperwork, the employee plans to dump the corpse in the Marketing Department so the death becomes someone else's problem.
summary: Faced with a manager who dreads paperwork more than a fatality, a worker quietly relocates the corpse to another department.

title: Consultant Teases Dilbert's Steaming Rage

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: You know what's funny? I'm getting paid to consult, but you're the smartest and most experienced person in the room.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: That must burn you like the heat of a thousand suns.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: That's my favorite sound!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tweeeeet

situation: A consultant sits across from Dilbert and points out that he is being paid for advice while Dilbert is actually the smartest and most experienced person present. He taunts Dilbert about how much that must burn. Dilbert's necktie whistles like a steam kettle as he fumes, and the consultant happily points at him.
punchline: The consultant is gleefully tormenting Dilbert over the unfairness of his pay, and Dilbert's anger literally makes his tie whistle, which the consultant enjoys.
summary: A smug paid advisor rubs in that the better-qualified engineer gets nothing for his expertise, then delights when the man's tie shrieks with steam.

file: 2006/2006-04-09_important sales call_secret weapon_ed from sales_prices identical_engineering staff_competitor_employs loser_act surprised.gif
title: Salesman's Secret Weapon Is Competitor's Employee

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: I need you to accompany me on an important sales call.

transcript.speaker: Balding Engineer
transcript.text: Me?

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: You're my secret weapon!

transcript.speaker: Balding Engineer
transcript.text: Well, okay.

transcript.speaker: Balding Engineer
transcript.text: What's your name?

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: I'm Ed, from Sales.

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: Only two companies make this type of product. The prices are identical.

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: The difference is that our engineering staff brings genius and innovation to everything it touches.

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: Whereas my competitor employs this loser.

transcript.speaker: Balding Engineer
transcript.text: Really? I wondered why you didn't look familiar.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sold!

transcript.speaker: Ed from Sales
transcript.text: You helped make a sale?

transcript.speaker: Balding Engineer
transcript.text: Why does everyone act all surprised?

setting: A customer's conference room during a sales call, then back at the office
situation: Ed from Sales brings an engineer along on a sales call, calling him his secret weapon without even knowing his name. In the meeting Ed pitches his company's engineers as geniuses and points at the engineer as the loser his competitor employs. The engineer, who actually works for the competitor, plays along and the customer buys from Ed.
punchline: The salesman's 'secret weapon' is an engineer from the competing company, and his willingness to be insulted is what closes the deal, leaving his colleagues surprised that he helped make a sale.
summary: A salesman recruits a stranger from the rival firm to be mocked in front of a client, and the stunt wins the contract.

title: Dilbert Lies to Manipulate Management

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In order to make an informed decision, you would need to know as much as I know.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's impossible, so instead, by mutual, implied agreement, I will feed you some lies that point you to the right decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we don't upgrade our servers, a herd of trolls will attack headquarters.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: No trolls!

setting: Conference room during a presentation to management
situation: Dilbert presents to The Boss and another manager, pointing at a diagram of information flowing into a head. He explains that the managers cannot know enough to decide properly, so he will feed them lies to steer them to the right decision. He then claims a herd of trolls will attack headquarters unless the servers are upgraded, and a manager reacts in alarm.
punchline: Dilbert admits that management can't make informed decisions, so he openly manipulates them with absurd lies, and the gullible manager immediately falls for the troll threat.
summary: An engineer tells his bosses he'll deceive them for their own good, then proves their gullibility by scaring them into approving a server upgrade with an imaginary monster attack.

title: Photographer Panda Mating Situation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The ex-photographer I hired isn't doing well in captivity.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is he dying?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not yet. It's more of a panda situation.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Would you like to mate?

transcript.speaker: Photographer
transcript.text: I couldn't be less interested.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk area and the photographer's cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Catbert that the laid-off photographer he hired is struggling to cope with being kept at the company. Catbert asks if he is dying, and the Boss says it's more of a panda situation. In the last panel a woman is brought to ask the slumped photographer if he'd like to mate, and he flatly refuses.
punchline: The Boss treats the hired photographer like a captive zoo panda, and the joke lands when a coworker is sent to ask him to mate, a reference to pandas' notorious reluctance to breed in captivity.
summary: A manager's new hire sulks like a zoo animal, so a colleague is sent to encourage breeding, with predictably dismal results.

title: Mordac Demands Imaginary Email Approval

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: You have exceeded your e-mail storage limit!

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: To increase your limit, you must get approval from your VP, the CIO, and one nonexistent person to be named later.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I'm thinking either a yeti or a bikini model who is also an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Erk!

situation: Mordac, the head of information services, storms up to an employee's desk and announces he has exceeded his e-mail storage limit. To get more space, the employee must obtain approvals from his VP, the CIO, and an imaginary person yet to be named. Mordac muses that this fictional approver might be a yeti or a bikini model who is also an engineer, while the employee squeaks in dismay.
punchline: The approval process for more e-mail storage is so absurdly bureaucratic that it requires sign-off from a made-up person, making the request effectively impossible.
summary: An IT enforcer makes getting extra mailbox space impossible by demanding sign-off from executives plus a fictional person he is still inventing.

title: Outsourcing Asok Back to India

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm outsourcing your job to India.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I moved here from India to take this job! Now I'll have to go back!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell Sandeep I need some photocopies.

situation: The Boss announces he is outsourcing Asok's job to India. Asok protests that he emigrated from India specifically to take this job and now will have to return. The Boss ignores the complaint and asks Asok to pass a photocopying request to Sandeep, presumably Asok's replacement in India.
punchline: The Boss is so indifferent to the human cost of outsourcing that he immediately asks Asok to relay a request to his replacement overseas, as if nothing meaningful has changed.
summary: A manager sends a worker's job back to the country the worker just left, then casually asks him to deliver a chore to the replacement.

title: Coffee-Powered Levitation Hits Wrong Target

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks to coffee, I can levitate objects with my mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bring... the mouse... bring the... mouse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not perfect yet.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: No problem. I appreciate the atten-tion.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a giant coffee mug strapped to his torso, tells Dogbert that coffee has given him the power to levitate objects with his mind. He concentrates hard and commands the computer mouse to come to him. Instead, Ratbert, the small orange pet, is flung through the air upside down.
punchline: Dilbert's caffeine-fueled telekinesis grabs the wrong thing, tossing Ratbert instead of the computer mouse, a pun on 'mouse' versus a rat-like creature, while Ratbert politely shrugs it off.
summary: A caffeine-soaked engineer tries to summon a computer mouse with his mind and accidentally launches a small pet through the air instead.

title: Dogbert's Space Shield Justified Instantly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My space defense shield detects an incoming threat. I am launching intercept rockets.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently the boys at Google used a death ray to blast the International Space Station out of orbit and toward our house.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you have a space defense shield?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that seem like a stupid question now?

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk with computer monitors
situation: Dogbert sits at his computer and announces that his space defense shield has detected an incoming threat and he is launching intercept rockets. He explains that Google used a death ray to knock the International Space Station toward their house. Dilbert, holding a mug, asks why Dogbert even has a space defense shield.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's reasonable question as stupid because the absurd threat he prepared for has actually materialized.
summary: A dog's seemingly paranoid orbital defense system turns out to be handy when a tech giant's weapon sends a space station hurtling toward home.

title: Time Traveler Wally Wants Coffee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And then we'll send the draft for review . . .

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bzzzzt!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Greetings. I am Wally from the year 2040.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In the future, time travel will be possible but highly unethical.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But it's only unethical if you make the mistake of changing anything from the past.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I was out of coffee so I came here to get a fresh cup.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ah, here we go.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have to run. Make sure nothing changes because of my visit or it will kill everyone in the future.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me be the first to say that this feels awkward.

situation: During a meeting, a flash of light reveals Wally arriving from the year 2040 in a green time-travel suit. He explains that time travel is unethical only if the past is changed, then admits he came back just to get a fresh cup of coffee. He warns everyone that nothing must change because of his visit or everyone in the future will die, leaving the group stunned.
punchline: Wally uses time travel for the most trivial reason, a coffee refill, and then burdens everyone with a catastrophic warning, which makes the meeting awkward.
summary: A future version of Wally pops into a meeting to steal coffee and threatens global doom if anyone alters the timeline because of it.

title: Safety Mascot Dog Costume Assignment

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's that thing doing here?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is my daughter, Traylor.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I brought her to the office so she can learn about working in a corporate environment.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay. Whatever. I have a new project for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some idiot cut his finger. Now we have to do a safety awareness campaign.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Put on this dog costume. You're the mascot for our "Spot" the safety hazard campaign.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whenever anyone walks by, you say, "Woof woof, don't use scissors."

transcript.speaker: Traylor
transcript.text: Can I get a tattoo?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure.

situation: Alice brings her young daughter Traylor to work to learn about corporate life. The Boss dismisses the child as a 'thing' and then orders Alice to wear a dog costume as the mascot for a safety awareness campaign, barking scissor warnings at passersby. Seeing this, Traylor asks if she can get a tattoo, and a humiliated Alice agrees.
punchline: After watching her mother degraded in a dog costume, the daughter's request for a tattoo is granted without argument, because Alice has completely lost any parental authority or dignity.
summary: A mother's demoralizing day at the office, wearing a silly costume at her boss's order, leaves her too humbled to refuse her child's request for body art.
enterprise_concepts: take your child to work day

title: Squirrels Hold Payroll Database Hostage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found a family of squirrels living inside our legacy system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They control our payroll database. They're making demands.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Leave the acorns and no one will get their deductions increased.

setting: Boss's office, then beside an old mainframe computer
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that squirrels have moved into the company's legacy system and now control the payroll database. In the final panel he carries a bowl of acorns to the mainframe, where a squirrel peers out from a window in the machine, and he delivers the squirrels' ransom demand.
punchline: The ancient legacy system is so poorly understood and fragile that squirrels have effectively taken it over, and the company has to bargain with them like hostage-takers to keep payroll deductions intact.
summary: A pack of squirrels nesting in an outdated mainframe ends up holding the company's payroll hostage until they receive a tribute of acorns.

title: Outsourced Back to India

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, my job has been outsourced to India.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's interesting because you came here from India.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you already think of that?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yes!

situation: Asok tells Wally, who is holding a coffee mug, that his job has been outsourced to India. Wally points out the irony that Asok originally came to the company from India, then asks if he has already thought of that. Asok, already upset, shouts that he has.
punchline: Wally points out the obvious irony of Asok's situation as if it were a helpful insight, and Asok, who has clearly been stewing on it, snaps back with an exasperated yell.
summary: A man laid off through outsourcing has the bitter irony of his situation pointed out by a coworker who treats it as a fresh observation.

title: Billionaire Buys Company To Stop Whining

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: You're always complaining about the management of your company so I decided to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: I used my billions to buy your company!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're going to fix management?

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: No, I just wanted to stop all the whining.

transcript.speaker: Ghost
transcript.text: You're fired.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: A small white ghost sits next to Dilbert on his couch and says it has used its billions to buy his company because he always complains about management. Dilbert hopefully asks if the ghost will fix management. The ghost reveals it only wanted to end the complaining, and fires him.
punchline: The wealthy owner's idea of dealing with employee complaints is not to improve management but to eliminate the person complaining by firing him.
summary: A rich ghost buys the company of his complaining friend, not to improve things but to dismiss him and end the grumbling.

title: Dogberto's Arson Lobby Art

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Famous artist Dogberto will tell us his plans for our lobby.

transcript.speaker: Dogberto
transcript.text: I plan to buy a drop cloth at Home Depot and drape it over the security desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Won't that be hard on the guard?

transcript.speaker: Dogberto
transcript.text: Not until I douse it with gas and light it.

situation: The Boss introduces a famous artist, Dogberto, who is a dog, to present his plans for decorating the company lobby. Dogberto describes draping a cheap drop cloth over the security desk, and when Dilbert worries about the guard, Dogberto reveals he intends to set it on fire.
punchline: The pretentious avant-garde artist's 'installation' is a cheap drop cloth over the security desk that he plans to burn, with the guard apparently in harm's way, mocking modern art's shock value and the executives who pay for it.
summary: A celebrity artist pitches a lobby installation that turns out to involve gasoline, fire and an endangered security guard.

file: 2006/2006-03-04_wise king salmon_fish are stupid_project_right or wrong.gif
title: Wise King Salmon Splits the Difference

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could do the project right for $100,000 or do it wrong for $25,000.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I believe that the wise King Salmon would say to split the difference and do it for $50,000.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fish are stupid.

situation: In a meeting, Dilbert tells the Boss the project can be done properly for $100,000 or badly for $25,000. The Boss decides to split the difference at $50,000, citing the wisdom of a fictional King Salmon. Dilbert later comes home in his coat, carrying a bag, and tells Dogbert that fish are stupid.
punchline: The Boss's compromise gets the worst of both options, a mediocre budget justified by an absurd fish authority, so Dilbert dismisses the whole idea by calling fish stupid.
summary: A manager picks a middle-of-the-road budget by invoking a royal fish's wisdom, leaving his engineer fuming about the intelligence of marine life.

title: Desperate Venture Capitalist Throws Money

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay, the world's most desperate venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I started in my garage...

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Take my money!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't you want to hear the rest?

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: I don't see how it could get any better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a product

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: I need a forklift and massage oil now!!!

setting: Office meeting table where Dilbert pitches to an investor
situation: Dilbert begins pitching his startup to Vijay, a venture capitalist, who is so desperate to invest that he immediately offers a bag of money before hearing anything. When Dilbert mentions he actually has a product, Vijay becomes so excited he demands a forklift and massage oil, presumably to carry and roll around in his cash.
punchline: The venture capitalist is so eager to invest that even the smallest detail, having a product, sends him into an absurd frenzy of excitement, mocking the irrational exuberance of venture funding.
summary: An investor so eager to hand over cash that a mere mention of a finished product sends him into ecstatic, absurd demands.

title: Kidney Stone Wins Kentucky Derby

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My first baby weighed 11 pounds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I once passed a kidney stone that was the size of a small horse.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I find that hard to believe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That kidney stone went on to win the Kentucky Derby!

situation: Carol, seated at her desk, mentions that her first baby weighed 11 pounds. Dilbert tops her story by claiming he once passed a kidney stone the size of a small horse. When Carol expresses doubt, he doubles down with an even more absurd embellishment.
punchline: Dilbert's exaggeration is so outlandish that when challenged, he escalates it further by claiming the horse-sized kidney stone won the Kentucky Derby, mocking one-upmanship in conversation.
summary: A coworker tries to outdo a story about childbirth with an impossibly exaggerated tale about a giant kidney stone that became a champion racehorse.

title: Idiot-Proof Software Means You're an Idiot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, we do claim that our software is idiot-proof.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you bought it, that's proof you're an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: High five!

situation: Dogbert works the phones at his own tech support desk while Dilbert stands in front of it holding a drink. Dogbert confirms that the software is advertised as idiot-proof, then argues that anyone who purchased it must be an idiot. He then asks for a high five.
punchline: Dogbert twists the 'idiot-proof' marketing claim into an insult, treating the customer's purchase as evidence of their idiocy, and cheerfully celebrates it.
summary: A tech support dog redefines a product's foolproof guarantee as an indictment of everyone who was foolish enough to buy it.

title: Unrealistic Sales Assumptions Land Kicks Hillbilly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Land of Unrealistic Business Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to find some assumptions about future sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dang! There's only one way across and it's blocked by an inebriated hillbilly.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In the Land of Unrealistic Assumptions, this guy is your only competitor.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Boot

setting: A fantasy landscape called the Land of Unrealistic Business Assumptions, with a grassy cliff and a log bridge
situation: Dilbert walks through a whimsical land looking for assumptions about future sales, accompanied by a small egg-like creature. He finds a drunken hillbilly asleep on a log blocking the only path across a chasm, with a sign reading 'Huge Sales' beyond it. Dogbert-style narration notes this guy is the only competitor, and the creature boots the hillbilly off the log into the chasm.
punchline: In an unrealistic business plan, the only competitor is a passed-out drunk who is easily eliminated, making huge sales projections seem trivially achievable.
summary: A trek through an imaginary land of rosy forecasts ends with a sleeping drunk, the sole rival, being kicked off a bridge to clear the way to enormous sales.

title: Free Training on Satan's Island

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: We'll send your engineers to our free training course.

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: The training is held on our own island retreat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going where?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fecalruba.

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: A devil-like vendor, labeled as Satan's vendor, offers to send the company's engineers to a free training course at his own island retreat. The Boss accepts, then tells Dilbert at his desk that he is being sent to an island with an unappealing name.
punchline: The 'free' vendor training is a trap: the island destination has a name that sounds like feces, implying the vendor is sending the engineers to something awful and the trip comes at the engineers' expense.
summary: A sinister vendor lures a manager into sending engineers to a free island training session, and the destination turns out to have a revolting name.

title: Tech Support Code Hidden in Landfill

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Before I can help you, I need your tech support product identification code.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can find it by going to your local landfill and digging until you see your product's original packaging.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But don't disturb the seagulls or they'll peck off your face.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center and the customer's desk, on the phone
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support headset, demands a product identification code before he will help a caller. He then instructs the customer to dig through a local landfill to find the original packaging. The customer listens on the phone with a blank, resigned expression while being warned about seagulls.
punchline: Tech support makes the customer do an absurdly unpleasant and dangerous task just to get a code, showing how little the support desk cares about helping.
summary: A tech support dog sends a caller to rummage through a garbage dump for a required code, with a warning about face-pecking birds.

title: Monthly Meeting of Insane Chicks

transcript.speaker: Woman at podium
transcript.text: Welcome to the monthly meeting of insane chicks.

transcript.speaker: Woman at podium
transcript.text: Our speaker today is Betty, and her topic is "All the people who are intentionally hurting us."

transcript.speaker: Woman at podium
transcript.text: The breakout session is titled "How to turn your imaginary problems into real ones."

setting: A conference room or meeting hall with a podium and seated audience
situation: A woman at a podium opens the monthly meeting of a group that she cheerfully calls 'insane chicks.' She introduces the speaker Betty, whose talk is about people who are deliberately hurting them, then announces a breakout session on turning imaginary problems into real ones. The seated audience of women listens with wide-eyed, anxious expressions.
punchline: The group's talks and workshops feed their paranoia and self-sabotage, so the meeting is literally designed to make their delusions come true.
summary: A support-group-style gathering for paranoid women schedules a lecture on imagined persecutors and a workshop on making imaginary troubles real.

title: Shy Bladder Drug Test Pressure

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've been randomly selected for a drug test.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a shy bladder. I can't produce under pressure!!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do it now or be fired.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for understanding.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do it! Do it! Do it! Do it!

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, hands Dilbert a cup and announces he has been randomly selected for a drug test. Dilbert explains that he has a shy bladder and can't perform under pressure, so Catbert threatens to fire him unless he complies immediately. Catbert then screams at him to hurry up, adding the very pressure Dilbert said he couldn't handle.
punchline: Catbert responds to Dilbert's stage-fright problem by piling on more pressure, shouting 'Do it!' which defeats the purpose and shows HR's cruelty disguised as procedure.
summary: An HR cat demands an immediate urine sample from a man who says pressure makes him unable to go, then yells at him to hurry.

title: Customers Fantasize About Beating You

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally in Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Researcher
transcript.text: According to my market research, ninety percent of your customers . . .

transcript.speaker: Marketing Researcher
transcript.text: . . . "Fantasize about beating you to death with your stupid product."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What about the other ten percent?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Researcher
transcript.text: They asked for your company address but didn't say why.

setting: Conference room in the marketing department
situation: Wally, working in marketing, sits at a table with a coffee mug while a market researcher reads out his survey findings. The researcher reports that most customers fantasize about violently attacking Wally with the company's product. When Wally asks about the remaining customers, the researcher reveals they requested the company's address without giving a reason.
punchline: The remaining ten percent are even worse than the violent fantasizers, since they apparently intend to act on their anger by showing up at the company.
summary: A researcher delivers market research showing customers despise a product so intensely that the few who are not merely fantasizing about violence seem to be planning a visit.

title: Coffee Addiction Doctor Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I tell if I'm drinking too much coffee?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: What would you do if I told you to quit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd jab you with a used needle.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: In that case, you're fine.

situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table holding an enormous coffee mug and asks the doctor how to tell whether he drinks too much coffee. The doctor asks how he would react to being told to quit, and Dilbert threatens to jab him with a used needle. The doctor calmly concludes that Dilbert is fine.
punchline: The doctor deems Dilbert's violent, withdrawal-driven threat to be a healthy reaction, which is the opposite of a sane diagnosis, since it clearly shows he is addicted to coffee.
summary: A patient hugging a giant coffee mug learns his caffeine habit is fine because he'd menace his doctor over giving it up.

title: Humiliated Company, No Friends to Notice

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Today the company restated its earnings from "a few frillion" to a loss of 1.3 billion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This would be humiliating if I had any friends.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your strategy of being unattractive is paying off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm ugly like a fox.

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit in armchairs watching a news report that his company has restated its earnings from a huge profit to a 1.3 billion loss. Dilbert remarks that the embarrassment would matter if he had friends, and Dogbert says his unattractiveness strategy is working. Dilbert replies that he is 'ugly like a fox'.
punchline: Dilbert's lack of friends and social appeal shields him from the embarrassment of his employer's accounting fiasco, and he spins his ugliness as cunning with a twisted 'crazy like a fox' line.
summary: A disastrous earnings correction on the evening news barely stings a lonely engineer whose isolation doubles as protection.

title: Salesman Honestly Dismisses Newer Version

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I buy this, how can I be sure you won't come out with a newer version next week?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I give you my word as a job-hopping commission junky with a gambling problem.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: And even if we did have a newer version, it sure wouldn't fix any of the problems that this one has.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle or office, across a desk
situation: Dilbert is considering buying a gadget from a salesman and asks for assurance that a newer version won't appear right after he buys. The salesman cheerfully describes himself as an untrustworthy, commission-driven gambler and then admits that any new version would not fix the flaws of the current product.
punchline: The salesman's brutally honest pitch, offering his worthless word and admitting the product is flawed and the upgrades won't help, undermines the very sale he is trying to make.
summary: A candid salesman reassures a wary buyer by confessing he is a commission-chasing gambler and that the product's flaws persist in every version.

title: The VP of HR Is a Ficus

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now that I know your résumé was embellished, you need to talk to the VP of Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you going to fire me?

transcript.speaker: VP of Human Resources
transcript.text: Nah. I'll let you in on a little secret.

transcript.speaker: VP of Human Resources
transcript.text: I'm the ficus tree that used to be in the lobby.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the Boss that his résumé was embellished and sends him to see the VP of Human Resources. The Boss nervously asks if he is going to be fired, and the VP leans back in his chair and promises to share a secret. In the last panel the VP reveals he is actually the ficus tree that used to be in the lobby, shown with a plant for a head.
punchline: The VP of HR admits he is just a lobby plant who got promoted, implying he is as unqualified as the Boss, whose résumé lies are therefore hardly worth punishing.
summary: A manager called in over a padded résumé learns that the executive judging him got his own job through an equally absurd route.

title: Appreciation Day Becomes Unpaid Weekend Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to have an employee appreciation day on the 8th!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the best day for a potluck lunch. You'll have all day Saturday to make a dish to share!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need a volunteer to organize everything. Let's see... Which one of you is the woman?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bring jackets. It's supposed to be about 45 degrees in the park that day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won't be able to attend because I do personal stuff on weekends.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take pictures!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hope no one else brought a pine cone appetizer.

setting: Office conference room, then a cold park
situation: The Boss announces an employee appreciation day, which turns out to be a Sunday potluck in a chilly park that employees must prepare for on their own time. He assigns the organizing to Alice simply because she is the woman, and Dilbert declines to attend. The Boss leaves, asking for photos, and in the final panel Alice and two coworkers shiver in the park.
punchline: The so-called appreciation day is really an unpaid weekend obligation where employees do all the work and freeze, while the Boss doesn't even show up and only wants photos.
summary: A manager's celebration of his staff turns out to be a weekend chore for the staff themselves, organized by the nearest woman and skipped by the manager.

title: Wally Dumped on Marketing Director

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The Director of Marketing needs an engineering resource.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving you to him because I hate his stupid guts.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketing
transcript.text: What did I do to deserve this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. I had to drown a burrito.

setting: Office cubicle and the Marketing Director's office
situation: The Boss tells Wally, who sits at his desk, that the Director of Marketing needs an engineering resource. He cheerfully admits he is assigning Wally out of spite toward that director. Wally then shows up late at the director's office holding a coffee mug and offers a bizarre excuse, leaving the director aghast.
punchline: The Boss treats Wally, a lazy and useless employee, as a weapon to punish someone he dislikes, and Wally's absurd excuse proves the director's suffering is well deserved.
summary: A manager offloads his laziest engineer onto a rival as an act of revenge, and the recipient's despair is immediate.

title: Boss's Management Listening Catheter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think what we should do is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whoa!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me a minute to install my management listening catheter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me about your excellent suggestion.

situation: Dilbert starts to offer a suggestion to his boss, who abruptly stops him. The boss then takes a minute to set up a funnel-and-tube device, a 'management listening catheter', with the tube draining into a bucket. Once it is in place, he invites Dilbert to continue, ready to 'listen'.
punchline: The boss's idea of listening is a catheter-like device that lets employees' suggestions flow in one ear and out into a bucket, showing that management treats employee input as waste.
summary: A manager rigs up a ridiculous drainage contraption so he can appear to listen to an employee's idea while it simply passes through him.

title: Dilbert Moves Dogbert for Meaning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I feel as if my life is nothing but moving things from one place to another.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've decided to seek a deeper connection with others to cure my emptiness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'm doing it wrong.

setting: Outdoor grassy field with a dirt path and rocks
situation: Dilbert walks outside with Dogbert and complains that his life feels like merely moving things from place to another. He then announces he will seek a deeper connection with others, and literally picks up Dogbert and places him on a rock. Dogbert just babbles blah blah blah, and Dilbert wonders if he is doing it wrong.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at a deeper connection is just physically moving Dogbert from one place to another, which is exactly the empty activity he was complaining about.
summary: A lonely man tries to cure his sense of emptiness by hauling his dog onto a boulder and discovers he is simply repeating the same hollow routine.

title: Hotness As A Super Power

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Did you hire Ellen just because she's hot?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, hotness is an important skill. It's like a super power.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: From now on, how much are you charging us for printer cartridges?

transcript.speaker: Office Supply Salesman
transcript.text: Fuh fuh free!

setting: The Boss's office, then the office hallway
situation: Carol confronts the Boss, asking whether he hired Ellen only because she is attractive. The Boss claims hotness is a legitimate skill, like a super power. In the last panel Carol, who is clearly attractive, uses the same logic to get a flustered salesman to give the company printer cartridges for free.
punchline: Carol takes the Boss's reasoning at face value and demonstrates that attractiveness really can be a workplace advantage by getting free printer cartridges from a dazzled salesman.
summary: After the boss defends hiring someone for her looks, a coworker proves his point by charming a vendor into handing over supplies at no cost.

title: Delegating a Financial Sinkhole

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're in charge of installing the system that Lyin' John sold to our biggest customer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lyin' John neglected to include the network and server in his sale. This is a financial sinkhole.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You take the joy out of delegating.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and assigns him to install a system that salesman Lyin' John sold to their biggest customer. He then reveals that John left the network and server out of the sale, making the project a money pit. Dilbert says nothing, and the Boss complains that Dilbert is spoiling his enjoyment of delegating.
punchline: The Boss dumps a doomed, underpriced project on Dilbert and then blames Dilbert's reaction for ruining his fun, showing he only delegates to offload problems.
summary: A manager pushes a salesman's botched deal onto an engineer and then complains that the engineer is making the handoff less enjoyable.

title: Dilbert Haggles Over a Penny

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: Here's a game card that gives you a chance to win groceries.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks. Just take a penny off of my bill and we'll call it even.

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: Um. . . I can't do that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why not? Isn't that game card worth a penny?

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: We don't have a procedure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's that my problem?

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: Look, maybe you could eat something that's worth a penny and I'll look the other way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a grape? I like grapes.

transcript.speaker: Grocery Clerk
transcript.text: It would have to be one that's been on the floor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It tasted like victory.

situation: At the checkout, a clerk offers Dilbert a game card for a chance to win groceries. Dilbert instead asks for a one-cent discount, which the clerk says he cannot give because there is no procedure. They settle on Dilbert eating a penny's worth of produce, specifically a grape that has been on the floor.
punchline: Dilbert wins a petty, rigid-policy standoff but pays for it by eating a dirty grape off the floor, calling it victory with deadpan pride.
summary: A shopper bargains with a checkout clerk over a worthless promotional card and ends up grudgingly claiming a floor-grape as his prize.

title: Non-Compete Agreement Demands Dagger Suicide

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you worked here, you signed a non-compete agreement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It clearly states that you are not allowed to earn money, sleep indoors, procreate or seek medical care.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Section 5B describes what you must now do with this ceremonial dagger.

setting: Conference room with a long table, viewed through the door in the final panel
situation: Dilbert sits across a conference table from The Boss and a pointy-haired colleague, who cite a non-compete agreement Dilbert signed when he worked there. The boss reads out increasingly absurd restrictions, such as being forbidden to earn money, sleep indoors, or seek medical care. The strip ends with the clause calling for a ceremonial dagger, implying Dilbert is expected to kill himself.
punchline: The non-compete agreement is so extreme that it effectively requires the former employee to commit ritual suicide, satirizing how legal contracts can strip ex-employees of any means of survival.
summary: A former employee is told the paperwork he signed bars him from nearly every basic necessity and then prescribes a grim use for a ceremonial blade.

title: Meaningless Folksy Sayings From Texas

transcript.speaker: Cowboy-hatted man
transcript.text: I come from a place where we have many colorful folk sayings!

transcript.speaker: Cowboy-hatted man
transcript.text: I'm happier than a wooden spoon at a spelling bee.

transcript.speaker: Cowboy-hatted man
transcript.text: Most of 'em don't mean nothin'.

situation: A man in a cowboy hat approaches Dilbert and boasts about the colorful folk sayings from his home region. He offers an example about a wooden spoon at a spelling bee, which makes no sense. He then admits that most of these sayings are meaningless.
punchline: The folksy saying is nonsensical, and the speaker cheerfully admits that most such sayings mean nothing, poking fun at folksy wisdom that sounds clever but says nothing.
summary: A cowboy-hatted newcomer proudly shares a quirky homespun saying, then casually concedes that such phrases are mostly gibberish.

title: CEO Asked to Return Unearned Bonus

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO is here to answer any of your questions about our restatement of earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you return your $25,000,000 bonus from last year, now that you acknowledge it was unearned?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: And what's your name?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dilbert

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss introduces the CEO to take questions about the company's restatement of earnings. Dilbert boldly asks whether the CEO will give back his $25 million bonus now that it has been admitted it was unearned. The CEO ignores the question and asks for Dilbert's name, while Dilbert sips from a mug.
punchline: The CEO deflects the question about returning the bonus by asking for Dilbert's name, an implied threat of retaliation against the employee who asked.
summary: A worker's pointed question about an unearned executive windfall gets met not with an answer but with a menacing request for his identity.

title: Wally Won't Work Either

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Your engineers think my project plan won't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll assign Wally to your project. He's a perfect fit.

transcript.speaker: Project Manager
transcript.text: Because he's a problem solver?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because he won't work either.

situation: A woman with a project plan tells the Boss that the engineers believe her plan is unworkable. The Boss offers to assign Wally to her project, calling him a perfect fit. She assumes it's because Wally is good at solving problems, but the Boss reveals the real reason.
punchline: The Boss plays on the double meaning of 'won't work': the plan won't succeed, and Wally famously refuses to do any work, so he's a 'perfect fit' for a doomed project.
summary: A manager facing a doubtful project plan is handed the office's most notorious slacker as a staff member, because the boss thinks both are equally hopeless.

title: Forgetting Your Job Over the Weekend

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you ever come to work on Monday and realize that you forgot how to do your job?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Only a total moron would forget over the weekend how to do his job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: O-o-okay. I'm starting to remember who you two are.

situation: Wally asks his colleagues at a meeting table whether they've ever arrived on Monday and forgotten how to do their jobs. Alice bluntly replies that only a total moron would forget over the weekend how to do his job. Wally, clearly the one who has forgotten, says he is only now starting to remember who Alice and Dilbert are.
punchline: Wally's confession was about himself, and his Monday memory loss is so complete that he can't even remember his coworkers, proving Alice's insult accurate.
summary: A coworker who has blanked on his entire job after the weekend gets called a moron and then admits he doesn't even recognise the people beside him.

title: Success Before Telling Alice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How was your conference call?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Very successful. Bill said he'd find a new supplier for the casing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or it might have been Ron, Ted, or Bob. They all sound the same on the phone.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hope it wasn't Bill. He never follows through.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ron is too overworked, Ted is a liar and Bob's a moron.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'd say the call was a waste of time. It might even be a huge step backward.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Success is the happy feeling you get between the time you do something and the time you tell a woman what you did.

situation: Alice asks Dilbert how his conference call went, and he cheerfully calls it a success because someone promised to find a new casing supplier. He can't even say who made the promise, and Alice picks apart each candidate and declares the call a waste of time or worse. Dilbert walks away deflated and tells Dogbert his definition of success.
punchline: Dilbert's sense of accomplishment lasts only until he tells Alice, who immediately points out why his work was pointless or harmful.
summary: A man proud of a vague phone meeting has his triumph demolished the moment he describes it to a skeptical colleague.
keywords: sounds the same on the phone

title: Tech Support Password Before Lunch

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, I need some tech support.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: What's your tech support password?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: I don't have one.

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: Well, then I can't help you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since when do you require a password?

transcript.speaker: Tech Support
transcript.text: Usually right before lunch.

setting: Tech support help desk and a caller's office
situation: A caller phones tech support for help and is asked for a tech support password he has never heard of. When he says he has none, the support worker refuses to assist him. Dilbert challenges the rule, and the worker admits the requirement only appears around lunchtime.
punchline: The tech support worker invents a password requirement as a convenient excuse to dodge work whenever it's nearly time for lunch.
summary: A help desk worker makes up a bogus security rule to avoid taking calls as the lunch hour approaches.

title: Satan's Vendor Meets Scissors-Wielding Customer

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: Wow. You're fast with those scissors.

transcript.speaker: Alice

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: A devil-horned software vendor gloats to a customer, Alice, that now that she has implemented his product, he can raise upgrade prices and delay patches with impunity. punchline: The vendor's lock-in threat is defeated instantly because Alice is willing to abandon the product and cut his tie in one decisive move, showing his leverage was only as strong as the customer's fear of switching.
summary: A gloating devilish salesman learns that his captive customer is perfectly willing to throw out his product and snip off his necktie.

punchline: Dogbert's 'communication' advice is really a self-serving way to avoid being questioned, since a seminar attendee who stops listening has nothing to ask.
summary: A self-serving seminar leader urges his audience to tune out everyone around them, quietly hoping it will spare him from having to answer anything.

summary: After being caught reselling stolen stationery online, a slacking engineer shrugs off the company's empowerment rhetoric as hollow talk.

title: Asking Customer to Pay 40% More

punchline: Dilbert misreads the customer's obvious fury (she snaps a pen in half) as thoughtful consideration of his outrageous demand to renegotiate a signed contract.
summary: A engineer asks a client to pay far above the agreed price to fix a salesman's overpromise, and mistakes her snapping rage for open-mindedness.

title: Dogbert's Work-Life Balance Seminar

punchline: The 'work-life balance' seminar reveals that employees have no real balance, since work and holidays consume nearly all their time and everything else must compete for a single remaining slot.
summary: A canine consultant lists everything people care about, then cruelly shrinks their available time down to almost nothing.

title: Circular Approval Needs Ballpark Numbers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't talk with vendors until our change control board approves the project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I can't do that without ballpark prices from the vendor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just take your best guess.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... I should make up a number so I can get approval to make a phone call and ask what the number should have been?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right. But first you need to get my approval to do the cost-benefit analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you approve it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd have to see the numbers.

situation: Dilbert wants to ask a vendor for ballpark prices to judge whether his idea is feasible. The Boss says he needs change board approval first, which requires a cost-benefit analysis, which in turn requires the vendor's prices. The Boss tells him to guess, then makes Dilbert seek his approval for the analysis, which he won't give without seeing the numbers.
punchline: Every step of the approval process depends on a later step, so nothing can ever be approved, and the Boss's final demand to see the numbers completes the circular trap.
summary: A bureaucratic approval loop leaves an employee unable to get permission to gather the data that permission requires.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I mean what are you trying to accomplish with the software?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won't know what I can accomplish until you tell me what the software can do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Try to get this concept through your thick skull: The software can do whatever I design it to do!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you design it to tell you my requirements?

situation: Dilbert asks Alice, the software designer, for her requirements before he starts designing, but the two keep talking past each other. Each insists the other must define what the software should do first. After a silent standoff, Dilbert suggests she design the software to tell her his requirements.
punchline: Because neither person will define the requirements, Dilbert proposes making the software itself work out what it should do, which mocks the circular, deadlocked nature of requirements gathering.
summary: Two coworkers are stuck in a standoff over who must specify what the software should do, until one proposes letting the program figure it out itself.

title: Alice's Hair Catches Fire

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know where Asok is?

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.text: Do you think it's my job to know the location of all employees? Do you? Do you? Do you?

situation: Dilbert asks Alice if she knows where Asok is, and she snaps at him, furious at being treated as the keeper of everyone's whereabouts. Dilbert then calmly asks a follow-up question about seeing Alice, while her hair is visibly on fire and she is screaming.
punchline: Dilbert ignores Alice's rant and the fact that her hair is burning, asking if he's seen her while she's right in front of him, showing his obliviousness and her escalating stress.
summary: After snapping at a coworker's simple question, a woman's rage literally ignites her hair while he keeps cluelessly asking after her.

title: Unluckiest Insurance Agent's Asbestos Stairwell

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob, the unluckiest insurance agent.

setting: Conference room or office with a wooden table
situation: Bob, an insurance agent, pitches hazard coverage to a prospective client across a table. The client signs the paperwork and hands it back, whereupon a huge cloud engulfs the office and Bob, holding the contract, warns the client not to flee down the stairwell because its steps are made of asbestos.
punchline: Bob's terrible luck turns the signing of the policy into an instant disaster, and his warning about asbestos stairs shows that the building is hazardous in exactly the ways the insurance is meant to cover.
summary: A jinxed insurance salesman seals a deal just as catastrophe strikes and calmly advises his new client about a toxic escape route.

title: Boss Insults Dilbert's Unimportant Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

Dilbert remarks that the conversation has turned ugly, and the Boss escalates by asking him to stop exhaling so much in the office.
punchline: The Boss's insults escalate from dismissing Dilbert's work to implying Dilbert is so worthless that even his breathing is an imposition.
summary: A request for project support is met with escalating contempt from a boss who finds his employee's very breathing objectionable.

The Boss suggests she work weekends and take weekdays off, and Alice erupts in rage. He smugly claims vacation reduces stress, then walks off thinking it should be obvious while Alice is heard punching the wall of her cubicle.
punchline: The Boss's 'solution' to the impossible workload is to make her work weekends, then claims vacations reduce stress, oblivious that his demand is exactly what is stressing her out.
summary: A manager insists his overloaded employee take her leave and still finish her project, offering a weekend-work scheme that only enrages her.

title: Dogbert's Garbage Barge Paradise

situation: Dogbert greets a group of new arrivals at the dock of his so-called floating paradise, then tells them to surrender their cell phones and anything else they could use to call for help. In the last panel the visitors stand on a barge covered in trash while a seagull looks on, and Dogbert admits there is more garbage than they'd expect.
punchline: The luxury floating paradise is really a garbage barge, and Dogbert has lured in victims who now have no way to call for help.
summary: A scheming dog lures visitors onto a supposed floating resort, confiscates their means of contacting the outside world, and then they find themselves stranded in a heap of trash.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as an artist in a beret, stands on the Boss's desk and pitches an art installation: covering the ugly courtyard sculpture with a giant tarp. He explains the supposed artistic message, then reveals that what really makes it art is that someone is winning, meaning he stands to profit. The Boss sits listening in his chair.
punchline: Dogbert drops the pretentious artistic justification to reveal that his real definition of art is whatever earns someone a prize or payout, implying that he plans to win the money.
summary: Dressed as an artist, Dogbert pitches a pretentious covered-sculpture project to the Boss before admitting that real art needs a winner.

punchline: The Boss offers a pretend shopping spree through a supply catalog as a substitute for a raise, and his awkward hedging reveals how cheap and insulting the gesture is.
summary: A manager tries to placate an underpaid employee by letting her daydream-shop in a stationery catalog rather than giving her more money.

summary: A husband cheerfully signs up for a tyrant's floating city while volunteering his wife as its first troublemaker.

situation: The Boss, interviewing a job candidate across a table, says he wants passionate employees. The candidate takes this literally and wildly threatens to cut off his own ear if he doesn't get the job. The Boss, apparently unfazed, remarks that he is a people person.
punchline: The Boss's claim to be a 'people person' is absurdly oblivious given that he is calmly treating a self-mutilation threat as a normal interview moment, and his demand for passion produces unhinged desperation.
summary: A manager asking for passionate hires gets a candidate so desperate he threatens self-harm, and the manager responds by praising his own people skills.

summary: A costumed bully tests an intern's obedience and he complies so thoroughly that he ends up shivering in his underwear while she coolly tells him to stand by.

summary: A manager turns down a hugely profitable idea because the money saved would show up on another department's books instead of his own.

summary: A coworker severs working ties over a secondhand rumor but won't reveal the accusation, hiding behind a convenient rule of secrecy.

situation: Wally, sitting in his cubicle, turns his monitor away so that nobody walking past can see what he is doing. Later the Boss, holding a coffee mug, complains that he cannot read people, while Ratbert in a pet carrier on his desk tells him to come back later.
punchline: The Boss cannot tell whether Wally is working because Wally is simply asleep, and the Boss's inability to read people is further underlined by him seeking insight from, and being brushed off by, a rat in a carrier.
summary: A lazy employee angles his screen away from view so he can nap undetected while his baffled supervisor cannot figure out whether anyone is actually working.

setting: Office, in a Wizard of Oz parody
situation: Wally pours coffee into the top of Dilbert's head, which is opened like the Tin Man's, joking that the Wizard can give him some ambition. Dilbert then asks if Wally fears the wicked witch's winged cat, which confuses Wally. In the last panel Alice, styled as the wicked witch with her winged cat Catbert beside her, demands headcount for her project.
punchline: The Wicked Witch's winged-monkey threat is recast as an angry manager demanding staff for her project, implying that a boss hunting for headcount is as menacing as a fairy-tale villain.
summary: In an Oz-themed office, a colleague tops up a tin-man-like coworker with coffee before the wicked witch appears wanting people for her project.

title: The Plunger of Blame

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to blame someone for the failure of Project Alpha.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Use the plunger of blame. It's the latest technology for randomly distributing blame.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: The Boss tells Catbert he needs someone to blame for the failure of Project Alpha. Catbert offers a 'plunger of blame' that randomly assigns blame to an employee. In the last panel, Dilbert stands holding coffee next to a coworker, and the plunger has hit him in the back.
punchline: Blame for a failed project lands on a random person like Dilbert rather than the person actually responsible, and he hopes the thing stuck to his back is just a friendly pat.
summary: A manager looking for a scapegoat gets a magic plunger that sticks blame on a random employee, and Dilbert ends up the unlucky target.

title: Robbie the Frightening Hobo Speaker

transcript.speaker: Robbie
transcript.text: Mumble mumble mumble

setting: Dogbert's speakers bureau office, then a company meeting room
situation: The Boss visits Dogbert's discount motivational speakers bureau looking for a cheap speaker who will make employees work harder without inspiring them to quit. Dogbert recommends a frightening hobo who mumbles incomprehensibly. In the final panel the huddled employees listen to him and are scared into clinging to their jobs.
punchline: The hobo is the perfect cheap speaker because he motivates through fear rather than inspiration, making employees desperate to avoid ending up like him.
summary: A bargain-hunting manager hires a mumbling, scary vagrant to give a talk that keeps staff working hard but never dreaming of anything better.

title: Dogbert Dismisses Loud Howard Requests
