transcript.speaker: Loud Howard
transcript.text: They love me!!!

setting: A pink-walled room with Dogbert seated at a desk, addressing the audience
situation: Dogbert, seated at his desk, tells the audience that many readers have asked for Loud Howard to return. He criticizes the character as one-dimensional, neither clever nor insightful, merely loud. As Dogbert wonders why anyone would want more of him, Loud Howard appears and screams that they love him.
punchline: Dogbert's insult that Loud Howard is only loud is answered by Loud Howard bursting in and shouting, which proves the point while also confirming his popularity.
summary: Dogbert grudgingly acknowledges reader demand for a one-note shouting character, who promptly appears and bellows his own approval.

When a coworker refuses to lend his guest chair, she disappears behind the cubicle wall and beats him up. She then returns with the chair and lectures the meeting that violence is part of succeeding in the business.
punchline: Alice treats physically assaulting a coworker over a chair as an essential qualification for corporate success, satirizing cutthroat office culture.
summary: After being stuck fetching a missing seat for a meeting, Alice brutally beats a coworker to get one and declares that's what the job demands.

title: Contractor's Dream Versus Candy and Emeralds

setting: Office, on and beside a desk
situation: The Contractor, a man with a carrot dangling from a propeller beanie, says his dream is to become a regular employee. Catbert, the evil HR cat, replies that his own dream is to eat candy and poop emeralds. He then points out that he is halfway successful, meaning he can eat candy but not produce emeralds.
punchline: Catbert equates the contractor's hope of ever being made a permanent employee with the impossible half of his own dream, implying the promotion will never happen.
summary: A hopeful contractor with a carrot on his head is told by a smug cat that his aspiration is about as realistic as a fantasy of jewel-producing digestion.

situation: Dilbert tries to make conversation on a first date, but his date says she is not interested in politics, science, war, sports or current events. She finally reveals she only wants to talk about her hair, and Dilbert reluctantly agrees. After a very short time, she complains about her hair color, and he is already asking if they're done with the topic.
punchline: After exhausting every other subject, Dilbert's date can only talk about her hair, and the topic is so dull he tries to wrap it up almost immediately.
summary: A man runs through every conversation topic with his date and is left with nothing but a discussion of her hair color.

title: Popcorn Masks Wally's Body Odor

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, I can't work with the smell of popcorn in the air. It makes me insane!

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Refueling the Hindenburg?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why are people so mean?

situation: Alice complains to Wally that the smell of his microwave popcorn drives her crazy. Wally explains he uses it to cover up his body odor and tells her to pick her poison. Dilbert walks in with a mug and mocks Wally's bag of popcorn, and Wally wonders why people are so mean.
punchline: Wally's popcorn is meant to hide his body odor, and Dilbert's Hindenburg quip implies the combined smell is explosive, leaving Wally hurt by the insult.
summary: A coworker's microwave snack turns out to be a cover for his poor hygiene, and a passing colleague adds a sharp historical jab.

title: Hoping the Boss Reviews It

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I need your comments on this before I submit it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just leave it here and hope I become the sort of boss who gets around to doing that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did someone tell you that hope works?

setting: Office, the boss's desk and a cubicle area
situation: An employee hands the boss a document and asks for comments before submitting it. The boss tells him to leave it and merely hope the boss someday becomes the type to review things. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, later asks the employee, who sits crossing his fingers at his desk, whether someone told him hope works.
punchline: The boss openly admits he is unreliable and that hoping is the employee's only strategy, and Dilbert mocks the idea that hope is an effective approach.
summary: A worker's request for feedback is met with an admission of managerial neglect, leaving him literally crossing his fingers.

title: Job Hopper With Rabbit Ears

transcript.text: You've had fifteen jobs in two months. How can I be sure you're not a job hopper?

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: Maybe I change jobs a lot. And maybe I have gigantic rabbit ears. But does that make me a hopper?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, okay, you're hired.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: I am so sick of this place!

situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate who has had fifteen jobs in two months and asks how he can be sure the man isn't a job hopper. The candidate, who has big rabbit ears, uses a pun to deflect the question and gets hired. In his thought bubble he reveals he is already sick of the place.
punchline: The applicant, a literal rabbit-eared 'hopper,' proves he is a job hopper by being fed up with the company before his first day even starts.
summary: A rabbit-eared applicant with a wild employment history jokes his way into a job he already resents.

situation: Dogbert stands next to Dilbert's desk holding a small spray canister and announces he has invented an external antidepressant. He explains that when he is in a bad mood he applies it to other people, then sprays Dilbert in the face. Dilbert recoils in agony as Dogbert reveals the product is just pepper spray.
punchline: Dogbert's so-called antidepressant only cheers him up by making someone else miserable, and it is just pepper spray rebranded as a wellness product.
summary: Dogbert pitches a mood-lifting invention and demonstrates it by spraying his unsuspecting friend in the face.

title: Wally Claims Dead Coworker's Monitor

situation: Wally asks a motionless coworker slumped at his desk whether the rumor of his death is true. The coworker doesn't respond, so Wally concludes he is dead, takes the man's computer monitor, and walks off with it while thinking that he'll be missed.
punchline: Wally's mourning is really opportunism: he is more interested in scavenging the dead man's monitor than in the death itself.
summary: Finding a coworker apparently deceased at his desk, Wally calmly helps himself to the man's monitor.

title: Consultant States the Obvious

situation: A consultant stops by Dilbert's cubicle and asks permission to share obvious generalities about information. He then delivers a banal statement about disorganized information being unhelpful for decisions. Dilbert asks whether he is a consultant or mentally slow, and the consultant admits he doesn't know.
punchline: The consultant is so devoid of useful insight that he can't tell whether he is a professional adviser or simply dim-witted, implying the two are hard to distinguish.
summary: A visiting adviser drones out an empty platitude and then confesses he cannot tell if his job title or a lack of brainpower explains it.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert a project to do in his spare time, and when Dilbert asks what spare time he has, the Boss lists his dating time, hygiene time, daydreaming and even his questions as time that can be taken. In the last panel Dilbert asks a bystander, Dogbert, whether his questions are stupid.
punchline: After the Boss insults Dilbert's questions as stupid, Dogbert tells him they're not as bad as his answers, piling on the insult.
summary: A manager carves up every personal moment of an employee's life to find free time for extra work, and the employee's own pet then adds one more insult.

Dilbert dismisses the worry, citing Google's 'Don't be evil' motto and noting they surely have no death ray. punchline: Dilbert's confident claim that Google has no death ray is immediately undercut by a scene of Google executives with what looks like exactly that weapon, suggesting the 'Don't be evil' motto is not to be trusted.
summary: A reassurance about a tech giant's friendly slogan is contradicted by a glimpse of its executives gleefully operating a giant ray weapon.

He ends by saying Wally is currently hunting for a workplace hazard to roll around in, implying a staged injury claim.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd legal threats suggest Wally is deliberately engineering a lawsuit so he can never be fired, exploiting disability and workplace safety laws.
summary: A canine attorney makes ridiculous legal claims on his lazy client's behalf to make him unfireable, hinting that a faked injury is next.

punchline: The Boss quietly admits that meetings are easier when no one with real knowledge is there to complicate things, revealing he deliberately excluded the expert.
summary: A manager happily reports a smooth meeting on a project he left its actual manager out of, and concedes that ignorance makes discussions easier.

situation: Dogbert runs a management school and gives each student a rock. He instructs them to throw it in the air, demand that it stay up, bribe it with non-monetary compensation, and yell at it. The rocks all fall and hit the students on the head.
punchline: Demanding the impossible from employees works about as well as ordering a rock to defy gravity, and the managers who believed it get literally hurt, which Dogbert rewards with a diploma.
summary: A canine instructor teaches would-be managers to command stones to float, and the lesson ends with a chorus of bruised heads.

summary: A lazy employee exploits his oblivious manager's inattention to get a bonus vacation on top of the one he already took.

The farewell speech lists Bob's failures, including falling margins and sales and confusing campaigns. It ends by asking everyone to wish for a piano to fall on his head.

summary: A farewell announcement for a long-serving marketing executive turns out to be a thinly veiled insult, wishing him a cartoon-style accident on his way out.

title: Best Workplace for Elderly Employees

Albert protests that he is only 54 and just ran a marathon. The Boss ignores this and says he has arranged for the cafeteria to stock food that is easy to gum.

summary: A manager chasing a workplace award patronizes a new hire by treating him as ancient, even though the man is fit and only in his fifties.

Dilbert reassures him, then explains that women have a thousand expressions meaning they want you dead, and he identifies each one. summary: A coworker flinches at a hostile stare, and a colleague cheerfully catalogues the many ways women's expressions wish death upon men.

title: Invited to a Schadenfreude Party

summary: A dog lures a trusting young man into accepting an invitation, then relishes the man's disappointment as the very thing the party celebrates.

summary: A project plan that schedules the manager's blunders is validated the moment the manager denies he could make any.

transcript.speaker: Devil Boss
transcript.text: Erk!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Bad dream?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't call it bad!

setting: A dream office, then Dilbert's bedroom
situation: In a dream, a horned devil version of the boss tells Dilbert, who is carrying a giant coffee mug, that he should cut down on coffee. Dilbert responds by using the Force to choke the boss in mid-air. He then wakes up in bed, and Ratbert asks if it was a bad dream.
punchline: Dilbert enjoyed the dream of choking his boss so much that he refuses to call it a bad dream.
summary: A dreaming Dilbert gets revenge on his devilish boss with a Star Wars-style chokehold and wakes up happy about it.

title: Coffee for the Hot New Hire

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That new employee is getting special treatment just because she's hot. It's unfair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's hot? Where is her cubicle? Maybe I should bring her some coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind brewing an extra pot? I don't know how big her mug is.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Alice stands at the coffee machine complaining that a new employee is getting special treatment because she is attractive. Dilbert, holding the coffee pot, immediately asks where the woman's cubicle is and offers to bring her coffee. He then asks Alice to brew an extra pot, proving her point.
punchline: Dilbert unwittingly demonstrates exactly the preferential treatment Alice is complaining about by eagerly fawning over the new hire, even asking Alice to do extra work for it.
summary: A woman's grievance about a colleague's perks is instantly validated when her coworker rushes to wait on the newcomer.

title: Alice Predicts Wally's Runaround

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, I came to ask you for the new design specs.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But we both know you'll send me to someone who doesn't have them. And that person will refer me back to you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When I return, you will have escaped to your secret hiding place.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ted has the specs.

situation: Alice approaches Wally's cubicle to request the new design specs. Before he can answer, she predicts his usual strategy of sending her to someone else, who will send her back, while he slips away to hide. Wally, holding his coffee mug, simply tells her that Ted has the specs.
punchline: Wally is so predictable at dodging work that Alice narrates his whole evasion routine in advance, and he skips the routine by pointing her to Ted, though her prediction suggests it is just the first step of the runaround.
summary: Alice pre-empts a coworker's habit of passing the buck by describing his entire dodge, only for him to calmly name someone else.

title: Baby Salesman Exploits Cuteness

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're too cute to work in engineering. I'm transferring you to sales.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No one wants to hurt a baby. Use that to your advantage.

transcript.speaker: Baby
transcript.text: And if you buy the deluxe package I won't be emotionally scarred for life.

setting: Office hallway, then a customer's office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a baby engineer he is too cute for engineering and reassigns him to sales. He advises the baby to exploit the fact that nobody wants to hurt a baby. In the final panel the baby, seated across a desk from a customer, uses that advantage to pressure her into buying the deluxe package.
punchline: The baby turns his cuteness into emotional blackmail, implying the customer will traumatize him if she refuses the upsell.
summary: A tiny employee is reassigned to sales and promptly weaponizes his adorable helplessness to guilt a client into spending more.

title: Alice Bonks Head Hiring Test

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, interview the guy in our conference room and see what he can do for us.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm going to bonk your head on the table. If it sounds empty, you'll work in Marketing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did it go?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I bonked too hard. We just got a new sales guy.

setting: Office cubicle area and conference room
situation: The Boss tells Alice to interview a candidate waiting in the conference room. Alice tells the seated man she will bonk his head on the table and assign him to Marketing if it sounds empty. Afterward, she reports she bonked too hard and the company has a new sales guy.
punchline: Alice's violent hiring test knocked the candidate unconscious, which she treats as a perfectly good qualification for a sales job, implying sales hires are empty-headed.
summary: A manager sends his coworker to vet a job applicant, and her unorthodox head-knocking test ends with the poor man being filed straight into the sales department.

title: Consultant Speaks Pure Buzzword Gibberish

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Mildly Retarded Consultant

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: You'll have to drink from the firehose unless...

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: ...you drill down and check the dashboard to see why the bloatware bubbled up from the bake-off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that mean anything?

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Don't ping my cheese with your bandwidth.

situation: A consultant addresses The Boss and Dilbert at a meeting table, stringing together corporate buzzwords and metaphors about firehoses, dashboards, and bloatware. When The Boss asks whether any of it means anything, the consultant responds with yet another nonsensical phrase instead of an answer.
punchline: The consultant's jargon is meaningless, and when asked directly to explain, he deflects with more gibberish, implying consultants hide emptiness behind buzzwords.
summary: A consultant buries his audience in meaningless business jargon and answers a request for clarity with even more nonsense.

title: Dilbert Impersonates Dogbert on Oprah

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oprah invited me to appear on her show to talk about my book. But I'm too busy. Can you pretend you're me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gosh... Normally I would never do something like that, but it's probably my only chance of being on Oprah. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oprah is a surprisingly good puncher.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, then his living room
situation: Dogbert, sitting on Dilbert's bed, asks Dilbert to impersonate him on Oprah's show because he is too busy. Dilbert eagerly agrees, seeing it as his only chance to be on Oprah. Later, Dogbert watches the TV from an armchair as Dilbert cries out in pain, and Dogbert remarks that Oprah punches well.
punchline: Dogbert tricked Dilbert into taking a beating in his place, and calmly watches it on TV while commenting on Oprah's punching skill.
summary: A flattered man agrees to stand in for his dog on a talk show, only to be pummeled on live television while the dog enjoys the show from home.

title: Carol Stonewalls Dilbert With Phone Call

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, I need some three-ring binders and a reservation for the conference room on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I don't like the way you asked, so I'm going to make a phone call until you give up and leave.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Yeah, the big jerk is still standing there.

setting: Office cubicle area, at Carol's desk
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the Boss's administrative assistant, for binders and a conference room reservation. Carol decides she dislikes his tone and picks up the phone, announcing she will keep talking until he gives up and leaves. Dilbert stays put, and she complains about him to whoever is on the line while he is still standing there.
punchline: Carol's passive-aggressive tactic of pretending to be on a call backfires on her goal, since Dilbert doesn't leave and she ends up openly insulting him to the caller while he waits.
summary: A surly administrative assistant tries to wait out a coworker's request by faking a phone call, but he simply stays put while she grumbles about him.

title: Clown Sets CEO Pay Level

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Executive Compensation Review Board

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: How much should we pay our CEO if he just shows up for work?

transcript.speaker: Clown
transcript.text: Fifty million dollars!!!

transcript.speaker: Clown
transcript.text: Honk honk

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: The clown makes a good argument.

transcript.speaker: Board Member
transcript.text: Aye!

setting: Executive compensation review board meeting room
situation: A compensation review board meets to decide how much to pay the CEO if he merely shows up for work. A clown seated among the board members shouts out fifty million dollars while honking a horn. The other board members treat this as a serious argument and vote in favor.
punchline: The board's decision-making is so absurd that a honking clown's outlandish figure for CEO pay is taken seriously and approved, satirizing inflated executive compensation.
summary: A board deciding executive pay accepts a horn-honking clown's wild salary figure as sound reasoning and votes yes.

title: Exit Interview: Creative Ways to Kill You

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Exit interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And what is your reason for leaving?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: To be honest, I was spending way too much time thinking about creative ways to kill you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you cleared out your desk?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Why don't you go check.

setting: Boss's office, during an exit interview
situation: The Boss conducts an exit interview with a departing female employee and asks why she is leaving. She calmly admits she kept fantasizing about creative ways to kill him. When he asks if she has cleared out her desk, she grins and tells him to go check for himself, implying she has left something unpleasant there.
punchline: The employee implies she has left a deadly trap or some sinister surprise in her desk, turning her murderous daydreams into a real threat.
summary: A quitting worker confesses homicidal fantasies about her manager, then slyly hints that her desk holds a nasty farewell gift.

title: Outsourced Employee Works From Old Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got a job at the Indian company where you outsourced my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I arranged to work from home, which, as you know, is my old cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Here's your assignment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: E-mail it to me. My day starts in 10 hours.

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's old cubicle
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has been hired by the Indian company that took over his outsourced job. He negotiated to work from home, which turns out to be his old cubicle in the same office. When the Boss hands him an assignment in person, Dilbert tells him to email it since his workday doesn't start for 10 hours.
punchline: Outsourcing has changed nothing except Dilbert's employer and time zone, so he is now an offshore contractor who still sits at the same desk and the Boss must treat him like a remote worker.
summary: After being outsourced, a man gets rehired by the foreign firm and keeps working at his same desk, now insisting on remote-worker rules.

title: Discounting Hell in the Business Case

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to write a business case for lobbying our government to attack Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the risk analysis section, do you want me to assume that hell is real or imaginary?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Real. But remember to discount the infinite future flows of agony to the present so it doesn't look so bad.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to write a business case for lobbying the government to attack Elbonia. Dilbert asks whether the risk analysis should treat hell as real or imaginary. The Boss says real, but tells him to apply present-value discounting to the eternal suffering so the numbers look better.
punchline: The Boss knowingly accepts that the plan will send him to hell but wants financial discounting techniques to make eternal damnation look like an acceptable cost.
summary: A boss orders a business case for warmongering and wants the eternal torment awaiting him massaged away with finance tricks.

title: Legacy System Is Ancient Machinery

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carl quit. He's the only one who knows how to program the legacy system.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It can't be that hard. Go figure it out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Frack.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then an equipment room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that Carl, the only person who knew how to program the legacy system, has quit. He brushes off Dilbert's concerns and orders him to figure it out. Dilbert is then shown facing the actual legacy system, a huge, antique mechanical contraption with a tiny screen showing a question mark.
punchline: The 'legacy system' turns out to be a literal old-fashioned machine with no documentation, so Dilbert is left helpless and muttering a mild curse.
summary: After the only expert on an outdated system leaves, a manager dismisses the difficulty and sends an engineer to confront a hulking relic of a machine.

title: Boss Rewards Asok With Pirate Story

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you've done a good job this quarter so I'm going to toss a little non-monetary compensation your way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell me some boring story about your life and I'll pretend to enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the story should involve pirates. Go.

setting: Boss's office, seated at a desk
situation: The Boss tells Asok he has done a good job this quarter and offers a non-monetary reward instead of money. The reward is that Asok may tell a boring life story while the Boss pretends to enjoy it. The Boss then adds a demand that the story involve pirates, and Asok looks on warily.
punchline: The 'reward' is actually a chore for the employee, since the Boss is only pretending to be interested and even dictates the story's content, which makes it a demand rather than a perk.
summary: A manager substitutes cash with the chance to bore him with a story, then insists it feature buccaneers.

title: Competent Not Obliged To Help

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was wondering if you could stop by this weekend and show me how to install my wireless network.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Under what theory are the competent obliged to help the incompetent?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow. This is awkward.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Watch what happens when I just stare at you.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to come over on the weekend and help set up his home wireless network. Dilbert coldly questions why skilled people should have to assist the unskilled. When the coworker admits the awkwardness, Dilbert simply stares at him in silence.
punchline: Dilbert refuses the request for free tech support and deliberately lets the awkward silence stretch, enjoying the other man's discomfort.
summary: A colleague's plea for weekend help with his home Wi-Fi is met with a pointed question and an uncomfortable, unbroken stare.

title: Nonsense Folksy Answers Evade Benchmark Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you start the benchmark tests?

transcript.speaker: Man in cowboy hat
transcript.text: I'm all over that like a caterpillar on my Sunday pants.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does that mean ...yes?

transcript.speaker: Man in cowboy hat
transcript.text: Do birds eat beans to fly faster?

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss asks a coworker wearing a big cowboy hat whether he has started the benchmark tests. The coworker answers with a nonsensical folksy simile. When the Boss asks if that means yes, the coworker replies with another absurd rhetorical question instead of a straight answer.
punchline: The coworker hides behind meaningless folksy sayings so he never has to give a clear yes or no, leaving the Boss, and everyone else, unsure whether any work has started.
summary: A hat-wearing colleague answers a simple status question with rambling country-style nonsense that never actually says whether the work was done.

title: Marketing's Data Comes From Guts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does marketing have any data on customer preferences?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Errr grunt!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is disturbing on so many levels.

situation: Dilbert asks a marketing colleague, whose hair is shaped like two pointed horns, whether marketing has any data on customer preferences. The colleague grunts and strains, then produces a sheet of paper, implying he has just passed the 'data' from his body. Dilbert is horrified.
punchline: Marketing's customer data is literally produced by grunting and straining, implying it is made up or comes straight from their backside.
summary: Asked for real customer information, a marketer physically strains and produces a paper, leaving his coworker appalled.

title: Elbonian MP3 Player Prototype Mistaken

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's our prototype from the Elbonian factory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I'm no expert, but this is obviously a good one of these.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an MP3 player.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We used to call them plumber's helpers!

situation: Dilbert presents the Boss with a crude prototype built by the Elbonian factory. The Boss, admitting he is no expert, confidently praises it as a good example of the wrong thing. Dilbert has to tell him it is an MP3 player, and the Boss says it looks like a plunger.
punchline: The outsourced prototype is so shoddy that it looks like a plunger rather than an MP3 player, and the clueless Boss cannot tell what the product is supposed to be.
summary: A boss fails to recognise a junk-looking prototype from an overseas factory as a music player and compares it to a plunger.

title: Wally Insults Marketing Product Name

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally in Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: We'll need a name for this product.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Woman
transcript.text: What do you call something that just occupies space and smells bad?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Man
transcript.text: What was your name again?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I don't like where this is heading.

setting: Marketing department conference table with a strange steaming gadget on it
situation: Wally has joined the marketing department, where colleagues gather around a smoking prototype product and discuss what to name it. A marketing woman asks what you call something that just occupies space and smells bad. Wally sips his coffee as the others glance toward him, and he realizes where the question is aimed.
punchline: The marketing team's description of something that occupies space and smells bad is a thinly veiled insult at Wally, who senses it right away.
summary: A product-naming brainstorm in marketing turns into a pointed jab at the newest team member sitting right there.

title: Boss Picks Authoritative Decision Style

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: What type of meeting decision-making style will we be using today?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Will it be authoritative, consultative, voting or consensus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shut your coffee hole.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker asks the group which decision-making style the meeting will use, listing four formal options. The Boss answers by rudely telling him to be quiet. The coworker acknowledges that this was effectively his answer.
punchline: By simply barking an insult, the Boss demonstrates the authoritative decision-making style, and the coworker admiringly concedes the point.
summary: A coworker's request to choose a formal decision-making method gets answered by his boss's blunt order to be silent, which settles the question by example.

title: Tina Rewrites Scope, Gets Rewarded Unpaid

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tina, you were only supposed to document our project status, not rewrite the entire scope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO loves the new project scope. We'll expect you to do that without extra resources.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Is this a "neener-neener" situation or more of a "who's your daddy?"?

situation: Dilbert confronts Tina for rewriting the entire project scope when she was only supposed to document project status. The Boss then shows up and announces that the CEO loves the new scope, and that the team must deliver it without any extra resources. Tina asks whether she is being taunted or gloating over Dilbert.
punchline: Tina's unauthorized scope expansion is praised by the CEO, so Dilbert's team is saddled with a bigger project and no extra resources, and Tina cheerfully asks whether the situation is a petty taunt or a show of dominance.
summary: A colleague's unauthorized rewrite of a project's goals impresses upper management, who happily pile the larger workload on the team without added support.

title: Wally's Plant Gets Coffee Dregs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We canceled our plant maintenance contract to save money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Each employee will adopt a nearby plant and water it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The unluckiest plant in the whole world

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now when I pour my coffee dregs on you, it will look like work!

transcript.speaker: Plant
transcript.text: Must... run...

situation: The Boss tells staff in a meeting that the plant maintenance contract has been cancelled to save money, so each employee must adopt and water a nearby plant. Wally ends up with a potted plant and gleefully plans to dump his leftover coffee on it, since that will make him appear to be working. The plant, drawn with a thought bubble, wants to flee.
punchline: Wally treats the plant duty as a way to look busy by dumping his old coffee on it, which is terrible for the plant and makes it the unluckiest plant in the world.
summary: After a cost-cutting move hands plant care to the staff, the laziest employee turns his stale coffee into a show of effort at the expense of his unfortunate plant.

title: Voters Pity Countries Without Choices

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: I heard that the guy you voted for just confessed to having an affair with a squirrel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up. The guy you voted for is being sued for choking his secretary.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: In some countries they don't get a choice of who to vote for.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel sorry for them.

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert and a bald coworker trade insults about each other's political candidates while getting coffee. One says Dilbert's candidate confessed to an affair with a squirrel, and Dilbert retorts that the coworker's candidate is being sued for choking his secretary. They then agree to pity people in countries with no choice of candidates.
punchline: Having a choice between scandal-ridden candidates is so dismal that they sarcastically feel sorry for people who don't get to vote at all, implying that voting is barely better than having no options.
summary: Two coworkers swap scandalous accusations about their preferred politicians, then sarcastically commiserate with people who lack the chance to make such terrible choices.

file: 2006/2006-04-06_asok_survival methods_indian institutet of technology_wounded rodent_tickle hawk_find highway.gif
title: Asok's Desert Survival Hawk Plan

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I must use the survival methods I learned at the Indian Institute of Technology.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Step one: pretend to be a wounded rodent.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now look for the highway and tickle the hawk with its own feather.

setting: Desert with mountains and a saguaro cactus
situation: Asok, lost and disheveled in the desert, tries to apply survival techniques he learned at his Indian technical institute. He follows the first step by pretending to be a wounded rodent, which attracts a hawk that grabs him and carries him into the air. Dangling from its talons, he thinks about the next step, tickling the hawk, while spotting a highway below.
punchline: Asok's textbook survival plan works so literally that pretending to be prey gets him snatched by a hawk, and he blithely treats being carried off as just the next step of the plan.
summary: A stranded engineer's theoretical survival checklist has him playing injured prey, and the predator he attracts promptly flies him away.

title: Frillion Isn't a Real Number

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: We might need to restate our earnings.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: It turns out that we're not allowed to make up numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Did you know that "frillion" isn't an actual number?

setting: Executive office or boardroom, across a desk
situation: A green dinosaur executive tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that the company may have to restate its earnings. He explains that making up numbers is not permitted, and then adds that 'frillion' is not a real number.
punchline: The company's earnings were apparently reported using invented numbers like 'frillion', implying accounting fraud treated as an innocent misunderstanding.
summary: A dinosaur executive casually admits that the company's financial results were padded with fictitious figures and now need correcting.

title: Dogbert Wins Internet Debates Repeatedly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm debating on the Internet!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'm winning every argument by saying the same thing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "How would you like it if Hitler killed you?"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, I debated you last night!

situation: Dogbert sits on the couch with a laptop, gleefully announcing he is debating people online. He reveals that he wins every argument by posting the same canned retort. Dilbert asks what it is, and when Dogbert recites it, Dilbert realizes he was one of the people Dogbert 'debated' the previous night.
punchline: Dogbert's one-size-fits-all insult is so formulaic that Dilbert recognizes it as the same tactic used against him, showing how online arguments are often just repeated, meaningless attacks.
summary: A scheming dog brags about triumphing in web arguments with one recycled line, only to have his own owner recognize it from being on the receiving end.

title: Dogbert Bribes Congressman Obviously, Again

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Lobbyist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Congressman, I will give you this bag of money if you vote for tax breaks for my client.

transcript.speaker: Congressman
transcript.text: Try to be less obvious than the last time.

transcript.speaker: Congressman
transcript.text: Yes! I vote yes!

transcript.speaker: Onlooker
transcript.text: Smooth.

setting: A congressman's office, then the legislative chamber
situation: Dogbert, working as a lobbyist, openly offers a congressman a bag of money in exchange for a vote on tax breaks for his client. The congressman asks him to be subtler than last time, then immediately takes the bag into the chamber and cheers a very public 'yes' vote while clutching the money.
punchline: The congressman's request for subtlety is hollow, since he carries the bag of cash into the chamber and loudly votes yes, making the bribery blatantly obvious, as an onlooker sarcastically notes.
summary: A lobbying dog hands a lawmaker a sack of cash for his vote, and the lawmaker's idea of discretion is waving the loot around in the legislature.

title: Customer Declines Voluntary Extra Payment

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Per your suggestion, I asked our customer to voluntarily pay us more money to cover our bidding error.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It might surprise you to learn that our customer doesn't like that idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You probably made it sound like a bad thing.

situation: Dilbert reports to The Boss that he followed the Boss's suggestion and asked a customer to voluntarily pay more to cover a bidding mistake the company made. The customer refused, and the Boss blames Dilbert for presenting the request in a negative light.
punchline: The Boss absurdly assumes the customer's refusal is due to Dilbert's phrasing, not the fact that asking someone to pay extra for your own mistake is inherently unappealing.
summary: After carrying out his manager's idea of asking a client to pay extra for the company's pricing blunder, an employee is blamed when the client says no.

title: Smokin' Jim's Rushed Warning

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Smokin' Jim

transcript.speaker: Smokin' Jim
transcript.text: I've got a nicotine addiction, a tiny bladder, and attention deficit disorder.

transcript.speaker: Smokin' Jim
transcript.text: So talk fast because I can't focus for more than ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Smokin' Jim
transcript.text: Gaa! I have to learn to give that warning faster!!!!

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: A co-worker named Smokin' Jim sits across from a woman and warns her about his nicotine addiction, tiny bladder and attention deficit disorder. He tells her to talk fast because he can only focus for ten seconds. By the time he finishes the warning, he is already jittery and fidgeting, wanting a cigarette.
punchline: His long-winded warning about his short attention span uses up the very ten seconds he says he can focus, so the warning itself defeats the purpose.
summary: A fidgety smoker cautions his meeting partner about his limited attention and then runs out of patience before she can speak.

file: 2006/2006-03-30_best marketing expert_resume_nobel prize_five olympic medals_marketing biathlon.gif
title: Marketing Biathlon Resume Fabrication

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to hire the best marketing expert we can find.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé says you've won the Nobel Prize in marketing, and five Olympic gold medals in the marketing biathlon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's a marketing biathlon?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You ski up to people who won't buy your crap and you shoot them.

situation: The Boss sits at his desk interviewing Dogbert, who is applying for a marketing expert position. The Boss reads off the absurd credentials on Dogbert's résumé, including Olympic medals in a made-up sport, and asks what a marketing biathlon is. Dogbert answers with a violent description of the sport.
punchline: Dogbert's invented credential is explained as shooting customers who refuse to buy, a darkly comic spin on aggressive sales tactics, while the Boss credulously accepts an obviously fake résumé.
summary: A gullible manager interviewing a canine candidate for a marketing job learns that the made-up sport on his résumé involves gunning down reluctant customers.

title: Wally Dodges Implementing Alice's Plan

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert says my plan won't work. I need a second opinion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hypothetically, if I say your plan is terrific, would I end up being the engineer who has to implement it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your plan reeks of infeasibility.

situation: Alice asks Wally for a second opinion on her plan after Dilbert said it wouldn't work. Wally, holding his coffee mug, first asks whether praising the plan would get him assigned to build it. When Alice admits that's possible, he immediately declares the plan infeasible.
punchline: Wally's evaluation of the plan depends entirely on whether a positive review would land him with the work, not on the plan's actual merits.
summary: A coworker seeking validation gets an honest-sounding verdict only after the reviewer confirms that approval would mean extra work for him.

title: Dogbert's Tech Support Satisfaction Secret

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: Hello, Tech Support, my computer is frozen.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try hanging up and slamming your hand in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My average call time is down and my job satisfaction is up.

situation: A customer calls tech support complaining that his computer is frozen. Dogbert, working as a support agent, tells him to hang up and slam his hand in a drawer. Dilbert then asks how work is going, and Dogbert cheerfully reports that his call times are shorter and he enjoys his job more.
punchline: Dogbert improves both his call-time metric and his own happiness by deliberately giving cruel, useless advice that ends calls quickly and amuses him.
summary: A tech support agent who happens to be a dog gets rid of a customer with painful advice and then boasts about his improved performance numbers.

title: Boss Urges Faking Benchmark Results

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: According to my benchmark tests, our product is the worst one on the market.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you can tweak the numbers.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Fake them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fake is such an ugly word.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just remember that your next raise depends on the sales of that product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And mistakes happen. A decimal place can be either here or there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I'm asking is that you do the tests again... while drinking.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I always wondered what job satisfaction felt like.

situation: Carol reports that benchmark tests show the company's product is the worst on the market. The Boss hints that she should tweak the numbers, reminds her that her raise depends on sales, and suggests she redo the tests while drinking so any errors look accidental. In the last panel Carol sits with her feet up, drinking, finally enjoying her job.
punchline: Being pushed to falsify test results, Carol finds that doing it drunk is the first time she has ever felt job satisfaction, which is a sarcastic comment on how miserable her job normally is.
summary: Told by her manager to massage unflattering product test data, an employee finds the only upside in the arrangement is a drink and a bit of contentment.

title: Fired Wearing an Idiot T-Shirt

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: This T-shirt goes to Ted for his work on the Alpha Project.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Your work was terrible. You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was frightening.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Were you scared shirtless?

situation: In a meeting, the Boss presents Ted with a T-shirt as an award for his work on the Alpha Project. As soon as Ted holds it up, the Boss fires him for terrible work, and the shirt is printed with the word 'IDIOT'. Later Dilbert tells Dogbert at home how frightening it was to watch.
punchline: Dogbert makes a pun asking if Dilbert was 'scared shirtless', a play on 'scared stiff' and the T-shirt that served as a humiliating insult rather than an award.
summary: A manager hands out a mocking shirt to a coworker and dismisses him in the same breath, which later inspires a wisecracking pun from a dog.

title: Decoy Dogbert Faces Bono Wrestling

transcript.speaker: Bono
transcript.text: Hello Dogbert. I am here to persuade you to give your billions to third world countries.

transcript.speaker: Bono
transcript.text: If guilt does not work, I am prepared to wrestle you for it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's your decoy working out?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He's got Bono in a headlock.

setting: A blue office and Dogbert's desk area
situation: A visitor in sunglasses, identified as Bono, confronts what he thinks is Dogbert and demands that the billionaire dog donate his fortune to third world countries, threatening to wrestle him for it if guilt fails. In the final panel, Dilbert asks the real Dogbert, sitting safely at his desk, how his decoy is doing, and Dogbert reports that the decoy has Bono in a headlock.
punchline: Dogbert sent a decoy to face the philanthropic celebrity, and the stand-in is winning the wrestling match, so Dogbert keeps his billions.
summary: A rock star tries to guilt a decoy dog into giving away a fortune, while the real, wealthy dog watches calmly from his desk as the stand-in puts the star in a headlock.

title: Racquetball Paranoia Support Group Rejects Reason

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Society of Insane Chicks

transcript.speaker: Woman in red sweater
transcript.text: I know he hates me because he likes to play racquetball.

transcript.speaker: Woman in yellow top
transcript.text: Maybe he just likes racquetball. And wants to stay healthy.

transcript.speaker: Woman in red sweater
transcript.text: Leave now.

setting: A circle of chairs at a support group meeting titled 'The Society of Insane Chicks'
situation: At a support group meeting, one woman claims a man hates her because he plays racquetball. Another member offers a calm, reasonable explanation, that he simply enjoys the sport and wants to be healthy. The first woman responds by ordering her to leave.
punchline: In a group built around irrational paranoia, offering a sensible, rational explanation is treated as a betrayal and gets you expelled.
summary: A member of a group for irrational women gets thrown out for suggesting that a man's hobby is just a hobby.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one will believe you're me unless you get all perfect scores.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why? You only did 300 push-ups for my online gym class!!!

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for earning only a B while secretly taking the boss's online ethics course in his place. He insists on perfect scores so nobody suspects the impersonation. When Dilbert says he was tired, the boss complains that he also only did 300 push-ups in the boss's online gym class.
punchline: The boss is outraged not by the cheating itself but by his employee's imperfect performance, while casually revealing he's also having Dilbert fake his way through an ethics course and a gym class.
summary: A manager berates his underling for imperfectly impersonating him in online classes, including a course on ethics, which he is plainly cheating on.
keywords: boss makes employee do his work

setting: A conference room table, then Dilbert's home living room
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for his honest opinion of her project plan and tells him not to hold back. Dilbert compares the plan to something written by a drunken lemur as a practical joke on other drunken lemurs. At home that evening, he tells Dogbert, who is sitting on the couch, what he learned from the exchange.
punchline: Dilbert took the invitation to be brutally honest literally, and the resulting insult was so absurd and offensive that he only learned afterward that people dislike drunken lemur analogies.
summary: After being urged to give blunt criticism of a colleague's plan, Dilbert offers a ridiculous animal comparison and later reflects on how poorly it landed.

title: Elbonian MP3 Player Lost in Translation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After seeing the Elbonian MP3 player prototype I scheduled a conference call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because of the time difference, the call was at 3 AM. I was groggy and they barely speak any English, but I think we got everything worked out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He was right. It does look better with the speakers.

setting: Dilbert's office, then an Elbonian workshop
situation: Dilbert explains that he held a 3 AM conference call with Elbonian engineers about their MP3 player prototype, which is a strange contraption of rods and parts. Groggy and facing a language barrier, he assumes everything was settled. The final panel shows two robed Elbonians admiring a ridiculous sculpture-like device, with the apparent result that the 'speakers' became decorative lamp-like horns instead of audio components.
punchline: Because of the language barrier and a sleepy 3 AM call, the Elbonians misunderstood the requirements and built something absurd, treating the 'speakers' as decoration, which Dilbert wrongly believed was all worked out.
summary: A sleep-deprived call with non-English-speaking overseas partners yields a bizarre, nonfunctional gadget that nobody realizes is wrong.

title: Quitting Gets You a Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't finish the project on time if you leave.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you a 20% raise if you stay.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay. I'll stay.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Huh.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, everyone, disloyalty is being rewarded!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: [Alice and a crowd of coworkers run excitedly toward the boss's office.]

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll probably get another raise for this.

setting: Office, the Boss's office and hallway
situation: Alice storms into the Boss's office and quits. The Boss panics because the project can't finish without her and offers a 20% raise to stay. Alice accepts, then realizes quitting pays off and alerts her coworkers, who stampede to the Boss's office to threaten to quit as well.
punchline: Rewarding an employee for threatening to leave teaches everyone that disloyalty pays, and Alice expects to be paid again for spreading the news.
summary: A boss caves to a resignation threat with a hefty raise, and the resulting stampede of coworkers proves how that decision backfires.

title: Zombies Versus Project Managers Training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's School for Zombies and/or Certified Project Managers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The training is the same for either profession. The main difference is that zombies get more sun.

transcript.text: Repeat after me: I want to calendar an on-site post cutover support review meeting.

setting: A classroom or training seminar, with Dogbert standing on a stool in front of an audience
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, welcomes a room of students to his school that trains both zombies and certified project managers. He explains that the training is identical for both professions, and then has the class repeat a piece of dull project-management jargon in a rote, mindless way.
punchline: Project managers are equated with zombies because their training is the same rote, mindless repetition of jargon, with the only real difference being that zombies get more sun.
summary: Dogbert runs a training school where the curriculum for the undead and for project managers turns out to be essentially the same.

title: Note-Taker Sent Instead of Boss

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My Pointy-Haired Boss couldn't make it, so he asked me to take notes.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: The entire reason for this meeting is to get his input. How the %*$!@ does taking notes help??

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: The... Entire...

situation: A meeting is held to collect the Boss's input, but he skips it and sends an employee to take notes instead. A frustrated attendee loudly objects that taking notes does nothing to provide the input the meeting was called for. In the last panel the attendees glare angrily while the note-taker sits nervously and the angry attendee starts repeating his point.
punchline: The boss sends a note-taker to a meeting whose sole purpose is to get the boss's input, completely defeating its point, and the messenger gets the blame for it.
summary: Someone is dispatched to record a gathering that exists only to hear from the absent manager, and the room's fury lands on the wrong person.

title: Cowboy Boss Speaks Nonsense Idioms

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I cannot decide if you are very wise or just a big stupid moron.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I'll tell you, little cowpoke, when the snake falls in love with the spaghetti, it's time to buy a new hat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You look more flustered than a barefoot squirrel at a tire store.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! They almost make sense!!!

setting: Office, at a desk or meeting table
situation: The Boss, wearing a cowboy hat, sits across from an employee who cannot tell whether the boss is wise or an idiot. The boss responds with absurd folksy idioms that make no sense. The employee holds his head in distress because the sayings almost sound meaningful.
punchline: The boss's meaningless cowboy-style sayings sound just plausible enough to leave the employee tormented, unable to tell wisdom from nonsense.
summary: A hat-wearing manager spouts bizarre homespun proverbs that leave his subordinate agonizing over whether any of it means something.

title: Fungible Oil Undermines Patriotic Car Purchase

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking about buying a more fuel efficient car.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's my patriotic duty to reduce this country's dependence on foreign sources of oil.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because then the countries that hate us will have less money to fund terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Actually, developing countries would buy the oil you saved, thus adequately funding those same terrorists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least I wouldn't be funding them myself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oil is a fungible commodity. The capitalist system virtually guarantees that you'll end up buying the lowest cost oil from sources unknown to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, maybe, but I want my car to make a statement.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And the statement would be "Hey, everyone, I don't understand what fungible means!"

setting: Dilbert's home and a grassy hillside outdoors
situation: Dilbert announces he wants a more fuel efficient car out of patriotic duty to cut foreign oil dependence and starve terrorists of funds. Ratbert and Dogbert dismantle his reasoning, pointing out that saved oil would be bought by others and that oil is fungible, so his purchases can't be traced. Dilbert falls back on wanting his car to make a statement.
punchline: Ratbert mocks Dilbert by saying the only statement his car would make is that he doesn't understand the word fungible.
summary: A man's noble-sounding plan to buy a greener car is picked apart by his pets until all that's left is a vanity statement that proves his ignorance.

transcript.text: This is Dilbert. He'll tell you why your idea is impossible.

situation: The Boss introduces his team to a visiting presenter before a proposal meeting. For each person he describes the unhelpful way they will react, from apathy to leaving early to doubting the idea. He finishes by admitting he himself will keep his eyes shut throughout.
punchline: The Boss warns the presenter that every attendee will be useless or hostile, then reveals that he will also be completely disengaged, so the presentation is pointless before it begins.
summary: A manager gives a presenter a cheerfully honest rundown of how each team member will fail to engage with the pitch.

punchline: Loud Howard announces a supposedly confidential reorganization at the top of his voice, then shouts about keeping it secret and threatens to shush others, which makes the secrecy absurd.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to his new coworker Phil, who is literally a potted plant that will sit in his cubicle. The Boss explains that Phil recites three annoying stories on repeat while Dilbert tries to work, and Dilbert ends up sobbing. In the last panel Catbert asks the Boss how he plans to cut expenses, and the Boss answers that performance bonuses are under control.
punchline: The potted plant is a stand-in for a typical annoying coworker, and the Boss's answer reveals that cost savings come from denying employees bonuses instead of fixing anything.
summary: A houseplant is assigned as a desk-mate to a tormented engineer, mirroring the tedious chatter of real coworkers, while management brags about saving money by withholding bonuses.

title: Boss Takes Online Exam Mid-Conversation

transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Is the online degree hard?

setting: Office cubicle and a nearby desk
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has enrolled in a distance learning class to earn his Master's degree, and Dilbert reacts with dread and then screams. Later the Boss chats with Catbert, who asks if the online degree is hard. The Boss casually reveals he is taking his midterm exam right now while holding a coffee mug, implying Dilbert is doing his exam for him.
punchline: The Boss is only taking his online midterm because Dilbert is secretly doing the work for him, so the degree isn't hard for the Boss at all.
summary: A manager brags about earning a graduate degree online while his subordinate, who is actually doing the coursework, screams in frustration.

title: Broken Chair, Upside-Down Solution

transcript.text: My chair is broken. May I use your extra one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have an extra chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure you do. It's right there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not an extra chair. It's my guest chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, whatever. The point is that the base broke off of my chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't sit on a chair that has no wheel base. It's unstable.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being a baby. Just turn your chair upside-down and it will be totally stable.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When did your chair break?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Last spring. You get used to it.

setting: The Boss's office, then the hallway outside
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a spare chair because his own chair's wheel base has broken off. The boss refuses, claiming the chair in his office is a guest chair rather than an extra one, and tells Dilbert to flip his broken chair upside-down and sit on it. Dilbert then asks a coworker with the same problem how long theirs has been broken, and learns it has been that way since last spring.
punchline: Management's cheap, dismissive fix is for employees to sit on upside-down broken chairs, and the coworker's resigned 'you get used to it' shows workers have simply endured it for months.
summary: A manager hoards a spare chair and tells a worker with a broken one to sit on it upside-down, a hack that other employees have already been living with for ages.

title: Caffeine Lets Dilbert Predict Conversations

setting: Office, at a desk beside an oversized coffee mug
situation: Alice begins to raise a work topic with Dilbert, who is sitting next to a giant coffee mug. Dilbert interrupts her, claiming the caffeine lets him see the future and predict the whole conversation. When Alice calls him a freak, he cheerfully says he knew she would, narrating his own next line.
punchline: Dilbert's supposed caffeine-fueled prescience is just him being annoying and presumptuous, and he mockingly scripts the exchange, including Alice's insult and his own reply.
summary: A heavily caffeinated engineer insists he can foresee an entire chat with a coworker and ends up predicting her put-down before she gives it.
keywords: I already know what you'll say

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert return from a four-mile walk, and Dilbert invites Dogbert to watch TV. Dogbert says he must finish a call first, then is shown wearing a headset at his desk running a tech support line, telling a caller that nothing in his database covers their problem.
punchline: Dogbert runs a tech support operation that offers customers no real help, brushing off their problems with the claim that the database has nothing on them.
summary: After a long stroll, a dog dons a headset to run his own helpline and tells a waiting caller that their issue is simply not covered.

title: Who Demotivates Whom First

transcript.text: You've never done a job well.

transcript.text: You have to go first.

The boss says Wally has never done a job well, and Wally replies that he is demotivated. They each insist the other must act first, until Wally points out that going first would make him the leader.
punchline: Both are deadlocked over who must act first, and Wally cleverly turns the boss's demand into an implication that the boss would be following him as the leader.
summary: A lazy employee and his manager trade blame over whose move must come first in a motivation standoff, and the employee flips the logic to claim leadership.

title: Coffee Cures Soul-Crushing Futility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, how do you cope with the soul-crushing futility of this job?

transcript.text: One day I realized that sadness is just another word for not enough coffee.

situation: Dilbert asks Wally how he copes with the futility of their job, and Wally says sadness is really just a lack of coffee. Dilbert takes the advice to an extreme and appears at home with a giant coffee pot strapped to his back and a tube in his mouth, wired on caffeine, while Dogbert looks on.
punchline: Dilbert takes Wally's coffee advice absurdly literally, hooking himself up to a giant coffee pot, which reveals he has become dangerously over-caffeinated.
summary: After hearing that unhappiness is merely a coffee shortage, a desperate engineer straps a huge pot of coffee to himself and sips from it nonstop.

title: Abusing the Occurrence Absence Policy

transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Every absence counts as one "occurrence" whether it is one day or more.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: I just got a headache. I'll see you in a year. Or as I like to call it, one occurrence.

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: If something is worth having, it's worth abusing.

situation: Catbert, as Evil Director of Human Resources, explains a policy that counts every absence as a single occurrence regardless of its length. A bald coworker immediately exploits the loophole, announcing he will take a year off over a headache. In the last panel his thought bubble reveals his attitude that any perk is meant to be abused.
punchline: A policy that treats a one-day absence and a year-long absence as the same single occurrence invites employees to abuse it by taking the longest possible leave.
summary: An HR rule that lumps every absence together as one event is promptly turned into a license for a coworker to vanish for twelve months.

title: Hiring Her Despite No Qualifications

transcript.text: You're so attractive that I'm blind to your complete lack of qualifications.

transcript.text: If I hire you, will you show up for work?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Not often, you ignorant lump.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha! It's cute the way you say it.
