transcript.text: Ha ha! I want your office.

situation: The Boss interviews an attractive woman and openly admits he is ignoring her lack of qualifications because of her looks. She insults him and says she will rarely show up, and he finds this charming. She then laughs and says she wants his office.
punchline: The Boss is so blinded by her looks that he laughs off her insults and admitted absenteeism, while she cheerfully sets out to take over his office.
summary: A smitten manager hires an unqualified interviewee who mocks him to his face and then eyes his corner office.

title: Three People's Work, Three Percent Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you did the work of three people this year and earned the highest raise in the department!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foom!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What made you all cumulo-nimbus?

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss praises Alice for doing the work of three people and earning the highest raise in the department. He then hands her a paper showing the raise is only 3%, and her hair explodes upward into a towering storm-cloud shape. Dilbert later asks what made her so cumulonimbus, and she simply repeats the number.
punchline: The 'highest raise in the department' is a pitiful 3%, which is enough to make Alice's hair swell into a thundercloud of fury.
summary: A glowing performance review turns explosive when the reward for triple productivity turns out to be a tiny pay bump.

title: Hating Customers Reduces Phone Center Stress

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your résumé looks great. I see no reason you wouldn't be an excellent phone center employee.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Mwab blah glob wobmah tob muh wah wah.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This job got a lot less stressful once I realized I hate our customers.

setting: Office interview room, then beside a desk
situation: A manager interviews a woman for a phone center job and praises her résumé. She replies with unintelligible gibberish because a long tongue-like appendage is hanging out of her mouth. In the final panel, Catbert holds a coffee mug and explains how he copes with the stress of the job.
punchline: The applicant's garbled speech doesn't matter for a phone center job, and Catbert's remark reveals that the real secret to coping with customer service is simply despising the customers.
summary: A hiring manager happily approves a candidate who can't speak intelligibly, while Catbert shares his cynical tip for surviving customer service.

title: Pushback Gets Presenter Fired

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Our CEO appreciates pushback.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The last thing he wants is a bunch of yes men.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Don't be afraid to stand your ground. He respects that.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: My plan is to form business units around each product line.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me. We tried that once and it didn't work.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: You're fired.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Leave now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Cruelty or convenience?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I needed a cubicle to store my extra binders.

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: Carol assures the team that the CEO welcomes pushback and respects people who stand their ground. When a presenter proposes reorganizing into business units, Dilbert points out that the approach was already tried and failed. The presenter fires Dilbert on the spot and tells him to leave, and Dilbert's cubicle is then needed for storage.
punchline: Despite claims that pushback is welcome, the person who speaks up is fired immediately, and the real motive turns out to be petty: Carol wanted his cubicle to store her extra binders.
summary: A manager's promise that dissent is valued evaporates the moment someone challenges a bad plan, and the firing turns out to be about office space.

title: The Boss Works His Snitch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, Asok, what have you heard about Ted's project?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: He seems to be in over his head and he's blaming you for cutting the wrong budget.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I hope this doesn't come back to bite me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not now, Carol. I'm working my new snitch.

situation: The Boss pumps Asok for gossip about Ted's troubled project, and Asok reports that Ted is blaming the Boss for cutting the wrong budget. Asok then worries aloud that informing on a colleague could backfire on him, while the Boss brushes off Carol, who is waiting with paperwork, because he is busy cultivating his new informant.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully admits he is using Asok as a snitch right in front of him, showing Asok has been manipulated into spying on coworkers and may suffer for it.
summary: A manager quizzes a junior employee for office gossip and openly calls him his new informant while dismissing an assistant.

title: Rental Car Clerk Offers One Glove

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I reserved a mid-sized car.

transcript.speaker: Rental Clerk
transcript.text: Let's see what's left.

transcript.speaker: Rental Clerk
transcript.text: We don't have any cars left. But I can let you borrow a glove from the lost-and-found bin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What good is one glove?

transcript.speaker: Rental Clerk
transcript.text: You wouldn't ask that if you had a frozen hand.

situation: Dilbert arrives at a rental car counter to pick up a mid-sized car he reserved. The clerk tells him there are no cars left and offers a glove from the lost-and-found as compensation. When Dilbert questions the usefulness of a single glove, she retorts that he'd feel differently if his hand were frozen.
punchline: The clerk offers a laughably inadequate substitute for a reserved car and answers his complaint with a defensive, illogical justification, mocking poor customer service.
summary: A rental agency with no vehicles available tries to appease a customer with a stray glove from its lost-and-found.

file: 2006/2006-04-05_concerns about work_teds work_team building exercise_test here_sent asok.gif
title: Boss Strands Ted in Desert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I listened to your concerns about Ted's work, so I tricked him into being left in the middle of the desert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He thinks it's a team-building exercise. Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We wanted you to transfer him, not kill him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? This is awkward.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this is Ted. Where's Asok?

setting: Conference room and an office building exterior
situation: During a meeting, the Boss proudly announces he acted on complaints about Ted's work by tricking Ted into being abandoned in the desert under the guise of a team-building exercise. Dilbert points out they only wanted Ted transferred, not killed. The Boss admits it is awkward, and in the final panel an angry Ted shows up and demands to know where Asok is.
punchline: The Boss takes a request to transfer a problem employee to mean leaving him to die in the desert, and the fuming Ted returns alive and looking for someone else (Asok) to blame.
summary: A manager misreads a request to move a coworker elsewhere and strands him in the wilderness, only for the furious man to walk back into the meeting.

title: Nemesis Is Now a Profession

transcript.speaker: Nemesis
transcript.text: Hi. I'm your new nemesis.

transcript.speaker: Nemesis
transcript.text: The nemesis function used to be handled informally. Now it's a profession, kind of like project management.

transcript.speaker: Nemesis
transcript.text: Stand by while I prepare my nemesis face and look for reasons to thwart you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sigh.

situation: A small horned man in a shirt and tie walks up to Dilbert's cubicle and introduces himself as Dilbert's new nemesis. He explains that the nemesis role has become a formal profession, then asks Dilbert to wait while he puts on a menacing face and searches for ways to obstruct him. Dilbert sighs.
punchline: Turning something as petty as having a rival into a bureaucratic profession mocks how corporate life formalizes and professionalizes everything, with a jab at project management being just as obstructive.
summary: A professional adversary shows up at Dilbert's desk, treating the job of being his enemy as a legitimate career path.

title: Boss Too Busy To Learn

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm too busy to learn anything about the projects I'm managing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I barely have enough time to make critical decisions about them.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Maybe you're lazy and stupid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's go down to the pond and throw rocks at the ducks.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that he is too busy to learn about the projects he manages, yet still makes critical decisions about them. Catbert suggests he may simply be lazy and stupid. The Boss ignores the insult and proposes going to throw rocks at ducks.
punchline: The Boss is too oblivious or unbothered to take in Catbert's accurate insult, and his suggestion of tormenting ducks proves he has plenty of time for pointless pastimes.
summary: A manager who claims he has no time to understand his projects shrugs off a blunt diagnosis of his character and plans a duck-pelting outing instead.

title: Hair Sample From Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you don't give us a urine sample to test, I have to fire you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a hair sample to test instead?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: How do I know it's your hair?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can take the sample yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Add this to the list of things you shouldn't trust Human Resources to do.

setting: Catbert's Human Resources office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Catbert, the HR director, threatens to fire Dilbert unless he provides a urine sample for drug testing. Dilbert offers a hair sample instead, and Catbert questions whether it would really be his hair, so Dilbert suggests Catbert collect it himself. At home, Dilbert tells Dogbert that the incident belongs on the list of things not to trust HR with.
punchline: Catbert's suspicion that a hair sample could be faked is easily defeated by letting him pluck the hair himself, which shows how HR creates needless obstacles and can't be trusted with even a simple task.
summary: When the HR chief demands a drug test, a simple workaround exposes how silly his objections are, adding to Dilbert's list of HR failings.

file: 2006/2006-04-10_less prodcutive_automatic promotion_hiring_work like idiot_look like idiot_pointy haired alice.gif
title: Boss Wants Alice Less Productive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I need you to be less productive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll get an automatic promotion if I can justify hiring one more direct report.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I'm going to work like an idiot, I might as well look like one.

situation: The Boss asks Alice to deliberately reduce her productivity so he can justify hiring another employee, because a larger headcount earns him an automatic promotion. Alice responds by showing up with her hair styled into the same pointy horns as the Boss's, while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: Alice sarcastically mimics the Boss's pointy hair, saying that if she has to act as foolishly as he asks, she may as well look as foolish as he does.
summary: Told to slack off so her manager can pad his headcount and win a promotion, Alice mocks the request by copying his distinctive hairstyle.

title: Cubicle Size Proves Slight Importance

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: This is a picture of my cubicle. As you can see, it's slightly larger than yours.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: That means I'm slightly more important than you.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And yet you've worked here much longer.

transcript.speaker: Man in white shirt
transcript.text: I get it!!!

situation: Tina, a woman with big curly hair, shows a male coworker a photo of her cubicle and claims its slightly larger size makes her slightly more important than him. She then points out that he has worked at the company much longer, and the coworker reacts with sudden shocked realization.
punchline: Tina's larger cubicle reveals that the company rewards status rather than seniority, and the coworker realizes how little his long tenure has earned him.
summary: A coworker shows off her bigger cubicle as proof of rank, then casually exposes that his longer tenure has gotten him nowhere.

title: Dogbert's Tech Support Ruins Lives

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's tech support. How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I get an error message every time I open an application.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try giving me all of your personal information and then checking into rehab.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll have someone steal your identity and move in with your wife.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: There's a good chance that the new guy will know how to fix your computer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When you get out of rehab, talk your wife into taking you back.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then never touch your computer again because it hurts the ones you love.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's work?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Everyone wants to talk to my supervisor.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center and Dilbert's office
situation: Dogbert runs a tech support line and answers a customer's simple error-message complaint by advising him to hand over his personal information and check into rehab. The advice escalates into identity theft and losing his wife before ending with a lecture on never touching the computer again. Dilbert then asks Dogbert how work is going.
punchline: Dogbert's deliberately abusive tech support wrecks the caller's life, so naturally every customer demands to speak to his supervisor.
summary: A tech support dog responds to a routine computer error with outrageous life-ruining advice and then wonders why callers keep escalating.

title: Seven Steps to Weaponized Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today I will teach you how to use your incompetence to achieve your goals.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 1: Be incompetent. (Also known as "the easy part.")

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 2: Volunteer for the most difficult and important projects

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 3: Convince your boss that an enemy within the company is slowing you down.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 4: Insist that competent people be pulled off of other projects to help you.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 5: Declare yourself the leader of the competent people

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 6: Claim credit for the work of the competent people.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Step 7: After you get promoted, fire the competent people to eliminate witnesses.

setting: Office conference rooms and cubicle area, ending outside a building window
situation: Dogbert coaches a bumbling employee through a seven-step plan for getting ahead through incompetence. The employee volunteers for hard projects, blames a corporate enemy, takes over competent coworkers, claims their credit, and finally gets them fired once promoted. The last panel shows a person falling from a high window.
punchline: The final step reveals that climbing the corporate ladder on others' work ends with eliminating the competent people who could expose you, played darkly as a literal defenestration.
summary: A dog mentors a hopeless worker on exploiting colleagues' talent to rise to the top and then silencing them.

title: The Internet Is Full

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, why isn't my e-mail working today?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The Internet is full.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Great! Now what do I do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if I'm supposed to see anything when it's draining.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Wally why his e-mail isn't working, and Wally lazily claims the Internet is full. The Boss believes it and asks what to do, then sits at his desk holding the computer's cable, apparently waiting for the Internet to drain.
punchline: The Boss is so technically clueless that he accepts the absurd claim that the Internet can be full and literally waits for it to drain like a tub, while Wally gets out of doing any work.
summary: Wally dodges a tech support request with a ridiculous excuse that his gullible boss swallows completely.

title: Patty Amplifies and Distorts Schedule

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Patty the Amplifier and Distorter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell the project team that we're pushing back the schedule by a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell you the reason because you would amplify and distort it.

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: The schedule is changing because Dilbert hates women!!!

situation: Dilbert asks Patty, a coworker with a megaphone strapped to her ear, to tell the project team the schedule is slipping by a week. He declines to give her the reason, saying she would amplify and distort it. Patty then announces to a coworker that the schedule is changing because Dilbert hates women.
punchline: Dilbert's refusal to explain was justified, since Patty distorts the message anyway and invents an outrageous reason that makes him look terrible.
summary: A coworker fitted with a literal amplifier proves her reputation by turning a simple delay notice into a shouted accusation.

title: Wally Doesn't Know His Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, what's the status on the RDP project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Am I working on that one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've been in charge of it for a year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Oh. In that case, it's almost done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Half of being a manager is living with a vague feeling of uneasiness.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Wally for a status update on the RDP project, and Wally has to ask whether he is even working on it. When told he has been in charge of it for a year, Wally instantly claims it is almost done. The Boss retreats to his desk and reflects that managers just have to live with a vague uneasiness.
punchline: Wally's instant, baseless claim that the project is almost done confirms the Boss's dim suspicion that he has no real idea what his employees are doing, and he simply accepts that unease as part of the job.
summary: A manager learns his employee has forgotten a year-long assignment, then shrugs off his worry as an occupational hazard.

title: Not Smart Enough to Debate Online

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want to debate with people on the Internet but I worry that I'm not smart enough.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll just read what the smart people are saying.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'm in.

setting: Dogbert's desk in front of a computer
situation: Dogbert sits at his computer and worries that he isn't smart enough to argue with people on the Internet. He decides to read what smart people are saying first, and then immediately announces he is ready to join the debate.
punchline: Reading a bit of what smart people say is enough to make Dogbert feel qualified, mocking how little it takes for people to feel entitled to argue online.
summary: After a brief moment of self-doubt, a dog decides that skimming smarter people's posts qualifies him to join online arguments.

title: Potato Battery Change Order Scam

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our sales guy vastly underbid a job. Now it's my project to install the system in a way that's profitable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Blame your customer for underspecifying the features then charge her through the nose for change orders.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Three million dollars for an electrical plug?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The base model uses a potato battery.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then a customer meeting at a table
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that a salesperson badly underbid a project and he must now make the installation profitable. Dogbert advises blaming the customer for vague requirements and then billing her heavily for change orders. In the final panel, a customer is shocked at a three million dollar charge for an electrical plug, and Dilbert explains that the base model only includes a potato battery.
punchline: The base product was so bare-bones that every real requirement becomes an expensive add-on, so the customer gets billed millions for something as basic as a plug.
summary: After a salesman lowballs a contract, a consultant's advice turns the cheap base product into a vehicle for enormous extra charges.

title: Squirrel Milking Management Wisdom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A business magazine is sending a reporter to interview me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They want to learn my best management practices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a little like milking a squirrel because you need butter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what that meant, but I like the way it sounded.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Describe your typical day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, let me tell you...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes you milk the squirrel, and sometimes the squirrel milks you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "He is like a Zen master. His words are peppered with squirrel-related wisdom."

setting: Office and the Boss's office, with a final scene in a break area or conference room
situation: The Boss announces that a business magazine wants to interview him about his management practices, and Dilbert sarcastically responds with a nonsensical squirrel analogy. The Boss, not understanding it but liking how it sounds, repeats a variation of it to the reporter. The resulting article praises him as a Zen master full of squirrel-related wisdom, which Dilbert reads with coworkers.
punchline: The Boss passes off Dilbert's sarcastic gibberish as his own insight, and the media mistakes meaningless nonsense for profound management wisdom.
summary: A clueless manager recycles a coworker's absurd insult as profound advice and ends up praised in print as an enlightened sage.

title: Ham Sandwich Is Workday Highlight

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: The highlight of my workday is this ham sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: From now until quitting time, nothing else will be as rewarding.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What do you do after work?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I think about the sandwich.

situation: Three coworkers, Bob, Dilbert and Alice, sit at a table at lunchtime while Bob eats a ham sandwich. He announces that the sandwich is the high point of his workday and that nothing else will match it before quitting time. Alice asks what he does after work, and he says he spends that time thinking about the sandwich.
punchline: Bob's whole life is so joyless that a ham sandwich is his sole source of satisfaction, both during work and after it.
summary: A coworker's sad little lunch becomes the one thing he lives for, occupying his thoughts even after hours.

title: Strong Leaders Schedule Weekend Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to work this weekend.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no work to do. I'm waiting for input.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't matter. Strong leaders make their people work on weekends.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then he asked me what the clueless leaders do, as if I would know that.

setting: Office cubicle area and break area
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to work the weekend even though Dilbert says there is no work available while he waits for input. The Boss insists that strong leaders make their people work weekends regardless. He then complains to Catbert, who holds a coffee mug, that Dilbert asked what clueless leaders do.
punchline: The Boss is the very definition of a clueless leader, yet he is oblivious to it and thinks Dilbert's question is unfair because he couldn't possibly know the answer.
summary: A manager demands pointless weekend work to prove his leadership and then grumbles that his employee asked an embarrassingly pointed question.

title: Patent Lawyer Sees Flying Monkey

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help to patent my search engine algorithm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I will become a billionaire and have attractive girlfriends.

transcript.speaker: Patent Attorney
transcript.text: Hold on... I have an emerging primate... and he's got wings!

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh! Ooh!

situation: Dilbert visits a patent attorney and asks for help patenting his search engine algorithm, explaining that he plans to become a billionaire with attractive girlfriends. The attorney interrupts to announce that a winged monkey is emerging from behind him, and he looks alarmed.
punchline: Dilbert's fantasy of getting rich and finding girlfriends is so unlikely that it is portrayed as the equivalent of pigs (or monkeys) flying.
summary: A man's grand plan for riches and romance via a patented algorithm is met with the sight of a flying monkey, hinting at how improbable his dream is.

title: Analogy Police Arrest the Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't start designing the product until someone tells us what features it should have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's like saying you can't play on the beach unless you know how many grains of sand there are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I don't think it's very much like that.

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police
transcript.text: Analogy Police. Come with me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you taking me to jail for making a bad analogy?

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police
transcript.text: The Analogy Police don't use a real jail. We use something similar.

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police
transcript.text: You'll be here with this beautiful woman.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? That's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: Analogy Police
transcript.text: She's the one being punished.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Your necktie is like Hitler at an ice rink.

setting: Office meeting room, then a green-walled room used as the Analogy Police's 'jail'
situation: Dilbert says the team can't design the product until someone defines its features, and the Boss responds with a ridiculous beach-and-sand analogy. When Dilbert points out the analogy is poor, an Analogy Police officer arrests the Boss. The Boss is placed in a 'jail' with a woman, thinking it's a good deal, but she is the one being punished and she lobs a bizarre analogy at him.
punchline: The Boss's punishment for bad analogies is being locked in a room with a woman who inflicts equally terrible analogies on him, which turns out to be torture for him (and her).
summary: A manager who defends vague requirements with a nonsensical comparison is hauled off by officers who punish bad comparisons with more of the same.

file: 2006/2006-03-02_center of excellence_presidentail library_honoring lifes work_asking questions.gif
title: Center of Excellence Is Boss's Library

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've been asked to design and build our Center of Excellence.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Which, as I understand it, is like a presidential library honoring my life's work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In time, people learn to stop asking me questions.

setting: Office meeting room with a presentation
situation: A pointy-haired manager type, standing beside a picture of a grand building, announces he has been asked to design and build the company's Center of Excellence. He explains that he sees it as a presidential library honoring his own life's work. A group of coworkers listening in a meeting looks on as he adds that people eventually stop asking him questions.
punchline: The manager treats the Center of Excellence as a monument to himself, and his closing remark implies that his coworkers give up on questioning him because his answers are never useful.
summary: A manager recasts a corporate excellence initiative as a personal monument and notes that his audience soon learns not to challenge him.

title: Space Heater Ban Loophole Uranus Joke

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Rep
transcript.text: Company policy says that space heaters are not allowed in cubicles.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: My heater doesn't heat space. It heats the air in my cubicle. That's okay, right?

transcript.speaker: Human Resources Rep
transcript.text: Why would anyone heat "space"?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: It keeps Uranus warm.

situation: At a meeting, a company representative reads out the policy that space heaters are banned in cubicles. Tina argues that her heater only warms the air in her cubicle, not space. When the rep asks why anyone would heat space, she answers with a crude pun.
punchline: Tina's deadpan reply that heating space keeps Uranus warm is a schoolyard 'your anus' pun that she delivers to mock the policy's silly wording.
summary: A woman uses a literal reading of a heater ban to question the rule, then slips in a juvenile planet pun when pressed.

title: Pop-Up Windows Blamed for Zero Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I tried to work, but pop-up messages kept telling me to update my computer's software.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I tried closing the pop-up windows, but they just kept coming back. There were too many of them!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you upgrade your software?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Great. I see whose side you're on.

situation: At a meeting, Wally explains that he got no work done all week because software update pop-ups kept appearing. He says he tried closing them but they kept returning. The Boss asks the obvious question of whether he simply upgraded the software, and Wally takes offense.
punchline: Wally's excuse for not working collapses when the Boss suggests the simple fix, and Wally reacts as if being asked to solve the problem is taking the pop-ups' side.
summary: A lazy employee blames nagging update prompts for a week of lost productivity and bristles when his manager suggests the obvious solution.

title: Garbage Man Consoles Unemployed Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now that I'm unemployed, I don't feel like a valuable member of society.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Consider this bag of garbage. It too is unemployed and yet it is worthy of love.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't love it.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: That's too bad because no one else will date you now.

setting: Outdoors on a street next to a trash can
situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man that being unemployed makes him feel worthless. The garbage man holds up a bag of trash and argues that it is unemployed yet still lovable. When Dilbert says he doesn't love the garbage, the garbage man points out that Dilbert's unemployment has made him undateable.
punchline: The garbage man's attempt at comfort turns into an insult, implying Dilbert is now as unwanted as trash and that his only romantic prospect is a bag of garbage.
summary: A sanitation worker tries to cheer up a jobless Dilbert with a trash-bag analogy, then undercuts it by saying his dating prospects have vanished.

title: Alice Knocks Out Marketing Guy

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: There's a little thing I like to do before any meeting with a marketing guy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BONK!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This way there's more congruence between the things you say and the way you look.

situation: Alice sits at a conference table across from a marketing guy and says she has a routine before meeting with marketing people. She punches him on the head, knocking him unconscious onto the table. She then explains that his dazed, out-of-it appearance now matches what he says.
punchline: Alice's violent 'routine' is justified as making a marketing guy look as brainless as the things he says.
summary: Before meeting a marketing person, Alice clobbers him so his dazed look fits his nonsense.

title: Trading Patents for Old Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If your lawyers are going to claim all of my patents, I demand my old job back.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

summary: After bargaining with the HR cat to get his former position back in exchange for his inventions, Dilbert cheerfully settles into a bland cubicle.

transcript.text: What meeting?

transcript.text: The budget meeting that you told me to schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You never told me when it was.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I sent you an e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, obviously you chose an uninteresting subject line.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Otherwise I would have opened it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a bad e-mail sender.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I also told you in person.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Boringly?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he missed the budget meeting that the Boss ordered him to schedule. The Boss claims he was never told when it was, and when Dilbert points to the e-mail he sent, the Boss blames Dilbert for writing a dull subject line so that he never opened it. Dilbert adds that he also told him in person, and the Boss asks if he did it boringly.
punchline: The Boss refuses all responsibility for missing the meeting, blaming Dilbert's boring communication style whether the message came by e-mail or face to face.
summary: A manager who skipped a meeting insists the real problem is that his employee is too dull to catch his attention, however the message is delivered.

title: Marketing Degree Ventriloquist Accusation

setting: Conference table in an office meeting or interview
situation: A woman with big curly hair tells the man across the table she is making an exception to her rule against judging by looks, predicting they will butt heads. The man, whose hair is shaped like a pair of buttocks, quietly states that he has a degree in marketing. She then asks why his lips aren't moving, implying his butt-shaped head is what is talking.
punchline: Because his head looks like a butt, the woman suggests the words about his marketing degree are coming out of it, insulting both his looks and his profession.
summary: A woman sizes up a man whose head resembles a backside and ends up implying that he is literally talking out of it.

summary: To get around laws against asking a candidate's age, the HR director has an interviewer wait for a sudden burst of ear hair to reveal that he is too old.

punchline: Dilbert's absurd but true explanation of his dismissal gets reduced by the form-filling counselor to a blunt, insulting label because it does not fit any standard checkbox.
summary: A job seeker's bizarre account of how his own pet ended his employment leaves a bureaucratic counselor with nothing to tick except an insult.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to get user data from Ed. Dilbert explains that Ed is completely unreachable: he ignores phone calls, messages and e-mail and is never at his desk. The Boss asks if Ed at least uses the restroom, and Dilbert says they suspect Ed has modified his briefcase instead.
punchline: Ed is so determined to avoid contact that coworkers believe he has rigged his briefcase to handle his bathroom needs, so he never has to leave his hiding place.
summary: An employee who dodges every form of communication is rumored to have even engineered a way to skip restroom breaks.

title: Project Zombie Lacks Joie de Vivre

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: A certified project management zombie opens a meeting by proposing a review of assumptions, risks, and constraints. A bald coworker complains that this project management style threatens his joie de vivre, then admits the joke is that he has none to begin with.
punchline: The coworker jokes that the dull project management process endangers his joy of life, but the real joke is that his job has already drained it completely.
summary: A colleague quips that rigid project management jargon is endangering his zest for life, then deadpans that he never had any.

title: Renaming Projects to Hide Overspending

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to read out the list of thirty projects he has assigned, to see which ones the Boss still remembers giving him. Dilbert reads through the list, which includes renaming the projects so the overspending is harder to spot. The Boss says none sound familiar but they all seem critical, and Dilbert winces.
punchline: The Boss can't recall assigning any of the projects, yet the new names make them all sound critical, so Dilbert's cover for the overspending has the unwanted side effect of making everything seem urgent.
summary: A manager quizzes his employee on a pile of forgotten assignments, and the fancy new project names only make every one of them sound essential.

title: Lobbyist Starts War to Sell Lederhosen

situation: Dogbert, acting as a lobbyist and standing next to a bag of money, pitches his services to the Boss. He promises to get Switzerland to attack Elbonia, which would boost sales of the Boss's Kevlar lederhosen. When the Boss seems uneasy, Dogbert reassures him that Elbonians believe dying in battle against a neutral country earns their souls candy.
punchline: Dogbert casually justifies manufacturing a war for profit by claiming the victims would be happy about it, since they believe they get candy in the afterlife.
summary: A lobbyist dog offers to provoke an international war to boost a client's product sales, then waves away the moral concern with an absurd religious belief.

transcript.text: I'm a people person!

punchline: The man preaches face-to-face communication, but his audience is so absorbed in their handheld devices that they tune him out entirely, proving his point about the old ways is moot.
summary: A coworker extols in-person conversation while everyone around him is too busy thumbing their phones to listen.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert because Human Resources reported that he refused a random drug test. Dilbert insists he did not refuse but has a shy bladder, a medical condition affecting 7% of men, and hopes the Boss will understand. The Boss responds by suggesting the condition is really a side effect of cocaine use.
punchline: The Boss sarcastically implies that Dilbert's supposed shy bladder is actually caused by cocaine ('nose candy'), meaning he doesn't believe the excuse and suspects Dilbert is hiding drug use.
summary: An employee blames a medical condition for skipping a mandatory screening, and his manager slyly accuses him of using the very drugs the test would reveal.

title: Police Charity Sticker Grants Driving Immunity

setting: Office reception desk, then a city street
situation: The Boss hands a woman at a desk a bumper sticker showing she donates to police charities, and explains it lets her break traffic laws freely. In the last panel he is driving a yellow car on a sidewalk-side street, running over a fire hydrant that sprays water while pedestrians flee in panic.
punchline: The Boss treats a charity sticker as a license to break the law, then immediately demonstrates reckless driving, hitting a hydrant and scattering pedestrians, while praising the sticker.
summary: A manager gives a coworker a sticker he believes buys immunity from traffic rules, then gleefully drives dangerously through town to prove it.

situation: Dilbert, unemployed, sits on his couch with a laptop and optimistically starts searching for jobs online. He finds a posting that seems promising because it needs no experience. Reading further, he discovers the job requires relocating and then being ground up in a blender and sold as a condiment.
punchline: The job listing's fine print reveals that the 'no experience needed' position is literally a death trap, mocking how too-good-to-be-true job ads hide terrible conditions.
summary: A jobless engineer browsing online listings finds an attractive opening whose small print turns out to be horrifyingly fatal.

A nervous coworker asks if he can still quit before the project damages his career. Dilbert reveals that the team photo is already printed on the team's coffee cups, so the coworker is already permanently associated with the project.
punchline: Dilbert's coffee cups bearing the team photo make it literally too late to distance yourself from the doomed project, trapping the coworker in permanent association with it.
summary: A worker tries to escape a swelling project only to learn his face is already printed on the team's mugs.

He adds that they will be happy forever unless they do something incredibly stupid. The Boss asks if they are building weapons of mass destruction, and the leader asks if that is a problem.
punchline: The leader has just described doing something incredibly stupid as the only threat to prosperity, then immediately shows he is about to do it by building weapons of mass destruction, a jab at countries that squander oil wealth on weapons.
summary: A foreign leader whose land has just struck it rich with oil cheerfully admits that only reckless folly could ruin him, then reveals he's pondering exactly that.

Dilbert responds with a comparison to the time he ran out of staples and had to use glue. Wally escalates with a sniper spotting him, and Dilbert caps it with a complaint about his bad glue.
punchline: Dilbert treats his trivial office supply mishap as equivalent to a life-or-death combat story, and keeps one-upping it with the absurdly small stakes of bad glue.
summary: Two coworkers swap stories over coffee, one recounting a battlefield close call while the other insists a stationery shortage was just as harrowing.

punchline: Ratbert gleefully rubs in Dilbert's embarrassing voting choice with an absurd scandal, and Dilbert's curt reply shows he knows he has no defense.
summary: A smug pet delivers absurd scandal news about a politician to the man who elected him, then offers to chat about it.

summary: A veteran employee boasts of a gadget-free upbringing with only tree bark to play with, and brushes off a squirrel jibe as mere maturity.

punchline: Alice answers a reprimand about dismissive expressions with a fresh dismissive expression, and even Catbert concedes it's allowed.
summary: A cat from HR scolds a coworker for her scornful faces and sounds, only for her to flash a new scornful look that he approves of.

title: Wally's Caffeinated Monster Plant

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, what are you feeding the plant outside your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a mulch of coffee dregs and my shredded status reports.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: You might want to switch to decaf.

setting: Office cubicle area, then an exterior view of the office building
situation: Dilbert asks Wally what he has been feeding the plant outside his cubicle. Wally explains it is a mulch of coffee grounds and his shredded status reports. The final panel shows a gigantic tree with grasping branches that has burst out of the top of the office building and is wrapping around it.
punchline: Wally's caffeine-laden fertilizer has turned the plant into a giant, rampaging tree that is swallowing the building, so he should switch to decaf.
summary: A coworker's odd homemade fertilizer has grown an office plant into a monstrous tree engulfing the whole building.

title: Alice's Body Language Betrays Her

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm sending you to a communication class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I've noticed that your words often say one thing while your body language says another.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frankly, it's creepy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Thank you. I appreciate the useful feedback.

situation: The Boss tells Alice she must attend a communication class because her words and body language don't match. He calls the mismatch creepy, and Alice thanks him for the feedback while visibly clenching her teeth in anger.
punchline: Alice demonstrates the exact problem the Boss describes: her polite words say 'thank you' while her snarling face and clenched teeth show she is furious.
summary: A manager criticizes an employee for saying one thing while her face says another, and she proves his point by thanking him through gritted teeth.

title: Catbert Enforces Cell Phone Ban

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah blah blah

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Seriously. Don't make me use the spoon.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Blah blah blah

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry it had to come to this.

situation: During a meeting, a coworker keeps talking on his cell phone while Dilbert looks on. A figure in a red devil costume holding a giant spoon (the devil outfit is used for the 'evil' enforcer role) orders him to hang up with a mild threat. When the coworker ignores him, the devil beats him with the spoon, leaving him sprawled across the table.
punchline: The devil's threats are comically mild ('I darn you to heck'), yet he still resorts to violence with a giant spoon, and then apologizes politely for it.
summary: A costumed devil politely threatens a rude phone talker with a giant spoon, then beats him senseless and apologizes.

title: Reality Blows Up the Spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens if I add the lies from Marketing to my boss's assumptions ... then factor in some reality?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: KABOOM!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid reality.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer wondering what will happen if he combines Marketing's lies with his boss's assumptions and then adds real data to the mix. His cubicle explodes with a loud KABOOM while the boss watches from a nearby cubicle. Dilbert is left singed and smoking, blaming reality.
punchline: Realistic data clashing with the fantasy numbers from Marketing and management literally blows up the project, and Dilbert blames reality rather than the lies.
summary: An engineer's attempt to reconcile fantasy projections with real figures ends in a literal explosion at his desk.

title: Budget Literally Written in Stone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're supposed to have our budget approved by Tuesday but that's not written in stone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes it is. I have it right here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was kind of lucky because this is the only one I brought to the meeting.

situation: The Boss tells a meeting that the budget approval deadline is not written in stone. A coworker takes this literally and produces an actual stone tablet with the budget deadline carved on it. He then remarks that he was lucky to have brought it, since it was the only one with him.
punchline: A coworker takes the idiom 'not written in stone' literally and produces a real stone tablet, then casually admits it was just luck that he had that one with him.
summary: A manager's figure of speech about a flexible deadline is answered by a staffer holding up a carved slab proving it is, in fact, set in stone.

title: Garage Startup Meets Homeowner Rules

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start a high tech company in the garage.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some of the most successful companies started in garages. It must help somehow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if those other guys had homeowner rules about not parking in the driveway.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room and garage
situation: Dilbert announces he will start a high tech company in his garage, reasoning that famous companies began in garages. He then sits in his car with a laptop, since he has to park in the garage to avoid breaking homeowner rules, and wonders how the famous garage startups handled the same restriction.
punchline: Dilbert follows the garage-startup legend literally, but his cramped setup, working from inside a parked car, shows how little the myth fits suburban reality.
summary: A would-be entrepreneur copies the famous garage-startup formula, only to find his car and the neighborhood rules getting in the way.

title: Lawyerpult Launches Patent Attorney

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got funding to start my own search engine company! Nothing can stop me now!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fire the lawyerpult.

transcript.text: I'd like to talk to you about your patent.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with a cutaway to Dogbert's lair
situation: Dilbert, holding a bag of money, announces that he has funding to start his own search engine company. Meanwhile, Dogbert orders his lawyerpult fired, and a lawyer is catapulted into Dilbert's home, crashing in a heap of papers and debris. The lawyer wants to discuss Dilbert's patent.
punchline: Any new tech venture will instantly be hit by patent lawyers, so Dilbert's confidence that nothing can stop him is shattered by a literally flying attorney.
summary: A confident new entrepreneur is promptly slammed by a lawyer hurled through his wall by a catapult.

title: Dogbert's Useless Retirement Seminar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't tell anyone that you retired. Just keep coming to work and collecting money for the weekly lottery pool. Then spend it on food.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want my dollar back.

setting: A seminar room where Dogbert presents from a stool
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, opens his retirement planning seminar. His entire advice is to secretly keep working and pocket the weekly lottery pool money to spend on food. Dilbert, sitting among the unimpressed attendees, demands a refund of his dollar.
punchline: Dogbert's retirement advice is so absurd and dishonest that the audience, Dilbert included, feels cheated and wants a refund of the dollar admission.
summary: A talking dog's seminar on securing your future turns out to be a scheme to skim lottery pool cash, leaving his audience asking for a refund.

transcript.speaker: Sound

situation: A vendor salesman brings his technical expert so the two geeks can talk shop while he and the saleswoman make out at the table. Dilbert and the technical salesman sit awkwardly discussing web service protocols next to the passionately kissing pair. Dilbert eventually wonders aloud if they are in the wrong jobs, and the other nerd refuses to kiss him.
punchline: The nerds are stuck doing the dull technical talk while the salespeople get the fun, and Dilbert's hopeful musing about being in the wrong jobs is shot down when his counterpart makes clear he wants no romantic involvement.
summary: Two engineers trade jargon at a meeting table while their sales counterparts get romantic beside them, leaving the geeks feeling left out.

transcript.text: How would I know you gave me a good one? Peer reviews are anonymous.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (silent panel)

situation: A coworker approaches Dilbert while both hold coffee mugs and warns that his 360 degree review could hurt his raise. He then offers to guarantee a positive review in exchange for half the value of the raise. Dilbert points out that anonymous reviews would make it impossible to verify the coworker kept his end of the deal.

summary: A scheming colleague tries to extort money in exchange for a glowing evaluation, then acts hurt when his target doubts him.

title: Six Sigma: New to Us

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company has decided to try something new.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Six Sigma

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: New? Six Sigma was developed in the 80s.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's new to us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't we jump on a fad that hasn't already been widely discredited?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way the false hope might sustain us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's nothing wrong with Six Sigma. All it does is reduce defects!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... Fortune magazine says... blah, blah... most companies that used Six Sigma have trailed the S&P 500.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. What did I miss while I was innovating?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces the company will adopt Six Sigma as something new. Dilbert points out it dates from the 1980s and has been discredited, and the Boss admits the point is false hope. Dilbert then cites a Fortune magazine finding that most Six Sigma companies have underperformed the market.
punchline: Management adopts an old, discredited fad and calls it new because it's new to them, while the one employee who shows up late claims he was busy innovating.
summary: A boss rolls out a decades-old management fad as the company's latest innovation, and his team calmly dismantles it with facts.

title: Employee of the Month by Alphabet

transcript.text: And we've moved to an alphabetical system for awarding "Employee of the Month." This is your month.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Stupid alphabet.

situation: The Boss tells a bald, bespectacled employee that he is being kept on only because the employee's lawyer threatened to sue over a firing for gross incompetence. He then adds that Employee of the Month is now awarded alphabetically, so it is this employee's turn. The employee walks away muttering in a thought bubble.
punchline: The employee, who is admittedly grossly incompetent, is getting an honor he clearly hasn't earned purely because of his name's place in the alphabet, and he grumbles about the arbitrary system rather than his own failings.
summary: A manager reluctantly retains a legally protected, incompetent worker and then hands him a recognition award that is based purely on alphabetical order.

title: Ask Legal Again Until Yes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the spirit!

situation: Dilbert informs the Boss that the legal department has declared his plan illegal. The Boss simply tells him to ask again in the hope they will change their minds. Dilbert sarcastically replies that he will do so after panning for gold in the water fountain, and the oblivious Boss praises his attitude.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic comparison of the Boss's request to an impossible task goes over the Boss's head, and he mistakes it for enthusiasm.
summary: Told that his scheme breaks the law, a manager just orders a re-ask, and his employee's sarcastic refusal is mistaken for eager cooperation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you lend me some money so I can open my own business?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, but I know some people on a barge who would.

Dogbert, sitting on the couch, boasts that he made a billion dollars by selling a garbage barge as oceanfront real estate. summary: After hearing about his friend's scrapped project, a scheming dog brags about swindling buyers with a trash barge and then redirects the request for startup cash to those same victims.

The Boss, holding up his hand, asks about fingernails, and the employee is baffled about why anyone would lick those.
punchline: The company's absurd fix for a product flaw is to tell customers to lick it off, and the Boss's follow-up question reveals he is only worried about an even stranger edge case, which the employee finds the more bizarre part.
summary: A team settles on telling customers to lick sticker residue off products, and the boss's only concern is about fingernails.

title: Wally Converts Vacation Into Sick Days

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I'm taking tomorrow as a sick day too. I still have eight bags left.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the Boss he wants to retroactively change a vacation day into a sick day because he got a stomachache. He admits the stomachache came from eating too many potato chips, then announces he will take tomorrow off sick too since he still has eight bags left to eat.
punchline: Wally openly admits he is deliberately making himself sick with junk food and plans to keep doing it, treating sick days as extra time off while the Boss does nothing about it.
summary: Wally cheerfully reveals that overeating snacks gave him a stomachache and that he intends to get sick again tomorrow to finish his supply.

title: Machines Have Taken Over Offices

transcript.text: The machines have taken over. Your job is to provide them with electricity.

transcript.text: And do you think those electronic voting machines care about your opinion?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, points out to Dilbert that the company's network equipment enjoys better working conditions than the human staff. He claims the machines have taken over and that Dilbert exists only to power them. He ends by noting that electronic voting machines don't care what Dilbert thinks, leaving Dilbert visibly distressed and gritting his teeth.
punchline: Dogbert escalates a joke about pampered servers into a paranoid warning that machines now rule us, capping it with a jab that electronic voting machines ignore human opinion.
summary: A dog tells his coworker that computers have better offices than people and that even voting machines have no interest in what he thinks.

Steve protests that as a former combat leader, he deserves better than trivial assignments. The boss responds by piling on another errand: buying a gift at the convenience store.
punchline: Steve's complaint about being overqualified for menial tasks backfires, as the boss just adds an even more trivial errand, showing he ignores employees' skills and dignity.
summary: A boss assigns his subordinate a petty gift-buying errand, and when the man objects that he once led troops in battle, he is simply given more chores.

punchline: Alice treats the buzzword-spouting project manager as a literal zombie and kills him, justified by the mind-numbing three-hour meeting she has just sat through.
summary: A jargon-spewing project manager gets treated like the undead and is dispatched by a sword-wielding coworker who has had enough of meetings.

transcript.text: Reduce employee turnover... check.

situation: The Boss addresses employees seated around a conference table, admitting that their jobs are awful and underpaid. He then tells them that every other company is just as bad. In a thought bubble, he ticks 'reduce employee turnover' off his to-do list.
punchline: The Boss thinks that convincing employees there is nowhere better to go counts as a successful retention strategy, instead of actually improving pay or conditions.
summary: A manager tries to keep his staff from quitting by assuring them that all employers are equally terrible.

situation: Dilbert has a plunger stuck to his back labeled "Blame", put there by his boss. situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, gives a retirement planning seminar and presents a plan to spend retirement on the golf course. summary: A seminar leader sells his audience on a grim retirement of carrying golf bags and living underground in sand traps.
