title: Satan's Vendor Pitches Benefits

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Satan's Vendor

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: You'll have many benefits after our technology is irrevocably implemented in your network,

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: For example, when one of our products stops working, we'll blame another vendor within 24 hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have free T-shirts?

transcript.speaker: Satan's Vendor
transcript.text: Yes, they're made of the finest allergens.

setting: Conference room or office meeting table
situation: A devil-horned vendor representing Satan pitches his company's technology to The Boss, promising that once it is irrevocably installed, any failure will be blamed on another vendor within a day. The Boss ignores the red flags and only asks about free T-shirts, and the vendor cheerfully offers shirts made of allergens.
punchline: The vendor's pitch is an openly hellish description of lock-in and blame-shifting, yet the boss only cares about free swag, which turns out to be just as nasty.
summary: A demonic salesman cheerfully lists the sinister perks of his product while the customer only wants free shirts.

title: Dogbert Lobbies Congress for Millions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Lobbyist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a million dollars I can have the government include your industrial waste in the recommended food pyramid.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For another million I'll have Congress authorize huge tax breaks for soulless, BlackBerry-using weasels with coffee breath.

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: I just want to hug you!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's another million.

situation: Dogbert, working as a lobbyist, sits at a conference table with corporate clients. He offers to buy government favors, first putting industrial waste in the food pyramid, then tax breaks for soulless executives. When a delighted client says he wants to hug him, Dogbert says that will cost another million.
punchline: Dogbert charges a million dollars for everything, even a hug, and his offers show how lobbying buys absurd and harmful government favors.
summary: A canine lobbyist prices corrupt political favors in million-dollar increments and even bills a grateful client for affection.

title: Shake Off Desert Abandonment

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You said it was a team-building exercise and you left me in the middle of the desert to die!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shake it off.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You wouldn't think that would work, but it does!

situation: A disheveled, tattered employee storms into the boss's office to complain that a so-called team-building exercise left him stranded in the desert to die. The boss dismisses the complaint with a bored 'Shake it off.' In the last panel the employee, now standing with a coffee mug beside Wally, is surprised to find that the advice actually worked.
punchline: The boss's dismissive, clichéd advice to 'shake it off' is absurdly applied to near-death abandonment, and the joke is that the employee cheerfully admits it somehow works.
summary: After being abandoned in the wilderness during a dubious company exercise, a worker gets brushed off by his boss and discovers the brush-off oddly cures him.

title: Dull Cubicle Dulls the Brain

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just saw a study that says the dull appearance of my cubicle is probably inhibiting the growth of neurons in my brain!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try sitting there for a few more hours and then tell me if you feel any different.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I can't remember what I was complaining about.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and an adjacent desk in the office
situation: Dilbert, holding a phone, complains that a study says his drab cubicle is stunting his brain's neuron growth. Catbert, sitting on a desk, suggests he stay in the cubicle a few more hours and see if he feels different. In the last panel Dilbert sits in the cubicle, thought bubble showing he has forgotten what he was complaining about.
punchline: Catbert's suggestion proves the study's point, as Dilbert's brain has been so dulled by his cubicle that he forgets his own complaint.
summary: A worker worried that his bland workspace is harming his brain gets a wicked suggestion that quickly demonstrates the problem.

title: Budget Troll Eats Prototype Planner

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And then we'll build a second prototype and...

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: It's not in the budget!

transcript.speaker: Troll
transcript.text: Oh, suddenly it's my fault for caring about the budget.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: An employee is presenting plans to Dilbert and a green troll from finance, proposing a second prototype. The troll roars that it isn't in the budget and swallows the employee. Afterward the troll sits there with the victim's phone, sulking that it's being blamed for caring about the budget.
punchline: The finance troll literally devours the employee for proposing something unbudgeted, then plays the victim by complaining that it is unfairly blamed for doing its job.
summary: A budget-obsessed troll gobbles up a colleague who suggests extra prototyping, then whines about being unfairly criticized.

title: Land of Unrealistic Business Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Land of Unrealistic Business Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Suddenly I feel as if anything is possible.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Gold (Take some)

transcript.speaker: Consumers
transcript.text: Hello! We're the consumers who have extraordinarily bad judgment!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need more than three of you.

transcript.speaker: Consumer
transcript.text: The hole's a thousand miles deep. The others thought it would be a good idea to come early.

transcript.speaker: Consumers
transcript.text: Ow! Ow!

setting: A fantasy landscape called the Land of Unrealistic Business Assumptions, with green hills, a money tree and free gold
situation: Dilbert wanders through a whimsical land where anything seems possible, accompanied by a small white creature. He meets a group of consumers sitting in a hole who announce they have extraordinarily bad judgment. Dilbert says he needs more than three of them, and they explain the hole is a thousand miles deep and the others came early and fell in.
punchline: Business plans often assume a limitless supply of consumers with terrible judgment who will buy anything, and the strip mocks that fantasy by showing them literally falling into a bottomless hole.
summary: In a fairy-tale realm of wishful corporate thinking, Dilbert finds the gullible customers every flawed business plan depends on, quite literally waiting in a pit.

file: 2006/2006-01-02_suggestions_audience_readers_resist perl pressure_unfunny comic_connect to network_email_note from author.gif
title: Author Draws Reader-Requested Unfunny Comic

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Note from the author

transcript.speaker: Scott Adams
transcript.text: Approximately one gazillion people have suggested I draw a comic based on the following idea.

transcript.speaker: Scott Adams
transcript.text: As you will see, this idea is not funny. But I give it to you anyway because I can't resist peer pressure.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Unfunny comic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you can't connect to the network, send a trouble report by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Scott Adams
transcript.text: Happy?

setting: Author's drawing desk, then an office with a computer
situation: The cartoonist appears as himself at his desk and explains that countless readers have urged him to draw a particular comic idea. He admits it isn't funny but draws it anyway. The comic shows the Boss telling an employee to email a trouble report when the network is down, and the author peeks in and asks 'Happy?'
punchline: The suggested joke, telling someone with no network access to report the problem by email, is a self-evident piece of illogical IT advice, and the author deliberately presents it as unfunny to mock the readers who insisted on it.
summary: The cartoonist reluctantly yields to reader demand and draws a deliberately flat gag about reporting a dead network by email.

title: Contract Worker Complains, Wally Unmoved

transcript.speaker: Contract Employee
transcript.text: It's stressful to be a contract employee. I only get paid for the hours I work.

transcript.speaker: Contract Employee
transcript.text: I can't enjoy my time off because it feels as if it costs me a fortune!

transcript.speaker: Contract Employee
transcript.text: Do you know what I mean?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yeah, I had a feeling once.

situation: A contract employee holding a folder complains to Wally that he only gets paid for hours worked, so time off feels expensive. Wally stands there with his coffee mug, and when asked if he understands, he gives a deadpan reply.
punchline: Wally sarcastically implies he is so emotionally numb and disengaged that he has only ever experienced a feeling once, showing he has zero sympathy or empathy for the complaint.
summary: A worried freelancer vents about unpaid days off to Wally, who responds with a flat, apathetic quip.

file: 2006/2006-04-14_the contractor_easy to get rid of_paperwork_point finger_firing finger.gif
title: Boss Threatens Contractor With Firing Finger

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No pressure, but do you have any idea how easy it would be to get rid of you?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There isn't even any paperwork. I just point my finger and you're history.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here comes the firing finger. Oooh... watch out!

situation: The Boss stands over a contractor at his desk and cheerfully reminds him that contractors can be dismissed with no paperwork at all. He demonstrates by pointing his finger at the contractor in a mock-menacing way. The contractor, wearing a carrot-like object on a propeller-style headband, sits calmly at his computer throughout.
punchline: The Boss revels in the fact that firing a contractor is so effortless that a mere pointed finger does the job, delivering a threat that is both casual and gleeful.
summary: A manager taunts a temp worker by gleefully demonstrating how a mere finger point can end his employment without any red tape.

title: Fire Warden Rolls On Fire

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you're my new fire warden for the floor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If there's a fire, your job is to roll around on it until it's out.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What if the whole floor is on fire?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one will be timing you.

situation: The Boss appoints Asok as the floor's fire warden and explains the duty is to roll around on any fire until it goes out. Asok asks what happens if the entire floor is burning, and the Boss reassuringly says no one will time him.
punchline: The Boss is cheerfully unconcerned that his fire safety plan means Asok burning himself, and his only reassurance about an impossible task is that there will be no deadline.
summary: A manager assigns an underling a ludicrously dangerous firefighting method and answers his worry about a larger blaze with a useless perk.

title: Elbonian Factory Translation Mix-Up

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: My Elbonian factory can manufacture your product for pennies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there any downside?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Minor translation issues.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: They either said "plastic" or "the spleen of a pig-footed bandicoot."

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We don't have any plastic.

setting: Boss's office, then an Elbonian factory
situation: An Elbonian factory owner pitches The Boss on manufacturing his product for pennies. When The Boss asks about downsides, the Elbonian downplays them as minor translation issues. At the factory, workers explain that the order for plastic may have been misread as a request for pig-footed bandicoot spleens, and they have no plastic anyway.
punchline: The 'minor translation issues' of cheap outsourcing turn out to be so severe that the product is being made from animal spleens instead of plastic.
summary: A bargain overseas manufacturing deal goes sideways when a language barrier turns a materials order into a pile of exotic animal organs.

title: Giving the MP3 Player Lips

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Marketing Guru

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your MP3 player is large and scary, but I can fix that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: All it needs is a set of Angelina Jolie lips and everyone will love it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Six months later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We must never speak of this.

setting: Engineering lab or office with a clunky prototype MP3 player
situation: Dogbert, posing as a marketing guru, tells engineers that their large, scary-looking MP3 player prototype just needs a pair of Angelina Jolie lips to be loved by everyone. Six months later, the robot-like device has been fitted with full red lips, and Dilbert, holding it, says they must never speak of it again.
punchline: The marketing guru's absurd advice was actually followed, producing a creepy lipped device so embarrassing that everyone wants to pretend it never happened.
summary: A consultant's ridiculous cosmetic fix for an ugly gadget gets implemented and leaves the team mortified.

title: Topper's Absurd War Story

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Return of Topper

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then we started taking RPG fire from a rooftop.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: I strangled 900 insurgents with my bare hands.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That seems unlikely.

transcript.speaker: Topper
transcript.text: That's what the first 600 said.

situation: Three coworkers sit at a table swapping war stories. One describes coming under RPG fire from a rooftop, and Topper, the one-upper, dismisses it and claims he strangled 900 insurgents bare-handed. When a coworker doubts him, Topper replies with a grim joke about his victims.
punchline: Topper's boast is so exaggerated that his answer to the skeptic implies the first 600 insurgents also doubted him right up until he strangled them.
summary: A braggart who must outdo everyone's tales claims a ridiculous body count and turns a doubter's skepticism into a menacing quip.

title: Wedding Attire Question Ends In Punching

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What are you going to wear to Ted's wedding?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whatever comes up in the rotation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then she shrieked some nonsense about spending six months shopping for shoes and started to punch me.

situation: Alice asks Dilbert what he will wear to Ted's wedding, and he casually says he'll wear whatever clothes come up in his regular rotation. In the last panel Dilbert tells Dogbert that Alice shrieked about spending six months shopping for shoes and then began punching him.
punchline: Dilbert's utter lack of concern about wedding attire, compared with Alice's months of careful preparation, provokes a violent reaction he finds baffling.
summary: A man's indifferent clothing plan collides with a co-worker's obsessive wedding preparations, and he ends up getting hit.

title: Wisdom From Bad Analogies

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I worry that all of my wisdom is derived from bad analogies.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, sometimes a good wine has to age before it is perfect.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So... I'll get smarter over time?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To the extent that you are like a grape.

setting: Dogbert's home, with Dogbert lounging on a yellow cushion
situation: Ratbert confides to Dogbert that he fears all his wisdom comes from bad analogies. Dogbert responds with a wine-aging analogy, and when Ratbert hopefully concludes he will grow smarter with time, Dogbert undercuts him by saying that only applies if Ratbert is like a grape.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance is itself a bad analogy, and he then dismisses Ratbert's hope by pointing out Ratbert is not actually a grape, so the comfort is meaningless.
summary: A worried rat is soothed by a dog's flawed winemaking metaphor that falls apart the moment it is applied to him.

title: Telecommuting Confession Falls Flat

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I said I was telecommuting but I really just stayed home and watched TV in my pajamas.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll never know how the TV got into my pajamas. Ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, you had to be there.

situation: Wally cheerfully admits to his coworkers that his week of 'telecommuting' was really just staying home watching TV in his pajamas. He follows up with a garbled joke about the TV getting into his pajamas, and the group stares at him in silence. Dilbert deadpans that you had to be there.
punchline: Wally's botched joke is so unfunny that Dilbert sarcastically uses the 'you had to be there' excuse, implying it wouldn't have been funny even in person.
summary: A slacker coworker confesses to goofing off at home, then bombs with a muddled joke that draws blank stares and a dry brush-off.

title: Because I Can: Plunger of Blame

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you attach the plunger of blame to me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The short answer is "because I can."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the long answer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I-I-I-I ca-a-a-n.

situation: Dilbert has a plunger labeled "Blame" stuck to his chest and asks his boss why it was put there. The boss replies that the short answer is "because I can." When Dilbert asks for the long answer, the boss just repeats the same reason in a drawn-out, sing-song way.
punchline: The boss has no real justification for blaming Dilbert, and the "long answer" is just the same power-trip excuse stretched out, showing he blames people simply because he has the authority to.
summary: A boss who has stuck a blame-labeled plunger on an employee admits he did it purely because he has the power, and stretching out the explanation adds nothing.

title: Dead Coworker, Paperwork Avoidance

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I just saw Mort in his cubicle. I think he's... dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I noticed that yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And you didn't say anything?!?! Were you thinking he's just as dead tomorrow and someone else can do the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wait. That's pretty good thinking...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was proud of it.

situation: Alice tells Dilbert she has just found their coworker Mort dead in his cubicle. Dilbert calmly says he noticed it the day before and kept quiet. When Alice angrily accuses him of hoping someone else would handle the paperwork, she reconsiders and admits it was clever, and Dilbert says he was proud of it.
punchline: Dilbert's callous plan to leave a dead coworker undiscovered just to dodge paperwork is so in tune with office self-interest that even Alice grudgingly approves.
summary: A worker's discovery of a deceased colleague reveals that a coworker deliberately stayed silent to avoid the bureaucratic hassle that follows.

title: Catbert Loses Cuteness Contest to Baby

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your powers of cuteness are formidable indeed, but can you do...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This?

transcript.speaker: Baby
transcript.text: Oh crud. You win. Why do I even try?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, confronts a baby in a diaper and concedes that the baby is formidably cute, then challenges him to match a move. Catbert flops onto his back with his legs in the air. The baby, impressed by the display, admits defeat.
punchline: Even a baby's natural cuteness cannot compete with Catbert simply rolling over helplessly, a classic cat move, so the baby gives up.
summary: A cat and a baby face off in a contest of cuteness, and the cat wins by flopping onto his back.

title: Allen Didn't Balance, Became CEO

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's seminar on work-life balance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Allen. He didn't balance his work and personal lives.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Allen did nothing but work, work, work. And now look at him.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: I'm the one who tried to balance everything. That's Allen. He's a %$*&! CEO now!

setting: A seminar room on work-life balance
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool, gives a seminar on work-life balance and points to an elderly man named Allen as a cautionary example of someone who only worked. Allen, leaning on a cane, then corrects him: he is the one who tried to balance everything, and the well-dressed man in the red suit nearby is the real Allen, who is now a CEO.
punchline: The workaholic who sacrificed everything for his job became a wealthy CEO while the person who balanced work and life ended up frail and worse off, undermining the premise of the seminar.
summary: A seminar speaker's warning about overworking backfires when the supposed bad example turns out to be a successful executive and the balanced person is the one who suffered.

title: Estimating Skill Versus Wally's Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project came in 10% over budget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it came in at exactly what I estimated.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You cut my budget by 10% because you wanted to feel like a leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume you'll give me a huge raise to reward my excellent estimating ability.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why can't you be like Wally? His project budget was $10,000,000 and he only spent $147.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you're so smart, explain that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's hard to explain without using the phrase "you gullible toad."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm next. What kind of mood is he in?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so good.

setting: The Boss's office during an annual review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert in his annual review that his project ran 10% over budget. Dilbert points out that it matched his original estimate and that the boss had arbitrarily cut the budget. The boss then holds up Wally's project as a model, claiming Wally spent only $147 of a $10,000,000 budget.
punchline: Dilbert implies that Wally's tiny spending can only be explained by the boss being a gullible fool who believed Wally's claims, and the insult leaves the boss in a foul mood for the next reviewee.
summary: A manager blames an employee for an overrun caused by his own budget cut, then praises a slacker's suspiciously cheap project as the ideal.

title: Recycling Zealot Sticks Paper on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Recycling Zealot
transcript.text: Gaaa! You put your gum on this recyclable waste material!!!

transcript.speaker: Recycling Zealot
transcript.text: How do you like it in your hair? Huh? Not so funny now is it, tree-killer!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The worst part is that I envy him for being passionate about his job.

situation: An agitated coworker who collects recyclable waste storms up to Dilbert, furious that gum was stuck on a piece of recyclable paper. He retaliates by slapping the gum-covered paper onto Dilbert's head. Afterward, Dilbert, with the paper still stuck to his hair, tells a bald coworker that what bothers him most is envying the man's passion.
punchline: Dilbert is so bored and disengaged at work that he envies even a fanatical, assaulting recycling zealot simply because the man cares about his job.
summary: After being attacked with a gum-covered sheet of paper, a weary engineer admits he is jealous of his attacker's zeal for work.

title: Programmers Don't Need the Specs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do I need to give the specs to the programmers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't need them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? Is it because they already know what to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes. Exactly. They know how to do that part.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, now I have a difficult choice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could call the programmers, prove you wrong, and suffer the consequences in a thousand subtle ways. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or I could do nothing and wait to get hosed for not providing the specs on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Geez. You complain when I don't give you choices too.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss when he should give the specifications to the programmers, and the boss says the programmers don't need them because they already know what to do. Dilbert realizes he is stuck choosing between contradicting the boss and suffering retaliation, or doing nothing and being blamed for missing the specs. The boss responds by complaining that Dilbert gripes even when given choices.
punchline: The boss thinks he is being generous by offering Dilbert two choices, when both are lose-lose options created by the boss's own bad instructions.
summary: A manager gives his engineer a no-win dilemma and then acts offended that the engineer isn't grateful for having options.

title: Free Engineering Solution During Interview

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We need someone who can solve the biggest engineering problem we have ever encountered.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just distribute the power supply across both functions and double the fan size.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. If I need anything else, I'll interview you again.

situation: Dilbert is interviewing for a job, and the interviewer hands him a diagram of their biggest engineering problem. Dilbert studies it and immediately offers a practical fix. The interviewer thanks him for the free solution and says he will just interview him again if he needs more help.
punchline: The company isn't hiring anyone at all; it is using job interviews as a way to extract free engineering consulting.
summary: A company poses its toughest technical problem to a job candidate, gets the answer on the spot, and cheerfully plans to keep harvesting solutions from future interviews.

title: Boss Shoves Bad Project Onto Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no good way to assign a bad project.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FWAP!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do it!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was a liberating thought.

setting: Office doorway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss stands holding a project folder and thinks that there is no good way to assign a bad project. He then smacks the papers into an employee and shoves him out the door, shouting at him to do it. Back at his desk, the Boss calmly reflects that the thought was liberating.
punchline: Realizing there is no good way to hand off a bad project, the Boss decides to do it in the worst way possible, treating that as a liberating excuse to stop caring about doing it decently.
summary: Having decided that delegating a terrible task can't be done nicely, a manager abandons all tact and simply forces it onto a subordinate.

title: Which One Is The Thimble?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you bring me up to speed before we go to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. You can't fit two gallons in a thimble no matter how fast you pour.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wait a minute... Which one of us is the thimble?

setting: Office hallway, then a conference room
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to quickly brief him on a topic before they go into a meeting. Dilbert replies that you can't pour two gallons into a thimble however fast you pour. In the conference room, the Boss slowly realizes he might be the thimble.
punchline: Dilbert's metaphor insults the Boss's capacity to absorb information, and the Boss only belatedly grasps that he is the one who is too small to hold it.
summary: A boss wanting a rushed briefing is told it's impossible to cram so much into so little, and then wonders who is being insulted.

title: Budget Chicken Over Infrastructure Funding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you fund the infrastructure project yet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm playing budget chicken with the Director of Operations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hoping that his department needs the infrastructure more than we do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I can bluff him into funding the project with his budget instead of mine, I win.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He'll be reprimanded for exceeding his budget and I'll get a bonus for being under mine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll use the bonus to buy a summer cabin by the lake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then I'll e-mail him pictures of my cabin and say, "I hope you're enjoying your infrastructure as much as I'm enjoying my cabin!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've reached a new low.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been thinking of firing you so I can get a fishing hat.

situation: Dilbert asks whether the Boss has funded the infrastructure project, and the Boss explains he is deliberately stalling to bluff the Director of Operations into paying for it from his own budget. The Boss plans to collect a bonus for staying under budget, buy a lake cabin, and gloat to the director by e-mail. Dilbert calls it a new low, and the Boss responds by musing about firing him to fund a fishing hat.
punchline: The Boss is so gleefully petty and self-serving that he casually considers firing Dilbert just to afford fishing gear for his cabin.
summary: A manager gambles with a rival department over who pays for needed systems so he can pocket a bonus, then jokes about sacking his employee for a fishing accessory.

title: Blaming Boss for Bigger Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't do any work this week because you gave Alice a bigger cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your favoritism had a corrosive effect on my morale, thus inhibiting my effectiveness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm optimistic that you'll do a better job of motivating me next week.

situation: Dilbert sits at a table with the Boss and Alice and explains that he got no work done all week because Alice was given a bigger cubicle. He frames this as the Boss's favoritism damaging his morale and productivity. He then calmly sips from a mug and says he hopes the Boss will motivate him better next week.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables by blaming his own lack of productivity on management's failure to motivate him, with polite corporate-speak sarcasm that shifts all responsibility onto the Boss.
summary: An employee coolly pins his week of idleness on his manager's cubicle favoritism and expects better motivation going forward.

title: Lawyerpult Claims Dilbert's Search Engine Idea

transcript.text: You thought up your search engine idea before we fired you. That means my company owns it.

transcript.speaker: Villain
transcript.text: That's why I used the Lawyerpult to hurl our attorney onto you.

transcript.speaker: Villain
transcript.text: Now I'm using the holograph device you invented. That thing is making us billions.

transcript.speaker: Attorney
transcript.text: Gaaa!!!

setting: Living room with a green couch
situation: A smug, horned-haired businessman lounges on a couch and explains that because Dilbert conceived his search engine idea while employed, his company owns it. He has used a Lawyerpult to fling an attorney onto Dilbert and Dogbert. He then reveals he is profiting from Dilbert's holograph device while the attorney flails in the air.
punchline: The villain uses a catapult to launch a lawyer at his victims to enforce intellectual property claims, literalizing how aggressively companies use legal tactics to seize employees' inventions.
summary: A ruthless ex-employer catapults a lawyer onto an inventor to enforce ownership of his ideas while getting rich off another of his inventions.

title: Too Much Coffee To Jog

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. I was behind a herd of slow walkers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I couldn't jog around them at the wide spots because my coffee cup was too full.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's all part of my can't-do approach to life.

situation: The Boss arrives late to a meeting, holding a coffee mug, and blames slow walkers in the hallway. He then admits he couldn't jog past them because his cup was too full, and sips his coffee while describing it as his can't-do approach to life. Dilbert, Alice and another attendee sit at the table listening.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully owns his defeatist attitude, turning a lame excuse for lateness into a personal philosophy of giving up at the first obstacle.
summary: A tardy manager explains that he gave up on hurrying because it might spill his coffee, proudly calling it his philosophy of never trying.

title: Desperate Venture Capitalist Begs Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay, the world's most desperate venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need a hundred billion to build an ocean city on barges.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Take my money!!! Take it, take it, take it!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do I get stock or something—

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thing?

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: How about an insincere wag?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Insincere wag!

situation: Dogbert pitches a hundred-billion-dollar plan to build an ocean city on barges to Vijay, a venture capitalist who is so desperate to invest that he frantically shoves bags of money at him. When Dogbert asks whether he gets stock in return, Vijay offers an insincere tail wag from Dogbert instead, and Dogbert obliges.
punchline: The venture capitalist is so desperate to invest that he demands nothing in return for his money, and the only thing he offers Dogbert is an insincere wag.
summary: A frantic investor throws money bags at a dog who asked for a ridiculous fortune, offering only a fake tail wag in place of equity.

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk along a trail of yellow sticky notes in a parody of the Yellow Brick Road, heading to see the Wizard of Landfill who supposedly can get Dilbert home. When they arrive, they encounter the groggy, caffeine-starved Boss mumbling about coffee. Dilbert hopes this isn't the wizard.
punchline: The great and powerful wizard who is supposed to solve Dilbert's problems might just be the clueless, zombie-like Boss, who can barely function without coffee.
summary: A Wizard of Oz spoof sends Dilbert down a sticky-note path toward an all-knowing wizard, only to find his incompetent boss muttering about coffee.

title: Patty Distorts Dilbert's Vendor Opinion

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Patty the Amplifier and Distorter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We got a proposal from a new vendor today.

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: Dilbert loves the new vendor! He thinks that anyone who disagrees is an idiot!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not what...

transcript.speaker: Patty
transcript.text: He's having an affair with the sales rep!

situation: Dilbert mentions at a meeting that a new vendor has sent in a proposal. Patty, a coworker with an ear trumpet who amplifies and distorts what she hears, repeats it to others as Dilbert loving the vendor and calling dissenters idiots. Each retelling grows more exaggerated, ending with a claim that Dilbert is having an affair with the sales rep.
punchline: A neutral statement about a vendor proposal gets escalated by the office gossip into an absurd and scandalous rumor within seconds.
summary: A harmless announcement about a vendor proposal is blown up by an office gossip into wild falsehoods.

title: Simple Solution Costs Coworker His Life

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been trying for six months to solve this engineering problem. It might be impossible.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Just turn it sideways and it will fit perfectly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... Now I have to kill you.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells a seated coworker that he has spent six months on an engineering problem that might be impossible. The coworker casually suggests turning the part sideways so it will fit. Dilbert, humiliated by how easy the answer was, announces he now has to kill him.
punchline: Being handed an obvious solution after half a year of struggle is so embarrassing that Dilbert decides the witness must be eliminated.
summary: A long-suffering engineer's months of effort are undone by a bystander's offhand tip, prompting a darkly comic threat.

title: Loud Howard Blurts Out Secret Reorg

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Loud Howard returns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Loud Howard, I'm planning a reorg and I need you to...

transcript.speaker: Loud Howard
transcript.text: A reorg?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...keep it to yourself.

transcript.speaker: Loud Howard
transcript.text: Can do!

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: The Boss tells Loud Howard he is planning a reorganization and begins to ask him for something. Loud Howard shouts 'A reorg?' before the Boss can finish, blowing the Boss's tie sideways. The Boss then asks him to keep it to himself, and Loud Howard cheerfully shouts 'Can do!' at full volume.
punchline: The Boss asks the one employee who can't speak quietly to keep a secret, and Loud Howard loudly agrees, so the secret is clearly not going to stay secret.
summary: A manager entrusts confidential restructuring plans to a coworker whose voice makes secrecy impossible.

title: Wally Agrees to Nothing Useful

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Wally, you've agreed to pull together all of the technical specifications by Thursday, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes, I'll look into pulling that stuff together.

transcript.speaker: Bob

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I agree.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Are you agreeing that I need it or agreeing to do it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You will have the list of who has the technical specifications by Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I don't need the list of who has them. I need the specifications!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I agree.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Forget it! I'll get them myself!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you help Bob get what he needs?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He'll have everything by Thursday.

situation: Bob, a coworker, tries to pin Wally down to a commitment to deliver technical specifications by Thursday. Wally keeps dodging with vague phrases like 'look into it' and 'I agree,' offering only a list of who has the specs. Bob finally gives up and does the work himself, and Wally then claims credit when the boss asks if he helped.
punchline: Wally evades all responsibility by agreeing to nothing meaningful, forcing Bob to do the work himself, and then takes credit for Bob's success.
summary: A frustrated coworker can't get a straight commitment out of a slippery colleague, ends up doing the job alone, and watches the slacker claim the credit.

title: Crime Doesn't Pay, Except Directly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And that's how I made a billion dollars in shady real estate deals.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The moral of the story is that crime doesn't pay...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Directly; it goes through escrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, don't ruin the rat.

setting: A pink-walled room with wooden floors, where Dogbert and Ratbert sit on round ottomans
situation: Dogbert tells Ratbert a story about making a billion dollars through shady real estate deals, then starts to deliver a moral about crime not paying. He undercuts it by explaining that the money arrives indirectly via escrow. Dilbert, watching from the side, scolds him for corrupting the rat.
punchline: Dogbert's moral that crime doesn't pay is subverted by the cynical technicality that the profits come indirectly through escrow, which is exactly the kind of lesson Dilbert doesn't want Ratbert to learn.
summary: A boastful dog-turned-con-artist twists a children's-story moral into a tip on laundering profits, prompting an objection from a concerned bystander.

title: Stinky Pete's Sewage Sandwich Story

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stinky Pete

transcript.speaker: Stinky Pete
transcript.text: I was jogging to work and eating my onion sandwich when I spotted a sewage spill.

transcript.speaker: Stinky Pete
transcript.text: So I did what anyone would do in that situation: I rolled around in it.

transcript.speaker: Stinky Pete
transcript.text: A penny for your thoughts.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I must insert my head into my buttocks so I can breathe.

setting: Office, a desk in a meeting or cubicle
situation: Stinky Pete, a smelly coworker, explains that he was jogging to work while eating an onion sandwich when he came across a sewage spill. He cheerfully says he rolled around in it, then asks his coworker what he's thinking. The coworker, overwhelmed by the stench, imagines folding himself up with his head in his rear end just to find breathable air.
punchline: The coworker's thought bubble shows the stench is so awful that the only imaginable way to breathe is to stick his head into his own buttocks, implying even that smells better than Stinky Pete.
summary: A reeking colleague boasts about wallowing in sewage after an onion-sandwich jog, and his horrified listener privately decides his own posterior smells better.

title: Government Mandate Means Mailman Looks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The product review board approved your business case for the government mandate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Diversity is very important to this company.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What do you think "government mandate" means?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've seen the way the mailman looks at me.

situation: The Boss tells Carol that the product review board approved her business case for a government mandate, then adds that diversity matters to the company. Carol walks away asking what he thinks 'government mandate' means, and he reveals he thinks it refers to a mailman who finds him attractive.
punchline: The Boss has completely misunderstood 'government mandate' as something to do with a mailman's romantic interest in him, showing he approved the project without understanding it and is self-absorbed and clueless.
summary: A manager approves a project he fundamentally misunderstands, confusing a regulatory requirement with a postal worker's admiring glances.

title: Combat Veteran Interrogates Coworker About Specs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it difficult to transition from leading troops in combat to the corporate life?

transcript.speaker: Ex-military Manager
transcript.text: Where are the product specs?!!

transcript.speaker: Ex-military Manager

situation: Dilbert asks a new colleague, a former combat leader, whether moving from military command to corporate work is hard. Instead of answering, the man grabs a coworker by the tie and angrily demands the product specs. He then calmly explains that the main difference is that good intelligence is harder to get in the office.
punchline: The ex-military manager treats a coworker like an enemy prisoner to extract information, showing that his only complaint about corporate life is that it is harder to get reliable intel.
summary: A former soldier answers a question about adjusting to office life while roughing up a colleague over missing documentation.

punchline: The coworker's deadpan 'Not really' implies that even sitting silently in a pointless meeting is no worse than the rest of his workday, which is equally unproductive.

punchline: Wally's business plan is absurdly vague, and Dilbert's 'good plan' is deadpan sarcasm about its total lack of substance.
summary: A coworker dreams of an eBay career with no idea what he would actually sell, and his friend sarcastically endorses the scheme.

situation: Coworkers walk in a line parodying The Wizard of Oz, saying they are off to see the 'Wizard of Landfill.' A young employee asks to join, listing what he needs (experience) and what the boss supposedly needs (brain, heart, soul, strategic vision). The Boss takes offense, denies needing any of it, and fires the employee, who adds that he needs a job.
punchline: Pointing out that the boss lacks a brain, heart, soul, and strategic vision gets the employee fired, giving him the one thing he now needs: a job.
summary: A parody march to a landfill wizard ends with a worker insulting his boss's missing qualities and promptly losing his job.

Dilbert's hesitant answer doesn't deter him, and he hands Dilbert a new assignment backed by a threat to punch him.
punchline: Rather than being alarmed that an employee was threatened, the boss treats it as a management technique worth copying and immediately threatens Dilbert with violence for more overtime.
summary: Hearing that intimidation got a coworker's project finished overnight, the boss decides to try the same tactic on the very person who told him.

As he lunges to strangle himself in despair, she calmly explains the time-report codes for attempted and successful self-strangulation.
punchline: The manager's bureaucratic obsession with tracking every minute is so absurd that she responds to his breakdown by supplying a time-report code for his suicide attempt.
summary: A man who once enjoyed freelance independence is crushed by micromanagement and driven to a meltdown that his boss treats as just another timesheet entry.

punchline: Asok finds a dry quality-standards joke hilarious and recognizes that his sense of humor has been warped by long exposure to corporate jargon.
summary: An intern cracks himself up with a quality-standards gag about lunch, then fears the job has changed him.

summary: After learning her coworker's terse message was innocent, an irritable engineer insists her grudge must still land somewhere else, and he shrugs it off.

summary: A failing manager is shrunk into a closet-sized job with a made-up title, then wanders onto a rooftop when told his only path back is someone else's fall.
