setting: A seminar room with Dogbert on a stool facing an audience
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool addressing attendees at his communication seminar. He announces the lesson will be about using a BlackBerry while pretending to listen. In the last panel he demonstrates by reciting noncommittal phrases while typing on his device without paying attention.
punchline: Dogbert's communication seminar teaches the opposite of communication, showing that he himself is ignoring the audience while tapping on his BlackBerry as he coaches them to fake listening.
summary: A seminar leader demonstrates the art of faking attention by typing on a handheld device while muttering stock replies.

title: Slightly Larger Cubicle Corrupts Alice

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, we're doing some construction and I have to move you to a slightly larger cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Muwhahaha! I will use the power of my slightly larger cubicle to rule my coworkers with an iron fist!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Get out of my way, you worthless microcuber!!

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and then the cubicle area
situation: The Boss tells Alice she must move to a slightly larger cubicle because of construction. Alice gleefully declares she will use the power of that extra space to rule her coworkers with an iron fist. She then shoves aside a startled coworker (Asok), calling him a worthless microcuber.
punchline: A trivially larger cubicle instantly goes to Alice's head, showing how petty office status symbols can turn people into tyrants over those with smaller cubicles.
summary: A tiny upgrade in cubicle size turns Alice into a power-mad bully who looks down on anyone with less floor space.

title: Vampire Promotes Blood Donation Competition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Vlad is here to tell us why it's so important to donate blood.

transcript.speaker: Vlad
transcript.text: Blood is totally delicious and I'm too lazy to bite necks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not with the Red Cross, are you.

transcript.speaker: Vlad
transcript.text: Compe-tition is healthy too.

situation: The Boss introduces a guest speaker, Vlad, who is there to urge employees to donate blood. Vlad, who is clearly a vampire, cheerfully admits he wants the blood for himself because he is too lazy to bite necks. The Boss realizes Vlad isn't from the Red Cross, and Vlad shrugs it off by praising competition.
punchline: The blood drive pitch is really a lazy vampire's scheme to get free blood, and he justifies it by calling it healthy competition with the Red Cross.
summary: A lazy vampire poses as a blood drive advocate so employees will hand over their blood without him having to bite anyone.

title: Exceeded Goals, Denied Raise

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You exceeded all of your goals this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I can't give you much of a raise because you didn't have the appearance of success.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to justify to management all large raises, and they don't know that you exist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who do they think accomplished all of my goals?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: Dilbert and The Boss sit at a table, The Boss looking tense.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll make it up to you next year.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Push

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Who was that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some vendor.

setting: The Boss's office and a nearby conference room
situation: The Boss conducts Dilbert's performance review, admitting Dilbert exceeded every goal but can't get a big raise because upper management doesn't know he exists. When Dilbert asks who they think did his work, The Boss shoves him out of the office. A visiting manager sees the exit and asks who it was, and The Boss passes Dilbert off as a vendor.
punchline: The Boss keeps Dilbert so invisible to upper management that he literally disowns him as a vendor, ensuring the raise problem never gets fixed.
summary: A boss admits an employee hit every target yet denies him a raise because executives have never heard of him, then hides him from a passing executive.

title: Violations for Every Letter Except Z

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I've documented all of your disciplinary issues in your personnel file.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have violations for every letter of the alphabet except Z. For some reason you missed that one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzzzzz

setting: Boss's office, at a conference table
situation: The Boss sits across a table from Wally with a tall stack of paper, explaining that he has documented Wally's disciplinary problems in his personnel file. He notes that Wally has violations covering every letter of the alphabet except Z. Wally responds by falling asleep, while Catbert sits quietly beside the Boss.
punchline: Wally, famous for doing nothing at work, supplies the missing Z by literally sleeping, and he is so unbothered by the lecture that he dozes off in the middle of it.
summary: A boss boasts of a huge disciplinary file covering nearly the whole alphabet, and the slacker employee being reprimanded provides the missing letter by nodding off.

title: Wally Confesses Before Being Fired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I have to let you go...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well, this was bound to happen.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I guess someone told you that I e-mailed our CEO and said you think his daughter looks like a chimp.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or is it because I built a guest house from stolen office supplies?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe it's because you found out that I've been taking a dollar out of your desk every day for seven years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, I was trying to say I have to let you go to a training class.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it someplace nice?

situation: The Boss begins telling Wally he has to let him go. Wally assumes he is being fired and preemptively confesses to a string of misdeeds: insulting the CEO's daughter, building a guest house from stolen office supplies, and pilfering a dollar a day from the Boss's desk. The Boss then reveals he only meant letting Wally go to a training class.
punchline: Wally, having needlessly confessed to years of wrongdoing, shrugs it off and asks whether the training class is somewhere nice, showing no shame or concern.
summary: A manager's ambiguous phrasing prompts an employee to blurt out a list of his own offenses before learning he was merely being sent to training.

title: Passionate Hires Curse the Air Conditioning

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new strategy is to hire passionate people instead of smart ones.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I curse the air conditioning system that blows such a cold wind!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can already feel our stock price going up.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces a new strategy of hiring passionate people rather than smart ones. An employee immediately stands up and passionately curses the air conditioning for blowing a cold wind. The Boss, pleased by the display of fervor, declares he can feel the stock price rising.
punchline: The Boss mistakes loud, irrational passion about a trivial thing for valuable corporate energy, showing that passion without intelligence is useless.
summary: A manager's plan to favor enthusiasm over brains gets its first test when a worker rages at the office air conditioning, and the manager is delighted anyway.

title: Wally's Mind Isn't On the Task

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, if I give you an assignment, what are the odds that you will actually do it right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I put my mind to a task, I do it well.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will you put your mind to it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. Good follow-up question.

situation: The Boss asks Wally how likely he is to do an assignment correctly. Wally says he does tasks well when he puts his mind to them. The Boss asks the obvious follow-up, whether Wally will actually put his mind to it, and Wally dodges by praising the question while sipping his coffee.
punchline: Wally's carefully conditional answer hides that he has no intention of applying effort, and he evades the direct question by complimenting the Boss.
summary: Wally gives a conditional promise of competence, and when pressed on whether he'll meet the condition, he sidesteps it with a sarcastic compliment.

title: Multitasking Coworker Drowns Drinking Water

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Amber Dextrous, your new co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: Nice to meet you. Nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She's going for the hug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh heck, I'll just go with the flow and for once not be the socially awkward one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: She wasn't going for the hug. She shakes with both hands.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's the perfect employee. She can do two things at the same time!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Human Resources surgically separated the two sides of her brain so she can multitask.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two days later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sorry to report that Amber drowned while trying to talk and drink water at the same time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Human Resources would like to see you after this meeting.

setting: Office cubicle area and a conference room
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Amber, a new coworker who greets him by saying everything twice and shaking with both hands, after Dilbert awkwardly tries to hug her. The Boss explains that Human Resources surgically split her brain so she can multitask. Two days later at a meeting, he announces she drowned trying to talk and drink water simultaneously, and tells Dilbert that HR wants to see him.
punchline: The company's obsession with multitasking led it to perform brain surgery on an employee, who died from the experiment, and the Boss's reaction is to summon Dilbert to HR, implying the blame or the next surgery lands on someone else.
summary: A manager proudly presents a surgically enhanced multitasking worker who promptly dies from doing two things at once, and then the next employee gets called in by HR.

title: Google Founders Bet on Death Ray

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Google Headquarters

transcript.speaker: Google Founder 1
transcript.text: Isn't it a little bit evil to kill Dilbert with our death ray?

transcript.speaker: Google Founder 2
transcript.text: Good point... What if I just blast the space station out of orbit and make it land on his house?

transcript.speaker: Google Founder 1
transcript.text: I'll bet you ten billion dollars you can't.

transcript.speaker: Google Founder 2
transcript.text: And the loser has to introduce himself as "the dumb one."

situation: Two Google executives stand next to a large death ray. One worries it is evil to use it to kill Dilbert, so the other proposes knocking a space station out of orbit onto Dilbert's house instead. They then turn the plan into a casual ten-billion-dollar bet, with the loser having to introduce himself as "the dumb one."
punchline: The Google founders' moral qualm is about the method rather than the murder, and they treat destroying a space station and a man's house as just another game, with absurd wealth making ten billion dollars a throwaway wager.
summary: Two wealthy tech founders casually debate whether a death ray is too evil, then swap it for dropping a space station on a man's home and make a bet out of it.

title: Winners Let Losers Clean Up

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be right back after I return these dishes to the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa, whoa!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Winners don't return dishes to the cafeteria.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then how do the dishes get back?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You must use your power of low standards.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Just place the dishes on the floor and wait for a loser with high standards.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa! Dishes on the floor!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Once again I have to clean up after slobs!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is like a miracle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now ask her to bring you back a yogurt.

situation: Dilbert is about to return his dirty dishes to the cafeteria when Wally stops him and explains his philosophy of low standards. Wally tells him to leave the dishes on the floor, and Alice, who can't stand the mess, angrily picks them up herself. Wally then suggests Dilbert push his luck by asking her to fetch him a yogurt.
punchline: Wally has turned his own laziness into a 'winning' strategy by exploiting coworkers like Alice, whose high standards compel her to do the work he won't.
summary: Wally shows Dilbert that leaving a mess lets someone fussier clean it up for free.

title: Arranged Marriage Advice From Wally

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My relatives want me to have an arranged marriage.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If they find someone who's totally hot and has low standards, ask if she has a sister.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What about love?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How can you not love that?

situation: Asok tells Wally at the coffee machine that his relatives want him to have an arranged marriage. Wally, holding the coffee pot, responds with self-serving advice about finding a hot woman with low standards and getting her sister's contact. When Asok asks about love, Wally insists that a hot woman with low standards is plenty lovable.
punchline: Wally sees an arranged marriage purely as a way to land a good-looking partner with low standards, treating that as the only thing worth loving.
summary: A coworker confides about family-arranged marriage plans and gets shamelessly shallow romantic advice from a cynical colleague.

title: Dilbert Trapped Beyond the Third Wall

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. Why am I still here? What's happening to me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I violated the third wall and now I can't get out!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert? Is that really you???

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I'm Toto. We must follow the yellow sticky-note road.

setting: A blank, empty void beyond the edge of the office set, with only the backs of the cubicle walls visible
situation: Dilbert finds himself stranded behind the scenery of his own comic strip after breaking the 'third wall', which is the boundary beyond the usual fourth-wall. He waves in distress, then meets Dogbert, who claims to be Toto from The Wizard of Oz and proposes they follow a trail of yellow sticky notes. The strip ends with 'Continued'.
punchline: Dogbert parodies The Wizard of Oz by casting himself as Toto and replacing the yellow brick road with a trail of office sticky notes.
summary: After stepping outside the boundaries of his own comic panel, Dilbert is lost in an empty void until Dogbert shows up pretending to be a movie dog and leading the way along a path of office stationery.

title: Boss Criticizes Presentation Without Reading

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you have a chance to review my PowerPoint presentation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's full of technical jargon and it's way too long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you even look at it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why would I look at something like that?

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss whether he reviewed his PowerPoint presentation. The Boss confidently criticizes it as too technical and too long. When Dilbert asks if he even looked at it, the Boss admits he never opened it.
punchline: The Boss delivers detailed criticism of a presentation he never read, assuming its flaws in advance and seeing no reason to actually look at it.
summary: A manager offers harsh feedback on a slideshow and then cheerfully admits he never bothered to open it.

title: Blackmail Rumor Backfires on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I need you to drop whatever you're doing and work all night to make this change to your system.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If you refuse to do my bidding, here's the rumor I will spread about you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! I'll say I was only scratching an itch.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Good luck with that.

situation: A woman hands Dilbert a document and demands he work all night on a change to his system. When he hesitates, she threatens to spread a rumor about him. Dilbert confidently says he'll just claim he was only scratching an itch, and she skeptically replies 'Good luck with that.'
punchline: The rumor is implied to be embarrassing and visibly self-evident, so Dilbert's lame excuse of scratching an itch is hopelessly unconvincing.
summary: A demanding coworker blackmails Dilbert into an overnight task with a threatened rumor, and his planned denial is shot down as laughably implausible.

title: Elderly Hire Mistaken for Fiddler

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, this is Albert. He's old but we need to call him mature.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Explain to him what the computers are, but don't let him touch anything. The elderly like to fiddle.

transcript.speaker: Albert
transcript.text: I was a chip designer in my last job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? Chocolate or poker?

situation: The Boss introduces a new older employee, Albert, to Asok and says he must be described as 'mature' rather than old. He instructs Asok to explain what computers are but not let Albert touch anything because old people fiddle. Albert says he was a chip designer, and The Boss assumes he means chocolate chips or poker chips.
punchline: The Boss is so ignorant and ageist that he thinks a semiconductor chip designer must have worked with chocolate chips or poker chips, while assuming Albert doesn't understand computers.
summary: A clueless manager condescends to a new older colleague about computers, then misunderstands his career in chip design.

title: Boss Forgot His College Major

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You know what's funny? I never studied engineering and I'm your boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In fact, I majored in... um... gosh, I don't remember.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You forgot your major?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't bother remembering things I can write down.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that it is funny he manages engineers without ever having studied engineering. He then tries to recall what he did major in and cannot remember. When Dilbert asks if he really forgot, the Boss says he doesn't bother remembering anything he could write down.
punchline: The Boss's excuse for not remembering his own college major is that he saves memory for things he can't write down, which shows how little he knows and how pleased he is about it.
summary: A manager with no engineering background cannot even recall what he studied and defends his lapse as sensible information management.

title: Boss Lets Vampire Run Blood Drive

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Is it true that you allowed a vampire to run the blood drive?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, and it takes a big man to admit he's wrong.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You admit you were wrong?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to lose weight instead.

situation: Catbert asks the Boss whether he really let a vampire run the company blood drive. The Boss replies that it takes a big man to admit he's wrong, then reveals that rather than admitting the mistake he chose to lose weight so he would be a smaller man instead.
punchline: The Boss twists the saying about being a big man by avoiding admitting fault and shrinking himself instead, refusing to ever acknowledge his error.
summary: Questioned about a poor decision, the boss dodges responsibility by making himself physically smaller rather than owning up to his mistake.

title: Mocking Dilbert's Honest Post-Mortem Answer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's use our process to figure out why Project Wolverine failed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There was only one reason: management discourages employees from voicing opinions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wanagewent duthcourages uth. Boo hoo!

setting: Conference room during a project post-mortem meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces they will use their process to find out why Project Wolverine failed. Dilbert honestly answers that management discourages employees from voicing opinions. The Boss responds by mocking him in a baby-talk voice instead of addressing the criticism.
punchline: Management asks for honest feedback about a failure, then proves Dilbert's point by ridiculing the criticism, showing that opinions really are discouraged.
summary: A boss requests an explanation for a failed project, then belittles the employee who truthfully blames management's attitude.

title: Lost-and-Found Glove Rental Car

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. The car rental place was out of cars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All they had was this glove from their lost-and-found. So I put it on and ran here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At least I got something.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Hey, that's my glove!

situation: Dilbert arrives late to a meeting and explains that the car rental company had no cars, only a glove from its lost-and-found, which he put on before running to work. Alice and a coworker look on in confusion. A coworker then recognizes the glove as his own.
punchline: Dilbert's absurd excuse for lateness backfires when the glove he took from lost-and-found turns out to belong to someone in the meeting.
summary: A tardy employee offers a ridiculous excuse involving a borrowed glove, only to have a colleague claim it as his.

title: Reselling a Half-Eaten Fundraiser Candy Bar

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Would you like to buy a candy bar for my daughter's school fundraiser?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks. I'm not hungry.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's not really the point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I buy an overpriced candy bar if I didn't plan on eating it right away?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'd do it because your coworker asked you to.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a reason?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes, it is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In that case, I'll take one.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Five minutes later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey, coworker, would you like to buy a half-eaten candy bar?

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert to buy a candy bar for her daughter's school fundraiser. Dilbert refuses because he isn't hungry, but gives in when she says the real reason is that a coworker asked him. Five minutes later he tries to sell a half-eaten candy bar to another coworker.
punchline: Dilbert turns the social obligation he just endured into a chain by passing it on, trying to sell a half-eaten candy bar to someone else.
summary: After being guilted into buying a fundraiser candy bar, Dilbert immediately tries to pass the pressure along by offering a bitten one to another coworker.

title: Integration Plan Exposes Boss's Blunder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, come up with a plan to integrate our product with the one we acquired through the merger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay. My plan is to throw away the competitor's product because it's just a cheap knock-off of our product.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about a plan that doesn't make our CEO look like a moron?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He could stop wearing sleeveless sweaters.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to plan the integration of a product acquired in a merger with the company's own product. Dilbert bluntly proposes scrapping the acquired product as a cheap knock-off, and the Boss asks for a plan that won't embarrass the CEO, who approved the deal. Dilbert responds with a jab at the CEO's fashion sense.
punchline: Dilbert implies the CEO already looks like a moron for buying a knock-off of his own product, so the only thing he can fix is his sleeveless sweaters.
summary: An engineer tells his boss the company just bought a copy of its own product, then deflects the demand to protect the CEO's image with a wardrobe insult.

title: Hiring Unqualified People With Good Attitudes

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We don't pay enough to attract qualified employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem. I'll hire unqualified people with good attitudes and train them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, when you get a second, train this guy.

transcript.speaker: New Hire
transcript.text: Yay!

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the human resources director, tells the Boss that the company's pay is too low to attract qualified employees. The Boss decides to hire unqualified people with good attitudes and train them instead. He then brings a cheerful new hire, shown as an empty suit, to Dilbert and dumps the training on him.
punchline: The Boss's cheap hiring plan means the training burden lands on Dilbert, and the empty-suit new hire suggests the company is hiring people with nothing to offer but enthusiasm.
summary: Rather than raise salaries to attract talent, management brings in cheerful but clueless recruits and hands the job of teaching them to an already busy engineer.

title: Dogbert's Secret Billionaire Underground City

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With your billions of dollars, I don't understand why you live here?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't. I live in an underground city of interconnected palaces. The elevator is in your linen closet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We billionaires only come topside to take your coffee and your women.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hola, Dogbert.

situation: Dilbert sits at his kitchen table with coffee and asks Dogbert why a billionaire would live in his modest home. Dogbert reveals he actually lives in an underground city of palaces accessed through Dilbert's linen closet. He adds that billionaires only come up to take Dilbert's coffee and women, and a woman then greets Dogbert warmly.
punchline: Dogbert's wealth lets him not only freeload on Dilbert's coffee but also charm away the women Dilbert is interested in, with Dilbert's flat 'Oh' showing he knows he's outclassed.
summary: A wealthy dog explains that his secret subterranean mansion lies beneath his owner's closet, and that his rich peers surface only to snatch coffee and romantic prospects.

title: Superconductor Genius Strangled By Necktie

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I worked on my own time to invent a room-temperature superconductor that could eliminate our need for oil.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You were supposed to be finding a new vendor for toner cartridges. What happened to that?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Must... not use... tele-kinesis...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why does my necktie seem so... ERK!!!

situation: Asok presents an invention he created on his own time, a room-temperature superconductor that could end the need for oil. The Boss ignores the breakthrough and asks why Asok hasn't completed his assigned task of finding a new toner cartridge vendor. Asok struggles to resist using his telekinetic powers on the Boss, and his own necktie begins choking him.
punchline: Asok's world-changing invention is dismissed by a boss who only cares about toner cartridges, and Asok's suppressed telekinetic rage ends up strangling himself with his own necktie.
summary: A young employee unveils a planet-changing discovery, but his manager only wants to know about office supply purchasing, pushing the employee's powers out of control.

title: Typing Under the Table During Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The first item of business is...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's that sound?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Airplane.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Scooter.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Locusts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why does it stop when you talk?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It landed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It parked.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They're napping.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... anyway, I wanted to thank you all for your attendance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know you were concerned that my meetings were using up all of the time you had for doing work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Productivity is up, but apparently we have locusts.

setting: A conference room during a staff meeting, ending with the Boss in a hallway with Catbert
situation: The Boss tries to start a meeting but is distracted by a constant clickety sound. The employees make up excuses, calling it an airplane, a scooter and locusts. The Boss accepts the explanations and later boasts that his meetings haven't hurt productivity, since everyone has been working through them.
punchline: The employees are secretly typing on keyboards under the table during the meeting, and the clueless Boss credits his meetings with higher productivity while blaming the noise on locusts.
summary: While their boss talks, the staff quietly do their real work under the table, and he believes strange insects explain the noise.

title: Assumptions Do Lie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can do this feasibility analysis in two minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's the worst idea in the world. Numbers don't lie.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO loves the idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Luckily assumptions do lie.

situation: Dilbert tells The Boss he can quickly complete a feasibility analysis, then concludes the project is the worst idea in the world. When The Boss reveals that the CEO loves the idea, Dilbert realizes the analysis must reach a favorable result and notes that he can simply tweak the assumptions to make the numbers say what leadership wants.
punchline: Because the CEO already likes the idea, Dilbert will fabricate favorable assumptions so the supposedly objective numbers justify a bad project.
summary: An engineer's honest verdict on a terrible proposal flips to a rigged one the moment he learns the top executive supports it.

title: Generic Leadership and Fake Conference Calls

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah, blah.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's 2 o'clock and my brain has shut down for the afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Blah, blah, blah, blah...

summary: A confident woman's friendly lunch invitation sends one nerdy coworker running and earns suspicion from the next one she tries.

punchline: The baby cheerfully dismisses the objection and floats a 'crazy idea', which suggests he has the same shaky reasoning as a typical meeting participant, or perhaps a baby's random thinking.

punchline: Catbert's idea of witness protection is hiding the employee in a litter box and masking the smell with his own asparagus-scented waste, which is humiliating and gross for Dilbert.

summary: When the HR cat reprimands Alice for slamming marketing staffers' skulls into furniture, she merely critiques the furniture options.

title: Project Plan Too Stupid To Read

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Dilbert and Wally refuse to support my project plan. Will you take a look at it?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: GAAA!!! The stupidity is leaping off the page and burrowing into my brain!!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Does anyone around here know how to say a simple "this won't work"?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gurgle

situation: Carol brings Alice her project plan, saying Dilbert and Wally won't support it, and asks Alice to look it over. Alice reads it and reacts with violent horror, collapsing back in her chair and gurgling. Carol is left wondering why no one can just say plainly that the plan won't work.
punchline: Carol's plan is so obviously terrible that Alice is physically overcome by reading it, yet Carol still wants a polite, simple 'this won't work' instead of dramatic reactions.
summary: A colleague asks Alice to review her rejected plan and Alice is nearly incapacitated by how foolish it is.

title: Dogbert Offers Unwanted Liberation

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're in luck. I've lobbied the governments of several countries to attack your country and liberate you and your oil.

transcript.speaker: Foreign Leader
transcript.text: We're already a democratic country! You're confusing us with North Elbonia!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For a nitpicker, you sure dress poorly.

setting: A foreign leader's office, with the leader seated behind a desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a lobbyist, tells a dark-robed foreign leader that he has persuaded several governments to invade the leader's country to liberate it and its oil. The leader objects that his country is already a democracy and that Dogbert has mixed it up with North Elbonia. Dogbert brushes off the correction by insulting the leader's clothes.
punchline: Dogbert's real interest is the oil, so the factual error about democracy is irrelevant to him, and he responds to the objection with a petty insult rather than an answer.
summary: A scheming lobbyist announces a planned invasion of a country for its oil, and when told he has the wrong country, he simply mocks the leader's outfit.

title: Asok's Telekinetic Doughnut Heist

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback: Indian Institute of Technology.

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Your telekinesis grades are very good, young Asok.

transcript.speaker: Teacher
transcript.text: Always remember that you may not use your powers in front of the ungifted.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Present day

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the...? I just blinked and the last doughnut disappeared!

setting: Flashback to the Indian Institute of Technology, then a present-day conference room
situation: In a flashback, a teacher praises young Asok's telekinesis grades and warns him never to use his powers in front of the ungifted. In the present day, the Boss is baffled when the last doughnut vanishes from a box on the meeting table while Asok sits nearby looking innocent.
punchline: Asok is secretly using telekinesis to steal the last doughnut during a meeting, obeying the letter of his teacher's rule by doing it only when the ungifted aren't looking.
summary: A flashback to Asok's gifted schooling explains why a doughnut mysteriously vanishes from a meeting table right under the boss's nose.

title: Wally Asks for Bonus Parity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our CEO got a $400,000,000 bonus this year. Can I get that too?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, he got that much because he's a million times more important than you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fair enough. Can I have the $400 that you say I'm worth?

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk holding his coffee mug and asks whether he can get a share of the CEO's enormous bonus. The Boss explains that the CEO is a million times more important than Wally. Wally accepts that logic and asks for the $400 it implies he is worth.
punchline: By accepting the Boss's own 'million times more important' logic, Wally exposes how the executive pay gap makes an employee's implied worth absurdly small.
summary: An employee turns his boss's justification for a gigantic executive payout into a request for a tiny matching sum.

title: Wally's Marketing Copy Compares Unfavorably

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally in Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Wally, I want you to design our sales collateral.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: The trick is to compare our product with things that are even worse.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Prettier than a skunk sandwich and cooler than a hobo's mittens."

situation: A marketing manager asks Wally to design the company's sales collateral and advises him to compare the product with things that are even worse. Wally, drinking coffee, then types up ad copy that favorably compares the product to a skunk sandwich and a hobo's mittens.
punchline: Wally follows the advice literally, so the product is only praised as better than absurdly bad things, which makes it sound terrible.
summary: Told to flatter the product by contrasting it with worse things, Wally writes slogans comparing it to rotten novelties.

title: Allergies Spark Medical Horror Story

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: My allergies are kicking up again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good gravy, man! Do you have any idea what you've just done?!!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Since you brought up the topic of health. . .

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: When I was having my bones set, the doctor noticed that I have a detached colon.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: My small intestines will eventually burrow up past my spleen and try to leave my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! Here it comes!!!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Gurgle

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: And don't get me started about my bunions.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker mentions his allergies, and Dilbert is horrified because he knows it will trigger the bald coworker to start talking about his health. The bald coworker launches into a gruesome description of his detached colon and intestines, while everyone else cringes and covers their ears. He ends up tangled in his own medical equipment, still complaining.
punchline: Mentioning any health problem in front of a chronic over-sharer unleashes an endless, graphic medical monologue that nobody can stop.
summary: One casual remark about sneezing sets off a coworker's nightmarish recitation of his bodily ailments that leaves the whole meeting in agony.

title: Alice's Mangled Sports Metaphors

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We can kick a field goal in the ninth inning if we use a full-court press.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Remember that you drive for show but you pick up the spare for dough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you been helping Alice with her sports metaphors?

transcript.speaker: Man in glasses
transcript.text: Perhaps.

situation: Alice presents at a whiteboard diagram and delivers a presentation filled with sports metaphors that mix up several different sports. Dilbert turns to a coworker drinking from a mug and asks if he has been coaching her on the metaphors. The coworker evasively answers 'Perhaps.'
punchline: Alice's sports metaphors are so hopelessly jumbled across baseball, football, basketball, golf and bowling that it seems someone must have deliberately fed her bad advice as a prank.
summary: A coworker's suspiciously nonsensical sports talk in a meeting suggests someone has been sabotaging her attempts at corporate jargon.

title: Scaling Back Responsibilities, Literally Flowers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All attempts to train you have failed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I don't want to fire you because there's a hiring freeze and I can't backfill.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I've decided to scale back your responsibilities.

transcript.speaker: Woman with flowers
transcript.text: Where do you want these?

situation: The Boss tells a seated employee, shown only as a chair with a shirt and no head, that training has failed. He cannot fire him because of a hiring freeze, so he will reduce his responsibilities. A woman then arrives with a bouquet and asks where to put it, implying the employee's new duties are trivial errands like receiving flowers.
punchline: The Boss's idea of scaled-back responsibilities is to hand the useless employee a trivial task like accepting a flower delivery, while keeping him only because a hiring freeze prevents replacing him.
summary: A manager who cannot fire an incompetent worker because of a hiring freeze demotes him to handling a flower delivery.

title: Salesman Gets Commission, Dilbert Does Work

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to accompany Alan on a sales call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll explain how our product works with their current system. Alan will crack jokes and collect a huge commission.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It might sound unfair, but these are good jokes.

transcript.speaker: Alan
transcript.text: Like "What can I do you for?"

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to go on a sales call with Alan, a salesman. Dilbert will do the technical explaining while Alan only tells jokes yet receives the large commission. The Boss admits it may seem unfair and defends it by saying the jokes are good, and Alan offers a cliché example.
punchline: The Boss justifies paying a salesman a huge commission for doing no real work by claiming his jokes are good, while the example joke is a tired cliché.
summary: A boss pairs an engineer with a joking salesman so the engineer does the real work while the salesman pockets the big payout.
keywords: what can I do you for
